Saying, "Blessed be thou of Jehovah," Micah’s mother makes an idol; and Micah expects the blessing of Jehovah because he has linked his idolatry to the ancient levitical order.

tribe There is here no mourning for sin, no humbling because of national transgression, no return to Jehovah. Accordingly, no word from Jehovah comes to them. They act wholly in self-will ({7.21.10}). CF.; 21:10; {27.9.3-13}.

records.o: Book Introduction - Ruth This lovely story should be read in connection with the first half of Judges, as it presents a picture of life in Israel at that time. Typically, the book may be taken as a foreview of the church (Ruth), as the Gentile bride of Christ, the Bethlehemite who is able to redeem. Ruth also gives a normal Christian experience: 1. Ruth deciding, Ruth 1 2. Ruth serving, Ruth 2. 3. Ruth resting, Ruth 3. 4. Ruth rewarded, Ruth 4. The events recorded in Ruth cover a period of 10 years (Ussher)

v: famine (See Scofield on {1.12.10}). Bethlehemjudah House of Bread and Praise.

records.o: Book Introduction - 1 Samuel This book represents the personal history of Samuel, last of the Judges. It records the moral failure of the priesthood under Eli, and of the Judges in Samuel’s attempt to make the office hereditary ({9.8.1}). In his prophetic office Samuel was faithful, and in him begins the line of writing prophets. Henceforth the prophet, not the priest, is conspicuous in Israel. In this book the theocracy, as exercised through judges, ends ({9.8.7}), and the line of kings begins with Saul. The book is in four parts: 1. The story of Samuel to the death of Eli, 1 Samuel {9.1.1} to {9.4.22}. 2. From the taking of the ark to the demand for a king, 1 Samuel {9.5.1} to {9.8.22}. 3. The reign of Saul to the call of David, 1 Samuel {9.9.1} to {9.15.35}. 4. From the call of David to the death of Saul, {9.16.1} to {9.31.13}. The events recorded in First Samuel cover a period of 115 years (Ussher).

v: Lord of hosts Jehovah (Lord) of Hosts, Heb. Jehovah Sabaoth. For the distinctive meanings of Jehovah, (See Scofield on {1.2.4}). Sabaoth means simply host or hosts, but with especial reference to warfare or service. In use the two ideas are united; Jehovah is LORD of (warrior) hosts. It is the name, therefore, of Jehovah in manifestation of power. "The Lord of Hosts, He is the King of glory" {19.24.10} and accordingly in the Old Testament Scripture this name is revealed in the time of Israel’s need. It is never found in the Pentateuch, nor directly in Joshua or Judges, and occurs but rarely in the Psalms; but Jeremiah, the prophet of approaching national judgment, uses the name about eighty times. Haggai in two chapters uses the name fourteen times, Zechariah in fourteen chapters calls upon the Lord of hosts about fifty times. In Malachi the name occurs about twenty five times. In the utmost extremity, the Psalmist twice comforts his heart with the assurance "the Lord of hosts is with us." {19.46.7}; {19.46.11}. The meanings and uses of this name may thus be summarized: (1) The "hosts" are heavenly. Primarily the angels are meant, but the name gathers into itself the idea of all divine or heavenly power as available for the need of God’s people {1.32.1}; {1.32.2}; {23.6.1-5}; {11.22.19}; {42.2.13-15}. (2) In use this is the distinctive name of Deity for Israel’s help and comfort in the time of her division and failure {11.18.15}; {11.19.14}; {23.1.9}; {23.8.11-14}; {23.9.13-19}; {23.10.24-27}; {23.31.4}; {23.31.5}; {37.2.4}; {39.3.16}; {39.3.17}; {59.5.4}. See other names of Deity, (See Scofield on {1.1.1}; {1.2.4}) {1.2.7} (See Scofield on {1.14.18}; {1.15.2}; {1.17.1}; {1.21.33}).
anointed A prophecy of Christ as King. Cf. {19.2.1-9}.
the word Or, a word from the LORD was unusual in those days; there was no public vision.

And David Cf. {9.17.55}; {9.17.56}. The order of events is: (1) David, whose skill on the harp, and valour in the combat with the lion and bear {9.17.34}; {9.17.36} were known to "one of the servants" of Saul, was brought to play before the king {9.16.17}; {9.16.18}. (2) David returns to Bethlehem {9.17.15}. (3) David is sent to Saul’s camp {9.17.17}; {9.17.18} and performs his great exploit. (4) Saul’s question {9.17.55}; {9.17.56} implies only that he had forgotten the name of David’s father --not remarkable certainly in an oriental king.
Selahammahlekoth i.e. The Crag (or Cliff) of Divisions.
reconcile Or, make himself pleasing. (See Scofield on {27.9.24}).

hit him Cf. {10.1.10}; {10.21.12}. The order is: (1) Saul is "hit"--wounded mortally, potentially "slain," by the Philistines; (2) either to escape agony, or insult by the enemy, he falls upon his sword, and his armour-bearer, supposing him to be dead, slew himself; (3) but Saul was not dead; raising himself upon his spear, he besought the Amalekite to put him to death. {10.1.10}; {10.21.12}.

records.o: Book Introduction - 2 Samuel As First Samuel marks the failure of man in Eli, Saul, and even Samuel, so Second Samuel marks the restoration of order through the enthroning of God’s king, David. This book also records the establishment of Israel’s political centre in Jerusalem ({10.5.6-12}), and her religious centre in Zion ({10.5.7}; {10.6.1-17}). When all was thus ordered, Jehovah established the great Davidic Covenant ({10.7.8-17}) out of which all kingdom truth is henceforth developed. David, in his "last words" ({10.23.1-7}), describes the millennial kingdom yet to be. The book is in four parts: 1. From the death of Saul to the anointing of David over Judah, in Hebron, {10.1.1-27}. 2. From the anointing in Hebron to the establishment of David over united Israel, {10.2.1} to {10.5.25}. 3. From the conquest of Jerusalem to the rebellion of Absalom, {10.6.1} to {10.14.33}. 4. From the rebellion of Absalom to the purchase of the temple-site, {10.15.1} to {10.24.25}. The events recorded in 2 Samuel cover a period of 38 years (Ussher).

v: new cart The story of David’s new cart and its results is a striking illustration of the spiritual truth that blessing does not follow even the best intentions in the service of God except as that service is rendered in God’s way. It is a constant point of failure. God had given explicit directions how the ark should be borne. {4.4.1-15} but David adopted a Philistine expedient. {9.6.7}; {9.6.8}. The church is full of Philistine ways of doing service to Christ. Cf.; {46.1.17-31}; {47.10.4}; {47.10.5}. See, also, {13.15.2}.

mercy {10.7.14-15} state the principle of judgment within the family of God. (See Scofield on {46.11.31}). It is always remedial, not penal {58.12.5-11}. Judgment of the wicked is penal, not remedial.

The Davidic Covenant The Davidic Covenant {10.7.8-17}. This covenant, upon which the glorious kingdom of Christ "of the seed of David according to the flesh" is to be founded, secures: (1) A Davidic "house"; i.e. posterity, family (2) A "throne"; i.e. royal authority (3) A kingdom; i.e. sphere of rule (4) In perpetuity; "for ever" (5) And this fourfold covenant has but one condition: disobedience in the Davidic family is to be visited with chastisement; but not to the abrogation of the covenant {10.7.15}; {19.89.20-37}; {23.24.5}; {23.54.3}. The chastisement fell; first in the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam, and, finally, in the captivities. {12.25.1-7}. Since that time but one King of the Davidic family has been crowned at Jerusalem and He was crowned with thorns. But the Davidic Covenant confirmed to David by the oath of Jehovah, and renewed to Mary by the angel Gabriel, is immutable {19.89.30-37} and the Lord God will yet give to that thorn-crowned One "the throne of his father David."; {42.1.31-33}; {44.2.29-32}; {44.15.14-17}. See, for the other seven covenants: EDENIC, (See Scofield on {1.1.28}) ADAMIC, (See Scofield on {1.3.15}) NOAHIC, (See Scofield on {1.9.1}) ABRAHAMIC, (See Scofield on {1.15.18}) MOSAIC, (See Scofield on {2.19.25}) PALESTINIAN, (See Scofield on {5.30.3}) NEW, (See Scofield on {58.8.8}).

kindness A lovely picture of salvation by grace. (1) What grace is -- kindness to a helpless one for another’s sake, {10.1.1-3}; {62.2.12}. (2) Grace gives the highest place, {10.1.11}. {49.1.1-6}. (3) Grace keeps the saved one, {10.1.13}; {43.10.28}; {43.10.29}.

But Absalom fled, and went to Talmai {9.27.8}. David, in the years of his wanderings, made a savage raid upon Geshur, and evidently bore away Maacah, daughter of the king of Geshur. Of her was born Absalom, and in him was her wild Bedouin blood, and the blood of a father who had been the reckless chief of a handful of desperate men.; {10.3.3}; {10.23.8-39} and whom only the divine love could tame. {10.22.36}. In Absalom David reaped from his own sowing.
revengers Heb. goel, Redemp. (Kinsman type). (See Scofield on {23.59.20}).

saw not the king’s face Not so had God taught David to forgive. Legalists have thought Absalom’s wilfulness to have been due to over-indulgence on the part of David. There is no such intimation in Scripture. Rather it would seem that had David at this time taken Absalom into intimacy, the rebellion might have been averted.
I have no son The pillar mentioned must have been reared before the birth of sons to Absalom. Cf. {10.14.27}. Another view is that his sons died in youth. They are not mentioned in the genealogies.
sons CF. {10.6.23}. The "five sons" were children of Michal’s sister Merab, wife of Adriel, "whom she brought up for Adriel". {9.18.19}.

in Israel Cf. {13.21.5}. The total military strength of Israel (the northern kingdom) was 1,100,000, and of Judah 500,000. The numbers actually set in array were, of Israel, 800,000; of Judah, 470,000.

records.o: Book Introduction - 1 Kings First Kings records the death of David, the reign of Solomon, the building of the temple, death of Solomon, division of the kingdom under Rehoboam and Jeroboam, and the history of the two kingdoms to the reign of Jehoram over Judah, and Ahaziah over Samaria. Includes the mighty ministry of Elijah. The book is in six parts: 1. From the rebellion of Adonijah to the death of David, 1 Kings {11.1.1} to {11.2.11}. 2. From the accession of Solomon to the dedication of the temple, 1 Kings {11.2.12} to {11.8.66}. 3. From the division of the kingdom to the death of Jeroboam and Rehoboam, {11.12.1} to {11.14.31}. 4. The kingdoms to the accession of Ahab, {11.15.1} to {11.16.28}. 5. Accession of Ahab to his death, {11.16.29} to {11.22.40}. 6. From the reign of Jehoshaphat to the accession of Jehoram over Judah, and Ahaziah over Samaria, {11.22.41-53}. The events recorded in First Kings cover a period of 118 years (Ussher).

v: high places Cf. {3.26.30}; {5.12.11-14}. The use of commanding elevations for altars seems to have been immemorial and universal. In itself the practice was not evil; {1.12.7}; {1.12.8}; {1.22.2-4}; {1.31.54}; {7.6.25}; {7.6.26}; {7.13.16-23}. After the establishment of Mount Moriah and the temple as the centre of divine worship; {5.12.5}; {14.7.12} the pentateuchal prohibition of the use of high places {5.12.11-14} which had looked forward to the setting up of such a centre, came into effect, and high places became identified with idolatrous practices. The constant recurrence to the use of high places, even for Jehovistic worship (See Scofield on {11.15.14}) and after the building of the temple, proves how deeply rooted the custom was. See {12.18.4-22}; {12.23.1-37}; {14.33.3}; {14.33.17}; {14.33.19} Note below refers to "Groves." (See Scofield on {7.3.7}).

the house of the Lord The typology of the temple, if indeed it has any typical significance, is most obscure and difficult. The N.T. invariably expounds the typology of the tabernacle, not of the temple. The symbolism of the latter may be revealed in the kingdom-age (see "Kingdom" O.T., (See Scofield on {1.1.26}; {38.12.8}) N.T.,; {42.1.32}; {46.15.28}. In the N.T. the usual Gk. word for sanctuary (naos) is used (1) of the temple in Jerusalem {40.23.16}. (2) of the believer’s body {46.3.16}; {46.3.17}; {46.6.19} (3) of the local church {47.6.16} and (4) of the true church {49.2.21} But in all these instances the thought is simply of a habitation of God. No reference to the structure of the temple, as in the case of the tabernacle {58.9.1} to {58.10.39}. Zif Second month, i.e. May.

windows of narrow lights Cf. {14.4.20}. In the holy of holies in the tabernacle no light but the shekinah glory was provided. In many ways Solomon’s temple manifests the spiritual deterioration of the people, and Jehovah’s condescension to it in grace.
they stretched forth Or, the cherubim stretched forth their wings.
doors Or, spaces and pillars were square in prospect.
Jachin i.e. He shall establish. Boaz i.e. in it is strength.

Then Solomon The consecration of the temple illustrates all consecration. The temple, like the believer {52.5.23} was threefold: the court, that which was outward, visible, answered to the body; the holy place, where everything appealed to the sacred emotions, answered to the soul; the holy of holies, the place of communion with God {2.25.22} answered to the spirit of man. The ark was the most all- inclusive type of Christ of any one of the vessels of the tabernacle. (See Scofield on {2.25.9}). When, therefore, the priests brought the ark into the court, the holy place, and the holy of holies, they were, in type, enthroning Christ over the body, with its powers and appetites; the soul, seat of the emotions and desires; and the mind, seat of the capacity to know and commune with God. (See Scofield on {1.1.26}) note 3. In Christian experience this answers to; {45.12.1-3}; {49.5.18}.
perfect The word implies whole-heartedness for God, single-mindedness, sincerity -- not sinless perfection.
eighth month i.e. November. {11.12.33}. altar See {11.12.25-33}; {5.12.4-14}. (See Scofield on {30.4.4}).
and an An impressive illustration of {48.1.8}; {48.1.9}. angel (See Scofield on {58.1.4}).

high places Cf. {14.14.3}. It appears that local sacrifices to Jehovah (though not according to the divine order) were offered in the times of the kings upon "high places" (cf) {9.9.12}. Apparently Asa’s mother had defiled one of these with an idol, {11.15.13}. Asa destroyed the idol and the idolatrous (but not the Jehovistic) "high places." But see "high places," (See Scofield on {11.3.2}).
Elijah Heb. "Elijahu," {42.1.17}; {42.4.25} called Elias. Ahab It was a small thing for a man whose life was passed in Jehovah’s presence to stand before Ahab.

Obadiah In such a time as the reign of Ahab and Jezebel a believer’s true place was by Elijah’s side. Obadiah is a warning type of the men of God who adhere to the world while still seeking to serve God. The secret of the Lord, and the power of the Lord were with Elijah, the separated servant. Cf. {55.2.20}; {55.2.21}. feared (See Scofield on {19.19.9}).

records.o: Book Introduction - 2 Kings This book continues the history of the kingdoms to the captivities. It includes the translation of Elijah and the ministry of Elisha. During this period Amos and Hosea prophesied in Israel, and Obadiah, Joel, Isaiah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, and Jeremiah in Judah. Second Kings is in seven parts: 1. The last ministry and translation of Elijah, {12.1.1} to {12.2.11}. 2. The ministry of Elisha from the translation of Elijah to the anointing of Jehu, {12.2.12} to {12.9.10}. 3. The reign of Jehu over Israel, {12.9.11} to {12.10.36}. 4. The reigns of Athaliah and Jehoash over Judah, {12.11.1} to {12.12.21}. 5. The reigns of Jehoahaz and Joash over Israel, and the last ministry of Elisha, {12.13.1-25}. 6. From the death of Elisha to the captivity of Israel, {12.14.1} to {12.17.41}. 7. From the accession of Hezekiah to the captivity of Judah, {12.18.1} to {12.25.30}. The events recorded in Second Kings cover a period of 308 years. (Ussher)

v: Jehoram Called Joram, {12.8.21}; {12.8.23}; {12.8.24}. began Heb. reigned, i.e. began to reign in consort with his father.

sinned Cf. {5.28.15-68}. From this captivity the ten tribes have never been restored to Palestine. A remnant of Judah returned under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, and individuals out of the ten tribes (called, after the division of Solomon’s kingdom, "Israel" in the historical books and Prophets, also "Ephraim" by the latter) went back, but the national restoration is yet to be fulfilled. See Palestinian Covenant, (See Scofield on {5.30.3}), Kingdom, {10.7.8-17}.

records.o: Book Introduction - 1 Chronicles The two books of Chronicles (like the two books of Kings) are but one book in the Jewish canon. Together they cover the period from the death of Saul to the captivities. They were written probably during the Babylonian captivity, and are distinguished from the two books of the Kings in a fuller account of Judah, and in the omission of many details. The blessing of God’s earthly people in connection with the Davidic monarchy is probably the typical significance of these books. First Chronicles is in three parts: 1. Official genealogies, {13.1.1} to {13.9.44}. 2. From the death of Saul to the accession of David, {13.10.1} to {13.12.24}. 3. From the accession of David to his death, {13.13.1} to {13.29.30}. Excluding the genealogies (1 Chronicles 1-9) the events recorded in First Chronicles cover a period of 41 years (Ussher).

v: Ataroth Or, Atarites, or, crowns of the house of Joab.
Jokmeam See {6.21.22-35} where many of these cities have other names:

castle of Zion Heb. castle. (1) Zion, the ancient Jebusite stronghold, is the southwest eminence in Jerusalem, called in Scripture the city of David, and associated with the Davidic royalty both historically and prophetically {13.11.7}; {19.2.6}; {23.2.3}. The word is often used of the whole city of Jerusalem considered as the city of God {19.48.2}; {19.48.3} especially in passages referring to the future kingdom-age; {23.1.27}; {23.2.3}; {23.4.1-6}; {29.3.16}; {38.1.16}; {38.1.17}; {38.8.3-8}; {45.11.26}. In {58.12.22} the word is used symbolically of heaven. (2) In {5.4.48} the name is given to a projection or peak of Mount Hermon.
It will be understood that the ancient tabernacle was now divided; the ark was brought into "Zion." (See Scofield on {13.11.5}).
Abishai Nephew of David, brother to Joab. {10.23.18}; {13.2.16}.

six hundred shekels of gold A discrepancy has been imagined in the two accounts, {10.24.24},; {13.21.25}; {10.24.24} records the price of the threshingfloor (heb. goren); {13.21.25} of the place (Heb. magom, lit. "home," {9.2.20}) same word or area on which afterward the great temple, with its spacious courts was built. {14.3.1}. David gave fifty shekels of sliver for the "goren"; six hundred shekels of gold for the "magom."
office i.e. their new office, since their former office of bearing the tabernacle was ended.
blessed Note the order: {13.29.3-8}, giving, {13.29.9}, joy, {13.29.10}, blessing, {13.29.11-19}, prayer, {13.29.20}, worship:

records.o: Book Introduction - 2 Chronicles This book continues the history begun in First Chronicles. It falls into eighteen divisions, by reigns, from Solomon to the captivities; records the division of the kingdom of David under Jeroboam and Rehoboam, and is marked by an ever growing apostasy, broken temporarily by reformations under Asa, (1 Chronicles 14-16); Jehoshaphat, ({13.17.1-19}); Joash, (1 Chronicles 24); Hezekiah, (1 Chronicles 29-32); and Josiah, (1 Chronicles 34-35). But the religious state of the people, even at the best, is described in Isaiah 1-5. The events recorded in Second Chronicles cover a period of 427 years. (Ussher).

v: court The tabernacle had no "court of priests."
river "The river," i.e. Euphrates, to the border of Egypt, but not to the "river of Egypt." Cf. {1.15.18} yet to be fulfilled:

Israel "Israel," the ten tribes other than Judah and Benjamin, often called "Israel" in distinction from Judah. The division of the kingdom marks an epoch of great importance in the history of the nation. Henceforth it is "a kingdom divided against itself." {40.12.25}. The two kingdoms are to be reunited in the future kingdom.; {23.11.10-13}; {24.23.5}; {24.23.6}; {26.37.15-28}. See "Kingdom" (O.T.), (See Scofield on {1.1.26}; {38.12.8}). (N.T.),; {42.1.31}; {46.15.28}. "Israel,"; {1.12.2}; {1.12.3}; {45.11.26}.
Michaiah Probably a grandchild of Absalom, called Abishalom, Cf. {14.11.20}; {11.15.2}.
when Asa Chapter 14 describes the outward prosperity of the kingdom, and Asa’s superficial reformation; chapter 15 the true reformation.
Israel i.e. the northen or ten-tribe kingdom.
to Asa i.e. none of his subjects. {14.16.5}; {14.16.6}; {14.15.9}.
father After the Jewish custom of calling a family, or tribal head, father; e.g. {43.8.53}.
Jehoram Jehoram reigned for a time as co-king with his father. {12.8.16}.
began Began, that is, as co-king. {14.22.2} (See Scofield on {14.21.1}).
Ephraim Used in a collective sense for the northern ten-tribe kingdom, called also "Israel."
reconciliation Or, an offering. (See Scofield on {27.9.24}). atonement (See Scofield on {2.29.33}).
third month i.e. June. seventh month i.e. October.
Also he Cf. {23.22.1-13} The divine view at this time:
came up See {12.24.1-6}; {24.25.1-9}; {27.1.1}; {35.1.6}. This was the first deportation of Judah. See {14.36.15-21}, the final deportation:

records.o: Book Introduction - Ezra Ezra, the first of the post-captivity books (Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi), records the return to Palestine under Zerubbabel, by decree of Cyrus, of a Jewish remnant who laid the temple foundations (B.C. 536). Later (B.C. 458) Ezra followed, and restored the law and ritual. But the mass of the nation, and most of the princes, remained by preference in Babylonia and Assyria, where they were prospering. The post-captivity books deal with that feeble remnant which alone had a heart for God. The book is in two parts: 1. From the decree of Cyrus to the dedication of the restored temple, {15.1.1} to {15.6.22}. 2. The ministry of {15.7.1} to {15.10.44}. The events recorded in Ezra cover a period of 80 years (Ussher).

v: are the children Probably individuals from all of the tribes returned to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel, Ezra and Nehemiah, but speaking broadly, the dispersion of the ten tribes (Ephraim- Israel) still continues; nor can they now be positively identified. They are, however, preserved distinct from other peoples and are known to God as such, though they themselves, few in number, know Him not {5.28.62}; {23.11.11-13}; {28.3.4}; {28.8.8}. The order of the restoration was as follows: (1) The return of the first detachment under Zerubbabel and Jeshua (B.C. 536), Ezra 1-6, and the books of Haggai and Zechariah; (2) the expedition of Ezra (B.C. 458), seventy-eight years later (Ezra 7-10); (3) the commission of Nehemiah (B.C. 444), fourteen years after the expedition of Ezra. {16.2.1-5}.

for we seek The people of the land sought to hinder the work in three ways: (1) by seeking to draw the Jews into an unreal union, {15.4.3}. (cf) {12.17.32}. (2) by "weakening the hands of the people of Judah," {15.4.4} i.e, by withholding supplies, etc.; and (3) by accusations lodged with Ahasuerus and Darius. The first was by far the most subtle and dangerous. The lives of Ezra and Nehemiah afford many illustrations of true separation. {47.6.14-18}; {55.2.19-21}.
Ahasuerus The Cambyses of secular history (529-521 BC); not the Ahasuerus of Esther, who is the Xerxes of secular history (485 BC). (See Scofield on {27.5.31}).

Artaxerxes The Artaxerxes of {15.4.7} is identical with Ahasuerus of {15.4.6}, i.e. the Cambyses of profane history. The Artaxerxes of {15.7.1} is the Longimanus of secular history, BC 418. But (See Scofield on {27.5.31}).

finished it The worship of Jehovah was thus re-established in Jerusalem, but the theocracy was not restored. The remnant which returned from the Babylonian captivity lived in the land by Gentile sufferance, though doubtless by the providential care of Jehovah, till Messiah came, and was crucified by soldiers of the fourth Gentile world-empire Rome, {27.2.40}; {27.7.7}. Soon after (A.D. 70) Rome destroyed the city and temple. See "Times of the Gentiles"; {42.21.24}; {66.16.19}.
first month i.e. April. fifth month i.e. August.
Machnadebai Or, Mabnadebai, according to some copies.

records.o: Book Introduction - Nehemiah Fourteen years after the return of Ezra to Jerusalem, Nehemiah led up a company (B.C. 444) and restored the walls and the civil authority. Of those events this book is the record. It is in eight divisions: 1. The journey to Jerusalem, {16.1.1} to {16.2.20} 2. The building of the wall, {16.3.1} to {16.6.19}. 3. The census, {16.7.1-73}. 4. The revival, {16.8.1} to {16.11.36}. 5. The census of the priests and Levites, {16.12.1-26}. 6. Dedication of the wall, {16.12.27-43}. 7. Restoration of the temple worship, {16.12.44-47}. 8. The legal order restored, {16.13.1-31}. The moral state of the time is disclosed by the prophet Malachi. This book affords many instances of individual faith acting on the written word (e.g. {16.1.8}; {16.1.9}; {16.13.1}). It is the principle of 2 Timothy 2. The events recorded in Nehemiah cover a period of 11 years (Ussher).

v: Chisleu i.e. December. Shushan Or, Susa, ancient capital of Persia.

Tobiah Two Tobiahs are distinguished by many: (1) "Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite," {16.2.10}; {16.2.19}; {16.4.3}; {16.4.7} {16.6.1}; {16.6.12}; {16.6.14}. (2) A Jew, unable to prove his genealogy. But the reference to the latter ({16.7.62}) indicates that he was already dead. But one Tobiah, and he the Ammonite, is active in this book.
sheep The sheep for sacrifice were brought in here. (See Scofield on {43.5.2}). tower The towers appear to have been on either side the sheep gate.
Nethinims i.e. dedicated (persons), probably descendants of the Gibeonites {10.21.1-3} devoted to the service of the Levites. But see {6.9.17-21}.
Ophel Trans. "tower," {12.5.24}; {14.27.3}; {14.33.14}. Perhaps part of the fort called Millo,; {11.9.15}; {14.32.5}.

for since the days of Jeshua It is not meant that there had not been some formal observance of the feast of tabernacles (cf) {14.8.13}; {26.3.4}, but that the people had not dwelt in booths since Joshua’s days.

madest known unto them This important passage fixes beyond all cavil the time when the sabbath, God’s rest {1.2.1-3} was given to man. Cf. {2.20.9-11}. In {2.31.13-17} the sabbath is invested with the character of a sign between Jehovah and Israel. (See Scofield on {40.12.1}).

records.o: Book Introduction - Esther The significance of the Book of Esther is that it testifies to the secret watch care of Jehovah over dispersed Israel. The name of God does not once occur, but in no other book of the Bible is His providence more conspicuous. A mere remnant returned to Jerusalem. The mass of the nation preferred the easy and lucrative life under the Persian rule. But God did not forsake them. What He here does for Judah, He is surely doing for all the covenant people. The book is in seven parts: 1. The Story of Vashti, {17.1.1-22}. 2. Esther made queen, {17.2.1-23}. 3. The conspiracy of Haman, {17.3.1-15}. 4. The courage of Esther brings deliverance, {17.4.1} to {17.7.10}. 5. The vengeance, {17.8.1} to {17.9.19}. 6. The feast of Purim, {17.9.20-32}. 7. Epilogue, {17.10.1-3}. The events recorded in Esther cover a period of 12 years (Ussher).

v: first month i.e. April; {17.3.12} twelfth month i.e. March; {17.3.13}
and many lay Heb. sackcloth and ashes were laid under many. {23.58.5}; {27.9.3}.

records.o: Book Introduction - Job Job is in form a dramatic poem. It is probably the oldest of the Bible books, and was certainly written before the giving of the law. It would have been impossible, in a discussion covering the whole field of sin, of the providential government of God, and man’s relation to Him, to avoid all reference to the law if the law had then been known. Job was a veritable personage ({26.14.20}; {59.5.11}), and the events are historical. The book sheds a remarkable light on the philosophic breadth and intellectual culture of the patriarchal age. The problem is, Why do the godly suffer? Job is in seven parts: 1. Prologue, {18.1.1} to {18.2.8}. 2. Job and his wife, {18.2.9-10}. 3. Job and his three friends, {18.2.11} to {18.31.40}. 4. Job and Elihu, {18.32.1} to {18.37.24}. 5. Jehovah and {18.38.1} to {18.41.34}. 6. Job’s final answer, {18.42.1-6}. 7. Epilogue, {18.42.7-17}. The events recorded in Job cover a period within 1 year.

v: land of Uz A region at the south of Edom, and west of the Arabian desert, extending to Chaldea. Uz See {24.25.20}. fear (See Scofield on {19.19.9}).
sons of God This scene is in heaven. Cf. {18.2.1-7}.

Eliphaz Eliphaz is a religious dogmatist whose dogmatism rests upon a mysterious and remarkable experience {18.4.12-16}. Did a spirit ever pass before Job’s face? Did Job’s hair of his flesh ever stand up? Then let him be meek while one so superior as Eliphaz declares the causes of his misfortunes. Eliphaz says many true things (as do the others), and often rises into eloquence, but he remains hard and cruel, a dogmatist who must be heard because of one remarkable experience.

Bildad Bildad is a religious dogmatist of the superficial kind, whose dogmatism rests upon tradition (e.g.) {18.8.8-10} and upon proverbial wisdom and approved pious phrases. These abound in all his discourses. His platitudes are true enough, but then every one knows them.; {18.9.1}; {18.9.2}; {18.13.2} nor do they shed any light on such a problem as Job’s.

Zophar Zophar is a religious dogmatist who assumes to know all about God; what God will do in any given case, why He will do it, and all His thoughts about it. Of all forms of dogmatism this is most irreverent, and least open to reason.
iniquity i.e. the punishment of his iniquity.

So these three Despite minor differences, Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar have one view of the problem of Job’s afflictions. He is a hypocrite. Outwardly good, he is, they hold, really a bad man. Otherwise, according to their conception of God, Job’s sufferings would be unjust. Job, though himself the sufferer, will not so accuse the justice of God, and his self-defence is complete. Before God he is guilty, helpless, and undone, and there is no daysman ({18.32.9}). Later, his faith is rewarded by a revelation of a coming Redeemer, and of the resurrection ({18.32.19}). But Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar are sinners also as before God, and yet they are not afflicted. Job refutes the theory of the three that he is a secret sinner as against the common moralities, but the real problem, Why are the righteous afflicted remains. It is solved in the last chapter.

Elihu Elihu has a far juster and more spiritual conception of the problem than Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar because he has an infinitely higher conception of God. The God of Eliphaz and the others, great though they perceive Him to be in His works, becomes in their thought petty and exacting in His relations with mankind. It is the fatal misconception of all religious externalists and moralizers. Their God is always a small God. Elihu’s account of God is noble and true, and it is noteworthy that at the last Jehovah does not class him with Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar (cf) {18.42.7} but he is still a dogmatist, and his eloquent discourse is marred by self-assertiveness (e.g); {18.32.8}; {18.32.9}; {18.33.3}. Jehovah’s judgment of Elihu is that he darkened counsel by words {18.38.2} the very charge that Elihu had brought against Job.; {18.34.35}; {18.35.16}. Furthermore, the discourse of Jehovah is wholly free from the accusations of Job with which even Elihu’s lofty discourse abounds. himself Heb. his soul.

The Lord answered Job The words of jehovah have the effect of bringing Job consciously into His presence. {18.42.5}. Hitherto the discussions have been about God, but He has been conceived as absent. Now Job and the Lord are face to face. It is noteworthy that Job does not answer Elihu. Despite his harsh judgment he has spoken so truly about God that Job remains silent. {18.38.1} might be paraphrased, "Then Jehovah answered for or on behalf of Job."

Wherefore I abhor myself The problem, of which the book of Job is the profound discussion, finds here its solution. Brought into the presence of God, Job is revealed to himself. In no sense a hypocrite, but godly and possessing a faith which all his afflictions could not shake, Job was yet self-righteous and lacking in humility. Chapter 29 fully discloses this. But in the presence of God he anticipates, as it were, the experience of Paul. {50.3.4-9} and the problem is solved. The godly are afflicted that they may be brought to self-knowledge and self-judgment. Such afflictions are not penal for their sins, but remedial and purifying. The book of Job affords a sublime illustration of the truth announced in; {46.11.31}; {46.11.32}; {58.12.7-11}. Best of all, such self-knowledge and self-judgment is the prelude to greater fruitfulness.; {18.42.7-17}; {43.15.2}. records.o: Book Introduction - Psalms The simplest description of the five books of Psalms is that they were the inspired prayer- and-praise book of Israel. They are revelations of truth, not abstractly, but in the terms of human experience. The truth revealed is wrought into the emotions, desires, and sufferings of the people of God by the circumstances through which they pass. But those circumstances are such as to constitute an anticipation of analogous conditions through which Christ in His incarnation, and the Jewish remnant in the tribulation (Is 10:21, refs), should pass; so then many Psalms are prophetic of the sufferings, the faith, and the victory of both. Psalms 22, 50 are examples. The former--the holy of holies of the Bible-- reveals all that was in the mind of Christ when He uttered the desolate cry, "My God, My God, why hast Thou forsaken Me?" The latter is an anticipation of what will be in the heart of Israel when she shall turn to Jehovah again ({5.30.1}; {5.30.2}). Other Psalms are directly prophetic of "the sufferings of Christ, and the glories which should follow" ({42.24.25-27}; {42.24.44}). Psalms 2 is a notable instance, presenting Jehovah’s Anointed as rejected and crucified ({19.2.1-3}; {44.4.24-28}) but afterward set as King in Zion. The great themes of the Psalms are, Christ, Jehovah, the Law, Creation, the future of Israel, and the exercises of the renewed heart in suffering, in joy, in perplexity. The promises of the Psalms are primarily Jewish, and suited to a people under the law, but are spiritually true in Christian experience also, in the sense that they disclose the mind of God, and the exercises of His heart toward those who are perplexed, afflicted, or cast down. The imprecatory Psalms are the cry of the oppressed in Israel for justice--a cry appropriate and right in the earthly people of God, and based upon a distinct promise in the Abrahamic Covenant (See Scofield on {1.15.18}), but a cry unsuited to the church, a heavenly people who have taken their place with a rejected and crucified Christ. ({42.9.52-55}). The Psalms are in five books, each ending in a doxology: Psalms 1-41. Psalms 42-72. Psalms 73-89. Psalms 90-106. Psalms 107-150.

v: king The second Psalm gives the order of the establishment of the kingdom. It is in six parts: (1) The rage of the Gentiles, the vain imagination of "people" (Jews), and the antagonism of rulers against Jehovah’s anointed {19.2.1-3}. The inspired interpretation of this is in {44.4.25-28} which asserts its fulfilment in the crucifixion of Christ. (2) The derision of Jehovah {19.2.4} that men should suppose it possible to set aside His covenant {10.7.8-17} and oath {19.89.34-37}. (3) The vexation {19.2.5} fulfilled, first in the destruction of Jerusalem, A.D. 70; and in the final dispersion of the Jews at that time; and to be fulfilled more completely in the tribulation {40.24.29} which immediately precedes the return of the King. {40.24.30}. (4) The establishment of the rejected King upon Zion {19.2.6}. (5) The subjection of the earth to the King’s rule {19.2.7-9} and (6) the present appeal to the world powers. {19.2.10-12}. See Psalms 8, next in order of the Messianic Psalms. (Note. Psalms 2, 8, 16, 22, 23, 24, 40, 41, 45, 68, 69, 72, 89, 102, 110, , 118. are considered as Messianic. For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels In Psalms 2. Christ was presented as Jehovah’s Son and King, rejected and crucified but yet to reign in Zion. That which the first man lost, the second man and "last Adam" more than regained. {58.2.6-11} in connection with Psalms 8, and {45.8.17-21} show that the "many sons" whom He is bringing to glory, are joint heirs with Him in both the royal right of Psalms 2. and the human right of Hebrews 2. All they that see me Psalms 22. is a graphic picture of death by crucifixion. The bones (of the hands, arms, shoulders, and pelvis) out of joint ({19.22.14}) the profuse perspiration caused by intense suffering ({19.22.14}); the action of the heart affected (v .14); strength exhausted, and extreme thirst ({19.22.15}); the hands and feet pierced ({19.22.16}) partial nudity with hurt to modesty ({19.22.17}), are all incidental to that mode of death. The accompanying circumstances are precisely those fulfilled in the crucifixion of Christ. {19.22.14-17}. The desolate cry of; {19.22.1}; {40.27.46}, the periods of light and darkness of; {19.22.2}; {40.27.45} the contumely of; {19.22.6-8}; {19.22.12}; {19.22.13}; {19.22.18}; {40.27.29-43} the casting lots of verse {19.22.18} ({40.27.35}), all were literally fulfilled. When it is remembered that crucifixion was a Roman, not Jewish form of execution, the proof of inspiration is irresistible.

Have This Psalm must ever be, in its successive steps, the mould of the experience of a sinning saint who comes back to full communion and service. Personally, it was David’s pathway to restored communion after his sin with Bathsheba. Dispensationally, it will be the pathway of returning Israel. {5.30.1-10}.

Hyssop Hyssop was the little shrub {11.4.33} with which the blood and water of purification were applied.; {3.14.1-7}; {4.19.1-19}. Cleansing in Scripture is twofold: (1) Of a sinner from the guilt of sin; the blood ("hyssop") aspect; (2) of a saint from the defilement of sin--the water ("wash me") aspect; (3) Under grace the sinner is purged by blood when he believes {40.26.28}; {58.1.3}; {58.9.12}; {58.10.14}. Both aspects of cleansing, by blood and by water, are brought out in; {43.13.10}; {49.5.25}; {49.5.26}. "He that is bathed needeth not save to wash his feet"; "Christ loved the church and gave Himself for it redemption by "blood, "hyssop," the "bath"] that He might sanctify and cleanse "it with the washing by the word": answering to the "wash me" of {19.51.7}.

All David’s prayers will find their fruition in the kingdom ({19.72.20}); {10.23.1-4}. {19.72.1} refers to the investiture of the King’s Son with the kingdom, of which investiture the formal description is given in {27.7.13}; {27.7.14}; {66.5.5-10}; {19.72.2-7}; {19.72.12-14} give the character of the kingdom. higher than the kings of the earth The eighty-ninth Psalm is at once the confirmation and exposition of the Davidic Covenant {10.7.9-14}. That the covenant itself looks far beyond David and Solomon is sure from {19.89.27}. "Higher than the kings of the earth" can only refer to Immanuel.; {23.7.13-15}; {23.9.6}; {23.9.7}; {33.5.2}. The Psalm is in four parts: (1) The covenant, though springing from the lovingkindness of Jehovah, yet rests upon His oath ({19.89.1-4}). (2) Jehovah is glorified for His power and goodness in connection with the covenant ({19.89.5-18}). (3) The response of Jehovah ({19.89.19-37}). This is in two parts: (a), it confirms the covenant ({19.89.19-29}), but (b), warns that disobedience in the royal posterity of David will be punished with chastening ({19.89.30-32}). Historically this chastening began in the division of the Davidic kingdom; {11.11.26-36}; {11.12.16-20} and culminated in the captivities and that subordination of Israel to the Gentiles which still continues. See "Gentiles, times of"; {42.21.24}; {66.16.14}. (4) The plea of the Remnant {23.1.9}; {45.11.5} who urge the severity and long continuance of the chastening ({19.89.38-52}). O give thanks unto the Lord The Messianic Psalms: Summary. That the Psalms contain a testimony to Christ our Lord Himself affirmed ({42.24.44}) and the New Testament quotations from the Psalter point unerringly to those Psalms which have the Messianic character. A close spiritual and prophetic character as surely identifies others. Christ is seen in the Psalms (1) in two general character, as suffering (for example Psalms 22), and as entering into His kingdom glory (for example Psalms 2; Psalms 24.) Compare ({42.24.25-27}). (2) Christ is seen in His person (a) as Son of God ({19.2.7}) and very God; ({19.45.6}); ({19.45.7}); ({19.102.25}); ({19.110.1}). (b) as Son of man ({19.8.4-6}) (c) as Son of David ({19.89.3}); ({19.89.4}); ({19.89.27}); ({19.89.29}). (3) Christ is seen in His offices (a) as Prophet ({19.22.22}); ({19.22.25}); ({19.40.9}); ({19.40.10}). (b) as Priest ({19.110.4}) and (c) as King (for example Psalms 2; Psalms 24.) (4) Christ is seen in His varied work. As Priest He offers Himself in sacrifice ({19.22.1-31}); ({19.40.6}); ({58.10.5-12}) and, in resurrection, as the Priest-Shepherd, ever living to make intercession; ({19.23.1-6}); ({58.7.21-25}); ({58.13.20}). As Prophet He proclaims the name of Jehovah as Father; ({19.22.22}); ({43.20.17}). As King He fulfils the Davidic Covenant ({19.89.1-52}) and restores alike the dominion of man over creation; ({19.8.4-8}); ({45.8.17-21}) and of the Father over all. ({46.15.25-28}). (5) The Messianic Psalms give, also, the inner thoughts, the exercises of soul, of Christ in His earthly experiences. (See, e.g, ({19.16.8-11}); ({19.22.1-31}); ({19.22.1-17}).
