records.o: Book Introduction - Proverbs This collection of sententious sayings is divine wisdom applied to the earthly conditions of the people of God. That the Proverbs were Solomon’s ({20.1.1}) implies no more than that he gathered into orderly arrangement sayings already current amongst the people, the wisdom of the Spirit, perhaps through many centuries ({21.12.9}). Proverbs 25-29 were current in Hezekiah’s time. Ecclesiastes 30-31 are by Agur and Lemuel. The book is in six parts: 1. To sons, Proverbs 1-7. 2. The praise of Wisdom, Proverbs 8-9. 3. The folly of sin, Proverbs 10-19. 4. Warnings and instructions, Proverbs 20-29. 5. The words of Agur, Proverbs 30. 6. The words of King Lemuel, Proverbs 31.

v: The Lord possessed me That wisdom is more than the personification of an attribute of God, or of the will of God as best for man, but is a distinct adumbration of Christ, is sure to the devout mind. {20.8.22-36}; {43.1.1-3}; {51.1.17} can refer to nothing less than the Eternal Son of God.

foolish son A "fool" in Scripture is never a mentally deficient person, but rather one arrogant and self-sufficient; one who orders his life as if there were no God. See, for illustration, {42.12.16-20}. The rich man was not mentally deficient, but he was a "fool" because he supposed that his soul could live on the things in the barn, giving no thought to his eternal wellbeing.

records.o: Book Introduction - Ecclesiastes This is the book of man "under the sun," reasoning about life; it is the best man can do, with the knowledge that there is a holy God, and that He will bring every-thing into judgment. The key phrases are "under the sun;" "I perceived"; "I said in my heart." Inspiration sets down accurately what passes, but the conclusions and reasonings are, after all, man’s. That those conclusions are just in declaring it "vanity" in view of judgment, to devote life to earthly things, is surely true; but the "conclusion" ({21.12.13}) is legal, the best that man apart from redemption can do, and does not anticipate the Gospel. Ecclesiastes is in five parts: 1. Theme, {21.1.1-3}. 2. Theme proved, {21.1.4} to {21.3.22}. 3. Theme unfolded in the light of human sufferings, hypocrisies, uncertainties, poverty and riches, {21.4.1} to {21.10.20}. 4. The best thing possible to the natural man apart from God, {21.11.1} to {21.12.12}. 5. The best thing possible to man under the law, {21.12.13-14}.

v: Vanity "Vanity," in Ecclesiastes, and usually in Scripture, means, not foolish pride, but the emptiness in final result of all life apart from God. It is to be born, to toil, to suffer, to experience some transitory joy, which is as nothing in view of eternity, to leave it all, and to die. See {45.8.20-22}.
good Or, as good as an inheritance, yea, better too.
Be not righteous See; {21.7.16}; {21.7.17} Natural wisdom: be moderately religious and moderately wicked.

there is no work {21.9.10} is no more a divine revelation concerning the state of the dead than any other conclusion of "the Preacher" {21.1.1} is such a revelation. Reasoning from the standpoint of man "under the sun" the natural man can see no difference between a dead man and a dead lion. {21.9.4}. A living dog is better than either. No one would quote {21.9.2} as a divine revelation. These reasonings of man apart from divine revelation are set down by inspiration just as the words of Satan; {1.3.4}; {18.2.4}; {18.2.5} are so set down. But that life and consciousness continue between death and resurrection is directly affirmed in Scripture.; {23.14.9-11}; {40.22.32}; {41.9.43-48}; {42.16.19-31}; {43.11.26}; {47.5.6-8}; {50.1.21-23}; {66.6.9-11}. grave Heb. "Sheol," (See Scofield on {35.2.5}).

records.o: Book Introduction - Song of Solomon Nowhere in Scripture does the unspiritual mind tread upon ground so mysterious and incomprehensible as in this book, while the saintliest men and women of the ages have found it a source of pure and exquisite delight. That the love of the divine Bridegroom should follow all the analogies of the marriage relation seems evil only to minds so ascetic that martial desire itself seems to them unholy. The interpretation is twofold: Primarily, the book is the expression of pure marital love as ordained of God in creation, and the vindication of that love as against both asceticism and lust--the two profanations of the holiness of marriage. The secondary and larger interpretation is of Christ, the Son and His heavenly bride, the Church ({47.11.1-4}). In this sense the book has six divisions: 1. The bride seen in restful communion with the Bridegroom, {22.1.1} to {22.2.7}. 2. A lapse and restoration, {22.2.3} to {22.3.5}. 3. Joy of fellowship, {22.3.6} to {22.5.1}. 4. Separation of interest--the bride satisfied, the Bridegroom toiling for others, {22.5.2-5}. 5. The bride seeking and witnessing, {22.5.6} to {22.6.3}. 6. Unbroken communion, {22.6.4} to {22.8.14}.

v: so is How poor are the similes of the bride as compared with those of the Bridegroom. To Him she is a "lily among thorns; she can only say that He is "as the apple tree among the trees of the wood."
our wall "Our wall." The bride had returned to her own home: the Bridegroom seeks her.

dove There is beautiful order here. First we have what the bride is as seen in Christ, "My dove." In herself most faulty; in Him "blameless and harmless" {50.2.15} the very character of the dove. The bride’s place of safety, "in the clefts of the rock"--hidden, so to speak, in the wounds of Christ. Thirdly, her privilege. "Stairs" speaks of access. It is not "secret places," as in A.V., but "the secret of the stairs"--the way and privilege of access to His presence; {49.2.18}; {51.3.1}; {58.10.19-22}. Fourthly, the order of approach: she is to come near before she speaks, "Let me see thy countenance," then "Let me hear thy voice." Lastly, now that she is near and has spoken, He speaks a tender word of admonition: "Take us the foxes," etc.

sister The word "sister" here is of infinitely delicate significance, intimating the very whiteness of purity in the midst of an ardour which is, like the shekinah, aglow but unspeakably holy. Sin has almost deprived us of the capacity even to stand with unshod feet before this burning bush.

sleep The bride is satisfied with her washed feet while the Bridegroom, His "head filled with dew," and His "locks with the drops of night," is toiling for others. See {42.6.12}; {42.14.21-23}. The state of the bride is not one of sin, but of neglect of service. She is preoccupied with the graces and perfections which she has in Christ through the Spirit; {46.12.4-11}; {48.5.22}; {48.5.23}. It is mysticism, unbalanced by the activities of the Christian warfare. Her feet are washed, her hands drop with sweet smelling myrrh; but He has gone on, and now she must seek Him (cf. {42.2.44}; {42.2.45}).
I sought him Observe, it is now the Bridegroom Himself who occupies her heart, not His gifts-- myrrh and washed feet {43.13.2-9}.
fitly set Heb. "sitting in fulness;" i.e. fitly placed, and set as a precious stone in the foil of a ring.
we may seek him So soon as the bride witnesses to the Bridegroom’s own personal loveliness, a desire is awakened in the daughters of Jerusalem to seek Him.
We have The reference here is obscure.

records.o: Book Introduction - Isaiah Isaiah is justly accounted the chief of the writing prophets. He has the more comprehensive testimony and is distinctively the prophet of redemption. Nowhere else in the Scriptures written under the law have we so clear a view of grace. The New Testament Church does not appear ({49.3.3-10}), but Messiah in His Person and sufferings, and the blessing of the Gentiles through Him, are in full vision. Apart from his testimony to his own time, which includes warnings of coming judgments upon the great nations of that day, the predictive messages of Isaiah cover seven great themes: Israel in exile and divine judgment upon Israel’s oppressors. The return from Babylon. The manifestation of Messiah in humiliation (e.g. Isaiah 53). The blessing of the Gentiles. The manifestation of Messiah in judgment ("the day of vengeance of our God"). The reign of David’s righteous Branch in the kingdom-age. The new heavens and the new earth. Isaiah is in two chief divisions: 1. Looking toward the captivities, {23.1.1} to {23.39.8}. Key verses, {23.1.1-2}. 2. Looking beyond the captivities, {23.40.1} to {23.66.24}. Key verses, {23.40.1-2}. These chief divisions fall into subdivisions, as indicated in the text. The events recorded in Isaiah cover a period of 62 years (Ussher).

v: Hear, O heavens The chapter, down to {23.1.23}, states the case of Jehovah against Judah. Chastening, according to Deuteronomy 28-29, had been visited upon Israel in the land ({23.1.5-8}), and now the time of expulsion from the land is near. But just here Jehovah renews the promise of the Palestinian Covenant of future restoration and exaltation {23.1.26}; {23.1.27}; {23.2.1-4}.
thy judges Under the kingdom the ancient method of administering the theocratic government over Israel is to be restored. Cf. {7.2.18}; {40.19.28}.
that the mountain A mountain, in Scripture symbolism, means a kingdom {27.2.35}; {66.13.1}; {66.17.9-11}.

branch A name of Christ, used in fourfold way: (1) "The Branch of Jehovah" ({23.4.2}), that is, the "Immanuel" character of Christ {23.7.14} to be fully manifested to restored and converted Israel after His return in divine glory {40.25.31}. (2) the "Branch of David" {23.11.1}; {24.23.5}; {24.33.15} that is, the Messiah, "of the seed of David according to the flesh" {45.1.3} revealed in His earthly glory as King of kings, and Lord of lords; (3) Jehovah’s "Servant, the Branch" {38.3.8} Messiah’s humiliation and obedience unto death according to; {23.52.13-15}; {23.53.1-12}; {50.2.5-8}. (4) the "man whose name is the Branch" {38.6.12}; {38.6.13} that is His character as Son of man, the "last Adam," the "second Man" {46.15.45-47} reigning, as Priest-King, over the earth in the dominion given to and lost by the first Adam. Matthew is the Gospel of the "Branch of David"; Mark of "Jehovah’s Servant, the Branch"; Luke of "the man whose name is the Branch"; John of "the Branch of Jehovah."

seraphims Heb. Burners. The word occurs only here. (See Scofield on {26.1.5}). The Seraphim are, in many respects, in contrast with the Cherubim, though both are expressive of the divine holiness, which demands that the sinner shall have access to divine presence only through a sacrifice which really vindicates the righteousness of God. (See Scofield on {45.3.24}; {45.3.25}; {45.3.26}) and that the saint shall be cleansed before serving. {1.3.22-24} illustrates the first; {23.6.1-8} the second. The Cherubim may be said to have to do with the altar, the Seraphim with the laver. (See Scofield on {19.51.7}; {43.13.10}). The Seraphim appear to be actual angelic beings.

Ephraim In the prophetic books "Ephraim" and "Israel" are the collective names of the ten tribes who, under Jeroboam, established the northern kingdom, subsequently called Samaria {11.16.24} and were (B.C. 722) sent into an exile which still continues. {12.17.1-6}. They are distinguished as "the outcasts of Israel" from "the dispersed of Judah." {23.11.12}. "Hidden" in the world {40.13.44} they, with Judah, are yet to be restored to Palestine and made one nation again.; {24.23.5-8}; {26.37.11-24}.

Hear ye now The prophecy is not addressed to the faithless Ahaz, but to the whole "house of David." The objection that such a far-off event as the birth of Christ could be no "sign" to Ahaz, is, therefore, puerile. It was a continuing prophecy addressed to the Davidic family, and accounts at once for the instant assent of Mary. {42.1.38}.
Butter and honey Indicating the plainness and simplicity of the life in which the young Immanuel should be brought up.
confederacy The reference is to the attempt to terrify Judah by the confederacy between Syria and Samaria. {23.7.1}; {23.7.2}.

signs The primary application here is to the two sons of Isaiah, Maher-shalal-hash-baz= "haste ye, haste ye to the spoil," a "sign" of the coming judgment of the captivity of Judah; Shear-jashub= "a remnant shall return," a "sign" of the return of a remnant of Judah at the end of the seventy years, {24.25.11}; {24.25.12}; {27.9.2}. The larger and final reference is to our Lord {58.2.13}; {58.2.14}.
not Omit, not. Isaiah complains that despite the wickedness of the northern kingdom her afflictions are light, her prosperity great.

throne of David The "throne of David" is a phrase as definite, historic, historically, as "throne of the Caesars," and as little admits of "spiritualizing." {42.1.32}; {42.1.33}. See "Kingdom (O.T.). (See Scofield on {38.12.8}). "Davidic Covenant," (See Scofield on {10.7.16}), {44.15.14-16}.

For all this his anger See {23.9.17}; {23.9.21}; {23.5.25}; {23.10.4} The context explains. Jehovah’s hand is outstretched still because His chastisement is followed by no amendment on the part of Israel.

that when A permanent method in the divine government of the earth. Israel is always the centre of the divine counsels earthward {5.32.8}. The Gentile nations are permitted to afflict Israel in chastisement for her national sins, but invariably and inevitably retribution falls upon them. See; {1.15.13}; {1.15.14}; {5.30.5-7}; {23.14.1}; {23.14.2}; {29.3.1-8}; {33.5.7-9}; {40.25.31-40}.

that day "That day": often the equivalent of "the day of the Lord" {23.2.10-22}; {66.19.11-21}. The prophecy here passes from the general to the particular, from historic and fulfilled judgments upon Assyria to the final destruction of all Gentile world-power at the return of the Lord in glory. (See "Armageddon,"; {66.16.14}; {66.19.21} "Times of the Gentiles,"; {42.21.24}; {66.16.19}, "The great tribulation,"; {19.2.5}; {66.7.14}, and (See Scofield on {23.13.19}).

The Davidic kingdom The order of events in Isaiah 10, 11, is noteworthy. Isaiah 10. gives the distress of the Remnant in Palestine in the great tribulation. {19.2.5}; {66.7.14} and the approach and destruction of the Gentile host under the Beast.; {27.7.8}; {66.19.20}. Is. 11. immediately follows with its glorious picture of the kingdom-age. Precisely the same order is found in Revelation 19, 20. (See "Kingdom," O.T.,; {1.1.26-28}; {38.12.8} N.T.; {42.1.31-33}; {46.15.28}. Also (See Scofield on {40.3.2}; {40.6.33}). That nothing of this occurred at the first coming of Christ is evident from a comparison of the history of the times of Christ with this and all the other parallel prophecies. So far from regathering dispersed Israel and establishing peace in the earth, His crucifixion was soon followed (A.D. 70) by the destruction of Jerusalem, and the utter scattering of the Palestinian Jews amongst the nations. shall come forth a rod This chapter is a prophetic picture of the glory of the future kingdom. This is the kingdom announced by John Baptist as "at hand." It was then rejected, but will be set up when David’s Son returns in glory {42.1.31}; {42.1.32}; {44.15.15}; {44.15.16}. Branch (See Scofield on {23.4.2}).

burden A "burden," Heb. massa= a heavy, weighty thing, is a message, or oracle concerning Babylon, Assyria, Jerusalem, etc. It is "heavy" because the wrath of God is in it, and grievous for the prophet to declare. Babylon The city, Babylon is not in view here, as the immediate context shows. It is important to note the significance of the name when used symbolically. "Babylon" is the Greek form: invariably in the O.T. Hebrew the word is simply Babel, the meaning of which is confusion, and in this sense the word is used symbolically. (1) In the prophets, when the actual city is not meant, the reference is to the "confusion" into which the whole social order of the world has fallen under Gentile world-domination. (See "Times of the Gentiles," {42.21.24}; {66.16.14}; {23.13.4} gives the divine view of the welter of warring Gentile powers. The divine order is given in Isaiah 11. Israel in her own land, the centre of the divine government of the world and channel of the divine blessing; and the Gentiles blessed in association with Israel. Anything else is, politically, mere "babel." (2) In {66.14.8-11}; {66.16.19} the Gentile world-system is in view in connection with Armageddon; {66.16.14}; {66.19.21} while in Revelation 17. the reference is to apostate Christianity, destroyed by the nations {66.17.16} headed up under the Beast; {27.7.8}; {66.19.20} and false prophet. In Isaiah the political Babylon is in view, literally as to the then existing city, and symbolically as to the times of the Gentiles. In the Revelation both the symbolical- political and symbolical-religious Babylon are in view, for there both are alike under the tyranny of the Beast. Religious Babylon is destroyed by political Babylon {66.17.16} political Babylon by the appearing of the Lord {66.19.19-21}. That Babylon the city is not to be rebuilt is clear from; {23.13.19-22}; {24.51.24-26}; {24.51.62-64}. By political Babylon is meant the Gentile world-system. (See "World,"; {43.7.7}; {66.13.8}) It may be added that, in Scripture symbolism, Egypt stands for the world as such; Babylon for the world of corrupt power and corrupted religion; Nineveh for the pride, the haughty glory of the world.

And Babylon {23.13.12-16} look forward to the apocalyptic judgments (Revelation 6-13.). {23.13.17-22} have a near and far view. They predict the destruction of the literal Babylon then existing; with the further statement that, once destroyed, Babylon should never be rebuilt (cf) {24.51.61-64}. All of this has been literally fulfilled. But the place of this prediction in a great prophetic strain looks forward to the destruction of both politico-Babylon and ecclesio- Babylon in the time of the Beast shows that the destruction of the actual Babylon typifies the greater destruction yet to come upon the mystical Babylons. Cf. (See Scofield on {23.13.1}). Babylon See note 2; (See Scofield on {23.13.1}).

son of the morning {23.14.12-14} evidently refer to Satan, who, as prince of this world-system (see "World," {43.7.7} (See Scofield on {66.13.8}) is the real unseen ruler of the successive world- powers. Tyre, Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome, etc. (see {26.28.12-14} Lucifer, "day-star," can be none other that Satan. This tremendous passage marks the beginning of sin in the universe. When Lucifer said, "I will," sin began. (See Scofield on {66.20.10}). See other instances of addressing Satan through another, {1.3.15}; {40.16.22}; {40.16.23}.

whole earth This universality is significant and marks the whole passage as referring, not merely to a near judgment upon Assyria, but in a yet larger sense to the final crash of the present world-system at the end of the age. (See "Times of the Gentiles," {42.21.24}; {66.16.14}; {27.2.44}; {27.2.45} "Armageddon,"; {66.16.14}; {66.19.17}. No other such universal catastrophe on the nations is known to Scripture.

Moab This "burden" had a precursive fulfilment in Sennacherib’s invasion, B.C. 704, three years after the prediction {23.16.14} but the words have a breadth of meaning which includes also the final world-battle. (See Scofield on {66.19.17}), {23.16.1-5} which is a continuation of this "burden," shows the "tabernacle of David" set up, the next event in order after the destruction of the Beast and his armies. Cf. the order in; {23.10.28-34}; {23.11.1-10}; {44.15.14-17}; {66.19.17-21}; {66.20.1-4}. burden See note 1; (See Scofield on {23.13.1}).

burden of Damascus As in the burden of Moab, there was doubtless a near fulfilment in Sennacherib’s approaching invasion, but Is 17:12-14 as evidently look forward to the final invasion and battle. ("Armageddon," {66.16.14} (See Scofield on {66.19.17}) Cf. {23.10.26-34}.
That sendeth ambassadors The local reference is evidently to an embassy from Egypt, resulting in the alliance denounced in Is. 30, 31, {24.37.7-11}.
Shebna Is 22:15-19. A foreigner and court favourite displaced as treasurer by Eliakim.; {23.36.3}; {23.37.2}.
open Here the prophecy looks forward to Christ. {66.3.7}.

thy dead men Eliminate the supplied words, men, and, together with. "Body" is in the plural, "bodies." {23.26.19-21} with Isaiah 27, constitute Jehovah’s answer to the plaint of Israel, {23.26.11-18}. {23.28.19} should read: "Thy dead shall live: my dead bodies shall rise" (i.e. the dead bodies of Jehovah’s people). The restoration and re-establishment of Israel as a nation is also spoken of as a resurrection {26.37.1-11} and many hold that no more than this is meant in {23.26.19}. But since the first resurrection is unto participation in the kingdom {66.20.4-6} it seems the better view that both meanings are here.

And I will camp Here, as often in prophecy, and especially in Isaiah, the near and far horizons blend. The near view is of Sennacherib’s invasion and the destruction of the Assyrian host by the angel of the Lord (Isaiah 36, 37.); the far view is that of the final gathering of the Gentile hosts against Jerusalem at the end of the great tribulation {19.2.5}; {66.7.14} when a still greater deliverance will be wrought. (See "Times of the Gentiles,"; {42.21.24}; {66.16.14}. The same remark applies also to {23.28.14-18} where there is a near reference to the Egyptian alliance ("we have made a covenant," etc.), while the reference to the stone {23.29.16} carries the meaning forward to the end-time, and the covenant of unbelieving Israel with the Beast. {27.9.27}.

Behold The imagery of {23.30.27}; {23.30.28} is cumulative. Judah is making an alliance with Egypt when she might be in league with Him whose judgment upon the world-powers will be like a terrible thunder-tempest ({23.30.27}), turning streams into torrents neck-deep ({23.30.28}, f.c.); who will sift the nations in their own sieve of vanity (or "destruction"), and put His bridle into the jaws of the peoples.

Tophet See {24.7.31}; {24.19.6}; {12.23.10} Historically a place in the valley of Hinnom where human sacrifices were offered. The word means "place of fire." The symbolic reference is to the lake of fire and the doom of the Beast. {66.19.20}.

king (See Scofield on {23.29.3}). In chapters 32-35. the same blended meanings of near and far fulfilments are found. The near view is still of Sennacherib’s invasion, the far view of the day of the Lord. {23.2.10-22}; {66.19.11-21} and the kingdom blessing to follow.

Comfort The first two verses of Isaiah 40. give the key-note of the second part of the prophecy of Isaiah. The great theme of this section is Jesus Christ in His sufferings, and the glory that shall follow in the Davidic kingdom. (See "Christ in O.T.," sufferings,) {1.4.4}; {58.10.18} glory,; {10.7.8-15}; {38.12.8} Since Israel is to be regathered, converted, and made the centre of the new social order when the kingdom is set up, this part of Isaiah appropriately contains glowing prophecies concerning these events. The full view of the redemptive sufferings of Christ (e.g. Isaiah 53) leads to the evangelic strain so prominent in this part of Isaiah. (e.g. {23.44.22-23}; {23.55.1-3}). The change in style, about which so much has been said, is no more remarkable than the change of theme. A prophet who was also a patriot would not write of the sins and coming captivity of his people in the same exultant and joyous style which he would use to describe their redemption, blessing, and power. In {43.12.37-44} quotations from Isaiah 53 and Isaiah 6 are both ascribed to Isaiah.
circle A remarkable reference to the sphericity of the earth. See, also, {23.42.5}; {23.44.24}; {23.51.13}; {18.9.8}; {19.104.2}; {24.10.12}.

the righteous man from the east The reference here seems to be to Cyrus, whose victories and rapid growth in power are here ascribed to the providence of God. {23.41.5-7} describe the effect upon the nations of the rise of the Persian power. They heartened each other, and made (Is 41:7) new idols. At {23.41.8} the prophet addresses Israel. Since it was their God who raised up Cyrus, they should expect good, not evil, from him ({23.41.8-20}). {23.41.21-24} form a contemptuous challenge to the idols in whom the nations are trusting.

servant Three servants of Jehovah are mentioned in Isaiah: (1) David {23.37.35} (2) Israel the nation {23.41.8-16}; {23.43.1-10}; {23.44.1-8}; {23.44.21}; {23.45.4}; {23.48.20} (3) Messiah {23.42.1-12}, Isaiah 49, entire chapter, but note especially {23.49.5-7}, where the Servant Christ restores the servant nation; {23.50.4-6}; {23.52.13-15}; {23.53.1-12}. Israel the nation was a faithless servant, but restored and converted will yet thresh mountains. Against the Servant Christ no charge of unfaithfulness or failure is brought. (See Scofield on {23.42.1}).

servant There is a twofold account of the Coming Servant: (1) he is represented as weak, despised, rejected, slain: (2) and also as a mighty conqueror, taking vengeance on the nations and restoring Israel (e.g. {23.40.10}; {23.63.1-4}). The former class of passages relate to the first advent, and are fulfilled; the latter to the second advent, and are unfulfilled.

for a light of the Gentiles The prophets connect the Gentiles with Christ in a threefold way" (1) as the Light He brings salvation to the Gentiles {42.2.32}; {44.13.47}; {44.13.48} (2) as the "Root of Jesse" He is to reign over the Gentiles in His kingdom. {23.11.10}; {45.15.12}. He saves the Gentiles, which is the distinctive feature of this present age.; {45.11.17-24}; {49.2.11}; {49.2.12} He reigns over the Gentiles in the kingdom-age, to follow this. See "Kingdom (O.T.),"; {1.1.26-28}; {38.12.8}. (3) Believing Gentiles in the present age, together with believing Jews, constitute "the church which is His body." (See Scofield on {49.3.6}).

former things That is, Isaiah’s prediction of Sennacherib’s invasion and its results, Isaiah 10, 37. See also, ({23.41.21-23}); ({23.43.8-12}); ({23.44.7}); ({23.48.3}); ({23.48.5}); ({23.48.16}). This appeal of the prophet to the fulfilment of his former predictions strongly confirms the unity of the book.
Jesurun i.e. upright. Symbolical name of Israel. {5.32.15}; {5.33.5}; {5.33.26}
redeemed Heb. goel, Redemp. (Kinsman type). (See Scofield on {23.59.20}).
Cyrus Cf. {11.13.2} where Josiah was mentioned by name three hundred years before his birth.

anointed The only instance where the word is applied to a Gentile. Nebuchadnezzar is called the "servant" of Jehovah {24.25.9}; {24.27.6}; {24.43.10} This, with the designation "My shepherd" {23.44.28} also a Messianic title, marks Cyrus as that startling exception, a Gentile type of Christ. The points are: (1) both are irresistible conquerors of Israel’s enemies. {23.45.1}; {66.19.19-21} (2) both are restorers of the holy city {23.44.28}; {38.14.1-11} (3) through both is the name of the one true God glorified {23.45.6}; {46.15.28}.

create evil Heb. "ra" translated "sorrow," "wretchedness," "adversity," "afflictions," "calamities," but never translated sin. God created evil only in the sense that He made sorrow, wretchedness, etc., to be the sure fruits of sin.
the redeemer Heb. "goel," Redemp. (Kinsman type). (See Scofield on {23.59.20}).
Verse Heading: Israel to preserved and restored The Lord Jesus and the believing remnant of Israel are here joined. What is said is true of both.
Sinim The word is supposed to refer to a people of the far East, perhaps the Chinese.
redeemer Heb. goel, Redemp. (Kinsman type). (See Scofield on {23.59.20}).
redeemer Heb. goel, Redemp. (Kinsman type). (See Scofield on {23.59.20}).
Art thou not The ref. is to Egypt {23.30.7} at the Exodus:

so marred The literal rendering is terrible: "So marred from the form of man was His aspect that His appearance was not that of a son of man"--i.e. not human--the effect of the brutalities described in {40.26.67}; {40.26.68}; {40.27.27-30}.

Redeemer Redemption: Kinsman type, summary. The goel, or Kinsman-Redeemer, is a beautiful type of Christ. (1) The kinsman redemption was of persons, and an inheritance {3.25.48}; {3.25.25}; {48.4.5}; {49.1.7}; {49.1.11}; {49.1.14} (2) The Redeemer must be a kinsman {3.25.48}; {3.25.49}; {8.3.12}; {8.3.13}; {48.4.4}; {58.2.14}; {58.2.15}. (3) The Redeemer must be able to redeem {8.4.4-6}; {24.50.34}; {43.10.11}; {43.10.18} (4) Redemption is effected by the goel paying the just demand in full {3.25.27}; {60.1.18}; {60.1.19}; {48.3.13}. (See Scofield on {2.14.30}; {45.3.24}). come to Zion The time when the "Redeemer shall come to Zion" is fixed, relatively, by {45.11.23-29} as following the completion of the Gentile Church. That is also the order of the great dispensational passage, {44.15.14-17}. In both, the return of the Lord to Zion follows the outcalling of the Church.
redeemer Heb. goel, Redemp. (Kinsman type). (See Scofield on {23.59.20}).

acceptable year of the Lord Observe that Jesus suspended the reading of this passage in the synagogue at Nazareth {42.4.16-21} at the comma in the middle of {23.61.2}. The first advent, therefore, opened the day of grace, "the acceptable year of Jehovah," but does not fulfil the day of vengeance. That will be taken up when Messiah returns {53.1.7-10} Cf.; {23.34.8}; {23.35.4-10}. The last verse, taken with the 4th, gives the historic connection: the vengeance precedes the regathering of Israel, and synchronizes with the day of the Lord.; {23.2.10-22}; {66.19.11-21}; {23.63.1-6}.
Hephzibah i.e. My delight is in her.
angel (See Scofield on {58.1.4}). redeemed Heb. "goel," Redemp. (Kinsman type). (See Scofield on {23.59.20}).

our Father Cf. {23.1.2}; {23.64.8}. Israel, collectively, the national Israel, recognizes God as the national Father (cf) {2.4.22}; {2.4.23} Doubtless the believing Israelite was born anew (cf); {43.3.3}; {43.3.5}; {42.13.28} but the O.T. Scriptures show no trace of the consciousness of personal sonship. The explanation is given in {48.4.1-7}. The Israelite, though a child, "differed nothing from a servant." The Spirit, as the "Spirit of His Son," could not be given to impart the consciousness of sonship until redemption had been accomplished. {48.4.4-6} See "Adoption"; {45.8.15}; {49.1.5}. (See Scofield on {49.1.5}). redeemer Heb. "goel," Redemp. (Kinsman type). (See Scofield on {23.59.20}).
our father Here the reference is to relationship through creation, rather than through faith, as in {44.17.28}; {44.17.29}. (See Scofield on {44.17.29}).

behold {23.65.17} looks beyond the kingdom-age to the new heavens and the new earth (see refs. at "create"), but {23.65.18-25} describe the kingdom-age itself. Longevity is restored, but death, the "last enemy" {46.15.26} is not destroyed till after Satan’s rebellion at the end of the thousand years. {66.20.7-14}.

records.o: Book Introduction - Jeremiah Jeremiah began his ministry in the 13th year of Josiah, about 60 years after Isaiah’s death. Zephaniah and Habakkuk were contemporaries of his earlier ministry. Daniel of his later. After the death of Josiah, the kingdom of Judah hastened to its end in the Babylonian captivity. Jeremiah remained in the land ministering to the poor Remnant ({12.24.14}) until they went into Egypt, whither he followed them, and where he died, early in the 70 year’s captivity. Jeremiah, prophesying before and during the exile of Judah, connects the pre-exile prophets with Ezekiel and Daniel, prophets of the exile. Jeremiah’s vision includes: the Babylonian captivity; the return after 70 years; the world- wide dispersion; the final regathering; the kingdom-age; the day of judgment on the Gentile powers, and the Remnant. Jeremiah is in six chief divisions: 1. From the prophet’s call to his message to the first captives, {24.1.1} to {24.29.32}. 2. Prophecies and events not chronological, {24.30.1} to {24.36.2}. 3. From the accession to the captivity of Zedekiah, {24.37.1-21}; {24.37.18}. 4. Jeremiah’s prophecies in the land after the final captivity of Judah, {24.40.1} to {24.42.22}. 5. The prophet in Egypt, {24.43.1} to {24.44.30}. 6. Miscellaneous prophecies {24.45.1} to {24.52.34}. The events recorded in Jeremiah cover a period of 41 years (Ussher).

v: word of the Lord The general character of the first message from Jehovah to Judah by Jeremiah is threefold: (1) He reminds Israel of the days of blessing and deliverance, e.g. {24.2.1-7}. (2) He reproaches them with forsaking Him, e.g. {24.2.13}. (3) He accuses them of choosing other, and impotent, gods, e.g. {24.2.10-12}; {24.2.26-28}. All these messages are to be thought of as inspired sermons, spoken to the people and subsequently written. Cf. {24.36.1-32}.

The Lord said The general character of the second message to Judah is: (1) of reproach that the example of Jehovah’s chastening of the northern kingdom {12.17.1-18} had produced no effect upon Judah, e.g. {24.3.6-10}. (2) of warning of a like chastisement impending over Judah, e.g. {24.3.15-17}. (3) of touching appeals to return to Jehovah, e.g. {24.3.12-14}. (4) of promises of final national restoration and blessing, e.g. {24.3.16-18}. Israel "Israel" and "Ephraim": names by which the northern kingdom (the ten tribes) is usually called in the prophets. When by "Israel" the whole nation is meant, it will appear from the context.

without form and void Cf. {1.1.2}. "Without form and void" describes the condition of the earth as the result of judgment; {24.4.24-26}; {23.24.1} which overthrew the primal order of {1.1.1}. SCOFIELD’S "GAP" THEORY! For Another Point of View: See Topic 401495 (Gap Theory) For Another Point of View: See Topic 8756

The word that came The general character of the message in the temple gate is, like the first and second messages, one of rebuke, warning, and exhortation, but this message is addressed more to such in Judah as still maintaining outwardly the worship of Jehovah; it is a message to religious Judah, e.g. {24.7.2}; {24.7.9}; {24.7.10}; {24.9.10}; {24.9.11}.

nor commanded Cf. (See Scofield on {2.20.4}), note 2, the threefold giving of the law. The command concerning burnt-offerings and sacrifices was not given to the people till they had broken the decalogue, the law of obedience.
Marg carcases See {24.19.11}; {12.23.10}; {26.6.5}. Fulfilled in part in all the destructions of Jerusalem, but with a final look toward {66.19.17-21}.

The word This, like the other messages, is made up of rebuke, exhortation, and warning, but in this instance these are based upon the violation of the Palestinian Covenant {5.28.1} to {5.30.9}. (See Scofield on {5.30.3}). The Assyrian and Babylonian captivities of Israel and of Judah were the execution of the warning, {5.28.63-68}.
holy flesh See {37.2.12} i.e. to what purpose the "holy flesh" of sacrifices? Its efficacy is "passed from thee" who rejoicest in evil. Cf. {23.1.13-15}.
swelling of Jordan i.e. under such a test as in {24.49.19}; {24.50.44}; {6.3.15}; {13.12.15}

dearth The significance of a drought at this time was very great. It was one of the signs predicted in the Palestinian Covenant {5.28.23}; {5.28.24} and already fulfilled in part in the reign of Ahab. {11.17.1}, etc. As that sign had been followed, even though after a long interval, by the Assyrian captivity of the northern kingdom, it should have been received by Judah as a most solemn warning.

the Lord said The Remnant, of whom Jeremiah was the representative, are carefully distinguished from the unbelieving mass of the people. The coming captivity, which they must share, for they too have sinned {24.15.13} though Jehovah’s judgment upon the nation, will be but a purifying chastisement to them, and they receive a special promise {24.15.11}. Verses {24.15.15-18} give the answer of the Remnant to verses {24.15.11-14}. Two things characterize the believing Remnant always-loyal to the word of God, and separation from those who mock at that word {24.15.16}; {24.15.17} Cf. {66.3.8-10}.

saying The sign of the unmarried prophet is interpreted by the context. The whole social life of Judah was about to be disrupted and cease from the land. But note the promises of verses {24.16.14-16}; {24.17.7}; {24.17.8}.
The word Israel (the whole nation) a vessel marred in the Potter’s hand, is the key to this prophetic strain. But Jehovah will make "it again another vessel" {24.18.4}.

restoration This final restoration is shown to be accomplished after a period of unexampled tribulation {24.30.3-10} and in connection with the manifestation of David’s righteous Branch {24.23.5} who is also Jehovah-tsidkenu {24.23.6}. The restoration here foretold is not to be confounded with the return of a feeble remnant of Judah under Ezra, Nehemiah, and Zerubbabel at the end of the 70 years {24.29.10}. At His first advent Christ, David’s righteous Branch {42.1.31-33} did not "execute justice and judgment in the earth," but was crowned with thorns and crucified. Neither was Israel the nation restored, nor did the Jewish people say, "The Lord our righteousness." Cf. {45.10.3}. The prophecy is yet to be fulfilled. {44.15.14-17}.

seventy years Cf. {3.26.33-35}; {14.36.21}; {27.9.2} The 70 years may be reckoned to begin with the first deportation of Judah to Babylon. {12.24.10-15}. B.C. 604 according to the Assyrian Eponym Canon, or B.C. 606 according to Ussher; or from the final deportation; {12.25.1-30}; {14.36.17-20}; {24.39.8-10}. B.C. 586 (Assyr. Ep. Canon), or B.C. 588 (Ussher). In the first case the 70 years extend to the decree of Cyrus for the return {15.1.1-3} B.C. (Assyr. Ep. Canon), or B.C. 536 (Ussher). In the second case the 70 years terminate B.C. 516 (Assyr.Ep. Canon) with the completion of the temple. The latter is more probable reckoning in the light of {27.9.25}.

all the inhabitants The scope of this great prophecy cannot be limited to the invasion of Nebuchadnezzar. If Jehovah does not spare His own city, should the Gentile nations imagine that there is no judgment for them? The prophecy leaps to the very end of this age. (See "Day of the Lord," {23.2.10-22}; {66.19.11-21} "Armageddon,"; {66.16.14}; {66.19.11-21}. I will call (See Scofield on {23.2.12}).
carried away captives Cf. {12.24.10-16}. The complete captivity of Judah came eleven years later. {12.25.1-7}.

The word The writings of Jeremiah in chapters 30 to 36, cannot with certainty be arranged in consecutive order. Certain dates are mentioned (e.g. {24.32.1}; {24.33.1}; {24.34.1}; {24.34.8}; {24.35.1} but retrospectively. The narrative, so far as Jeremiah gives a narrative, is resumed at {24.37.1}. These chapters constitute a kind of summary of prophecy concerning Israel as a nation, looking on especially to the last days, the day of the Lord, and the kingdom-age to follow. If the marginal references are carefully followed the order will become clear. But these prophecies are interspersed with much historical matter concerning Jeremiah and his time.

Write Three "writings" by Jeremiah are to be distinguished: (1) This is impersonal--a general prophecy, and probably the earliest. {24.30.1} to {24.31.40}. (2) The prophecy destroyed by Jehoiakim. {24.1.1} to {24.36.23}. (3) The destroyed writing re-written doubtless the writing preserved to us. {24.36.27}.
redeemed (See Scofield on {23.59.20}; {2.14.30}). ransomed Heb. "goel," Redemp. (Kinsman type). (See Scofield on {23.59.20}).

bought (1) A sign of Jeremiah’s faith in his own predictions of the restoration of Judah {24.32.15} for the field was then occupied by the Babylonian army; and (2) a sign to Judah of that coming restoration.

In those days See "Davidic Covenant" (See Scofield on {10.7.16}). "Kingdom (O.T.)" {1.1.26}. (See Scofield on {38.12.8}). "Kingdom (N.T.)"; {42.1.31-33}; {46.15.28}. Branch (See Scofield on {23.4.2}).

And it came to pass Five phases of Jeremiah’s prison experiences are recorded: (1) He is arrested in the gate and committed to a dungeon on the false charge of treason {24.37.11-15}. (2) he is released from the dungeon, but restrained to the court of the prison; (3) he is imprisoned in the miry dungeon and kept in prison court {24.38.1-6}. (4) he is again released from the dungeon and kept in the prison court {24.38.13-28} until the capture of the city; (5) carried in chains from the city by Nebuzar-adan, captain of the guard, he is finally released at Ramah. {24.40.1-4}.
let this man See {24.26.11}. The fundamental reason why the prophetic warnings of the Old and New Testaments are unwelcome to an unreasoning optimism.

Babylon Here began the "times of the Gentiles," the mark of which is that Jerusalem is "trodden down of the Gentiles," i.e. under Gentile overlordship. This has been true from the time of Nebuchadnezzar to this day. See "Times of the Gentiles" (See Scofield on {42.21.24}; {66.16.19}).

Gentiles A near and a far fulfilment of these prophecies against Gentile powers are to be distinguished. In Chapter 46, the near vision is of a Babylonian invasion of Egypt, but verses {24.46.27}; {24.46.28} look forward to the judgment of the nations. (See Scofield on {40.25.32}), after Armageddon {66.16.14}, (See Scofield on {66.19.17}) and the deliverance of Israel ("Israel," {1.12.2}; {1.12.3} (See Scofield on {45.11.26}). {24.50.4-7} also looks forward to the last days.
day of the Lord See Day (of Jehovah) note, (See Scofield on {23.2.12}).
O destroying mountain See note 2 on Babylon, {23.13.1}; {38.4.7}, (See Scofield on {23.13.1}).

records.o: Book Introduction - Lamentations The touching significance of this book lies in the fact that it is the disclosure of the love and sorrow of Jehovah for the very people who He is chastening--a sorrow wrought by the Spirit in the heart of Jeremiah ({24.13.17}; {40.23.36}; {40.23.38}; {45.9.1-5}). The chapters indicate the analysis, viz., five lamentations.

v: The literary form of Lamentations is necessarily obscured in the translation. It is an acrostic dirge, the line arranged in couplets or triplet, each of which begins with a letter of the Hebrew alphabet. In the third Lament, which consists of sixty-six stanzas instead of twenty-two, each line of each triplet begins with the same letter, so that the entire sixty six verses are required to give the twenty-two letters of the alphabet. Thus {25.3.1-3} or our version form but three lines of the original, each line beginning with A, etc.

records.o: Book Introduction - Ezekiel Ezekiel was carried away to Babylon between the first and final deportation of Judah ({12.24.11-16}). Like Daniel and the Apostle John, he prophesied out of the land, and his prophecy, like theirs, follows the method of symbol and vision. Unlike the pre-exilic prophets, whose ministry was primarily to either Judah or the ten-tribe kingdom, Ezekiel is the voice of Jehovah to "the whole house of Israel." Speaking broadly, the purpose of his ministry is to keep before the generation born in exile the national sins which had brought Israel so low (e.g. {26.14.23}); to sustain the faith of the exiles by predictions of national restoration, of the execution of justice upon their oppressors, and of national glory under the Davidic monarchy. Ezekiel is in seven great prophetic strains indicated by the expression, "The hand of the Lord was upon me." ({26.1.3}; {26.3.14}; {26.3.22}; {26.8.1}; {26.33.22}; {26.37.1}; {26.40.1}). The minor divisions are indicated in the text. The events recorded in Ezekiel cover a period of 21 years (Ussher).

v: living creatures The "living creatures" are identical with the Cherubim. The subject is somewhat obscure, but from the position of the Cherubim at the gate of Eden, upon the cover of the ark of the covenant, and in Revelation 4, it is clearly gathered that they have to do with vindication of the holiness of God as against the presumptuous pride of sinful man who, despite his sin, would "put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life" {1.3.22-24}. Upon the ark of the covenant, of one substance with the mercy-seat, they saw the sprinkled blood which, in type, spake of the perfect maintenance of the divine righteousness by the sacrifice of Christ {2.25.17-20}. (See Scofield on {45.3.24}; {45.3.25}; {45.3.26}). The living creatures (or Cherubim) appear to be actual beings of the angelic order. Cf. (See Scofield on {23.6.2}). The Cherubim or living creatures are not identical with the Seraphim. {23.6.2-7}. They appear to have to do with the holiness of God as outraged by sin; the Seraphim with uncleanness in the people of God. The passage in Ezekiel is highly figurative, but the effect was the revelation to the prophet of the Shekinah glory of the Lord. Such revelations are connected invariably with new blessing and service. Cf.; {2.3.2-10}; {23.6.1-10}; {27.10.5-14}; {66.1.12-19}.

Son of man "Son of man," used by our Lord of Himself seventy-nine times, is used by Jehovah ninety one times when addressing Ezekiel. (1) In the case of our Lord the meaning is clear: it is His racial name as the representative Man in the sense of {46.15.45-47}. The same thought, implying transcendence of mere Judaism, is involved in the phrase when applied to Ezekiel. Israel had forgotten her mission. (See Scofield on {1.11.10}) {26.5.5-8}. Now, in her captivity, Jehovah will not forsake His people, but He will remind them that they are but a small part of the race for whom He also cares. Hence the emphasis upon the word "man." The Cherubim "had the likeness of a man" {26.1.5} and when the prophet beheld the throne of God, he saw "the likeness as the appearance of a man above upon it" {26.1.26}. (See Scofield on {40.8.20}) {66.1.12}; {66.1.13}. (2) As used of Ezekiel, the expression indicates, not what the prophet is in himself, but what he is to God; a son of man (a) chosen, (b) endued with the Spirit, and (c) sent of God. All this is true also of Christ who was, furthermore, the representative man--the head of regenerate humanity.
eat it Cf. {26.2.10}; {66.10.9}. Whatever its message, the word of God is sweet to faith because it is the word of God.

take The symbolic actions during the prophet’s dumbness were testimonies to the past wickedness and chastisement of the house of Israel (the whole nation), and prophetic of a coming siege. They therefore intermediate between the siege of {12.24.10-16} at which time Ezekiel was carried to Babylon, and the siege of {12.25.1-11} eleven years later.

visions Visions, that is, of former profanations of the temple, and of the wickedness because of which Israel was then in Babylon, show the prophet that he might justify to the new generation born in Assyria and Babylonia during the captivity, the righteousness of God in the present national chastening. The visions are retrospective; Israel had done these things, hence the captivities. This strain continues to {26.33.20}. It is the divine view of the national sinfulness and apostasy, revealed to Ezekiel in a series of visions so vivid that though the prophet was by the river Chebar,; {26.1.1}; {26.1.3}; {26.3.23}; {26.10.15}; {26.10.20}; {26.10.22}; {26.43.3} It was as if he were transported back to Jerusalem, and to the time when these things were occurring. These visions of the sinfulness of Israel are interspersed with promises of restoration and blessing which are yet to be fulfilled. See "Israel"; {1.12.2}; {1.12.3}; {45.11.26}. Also "Kingdom, (O.T.)"; {1.1.26-28}; {38.12.8}.

Son of man The combined purport of the four visions of profanation in Ezekiel 8, is idolatry set up in the entire temple, even in the holy of holies {26.8.10}; {26.8.11} women given over to phallic cults {26.8.14} and nature-worship {2.8.16}.

was gone It is noteworthy that to Ezekiel the priest was given the vision of the glory of the Lord (1) departing from the Cherubim to the threshold of the temple {26.9.3}; {26.10.4}. (2) from the threshold {26.10.18}. (3) from temple and city to the mountain on the East of Jerusalem (Olivet, {26.11.23}) and (4) returning to the millennial temple to abide. {26.43.2-5}.

for in It must constantly be remembered that though the prophet was in Babylonia he prophesies as if in the land, and during the eleven years’ interval between the first and final deportation. (See Scofield on {26.8.3}).
though Important contemporaneous testimony to the character and historicity of Daniel who was yet living. Cf. {24.15.1}; {26.14.16},; {26.14.18}; {26.14.20}; {24.7.16}; {24.11.14}; {24.14.11}.

rod The passage is a prophecy of the future judgment upon Israel, regathered from all nations (see "Israel," {23.1.24-26} refs. into the old wilderness wanderings. {26.20.35}. The issue of this judgment determines who of Israel in that day shall enter the land for kingdom blessing.; {19.50.1-7}; {26.20.33-44}; {39.3.2-5}; {39.4.1}; {39.4.2} see other judgments, (See Scofield on {43.12.31}; {46.11.31}). (See Scofield on {47.5.10}; {40.25.32}). (See Scofield on {65.1.6}; {66.20.12}).

Thus The prophecies upon Gentile powers, extending to {26.32.32} have doubtless had partial fulfilments of which history and the present condition of those cities and countries bear witness, but the mention of the day of Jehovah {26.30.3} makes it evident that a fulfilment in the final sense is still future. See "Day of Jehovah" {23.2.10-22}. (See Scofield on {66.19.19}). Also "Armageddon" {66.16.14}. (See Scofield on {66.19.17}). Those countries are once more to be the battle ground of the nations.

Thou Here ({26.28.12-15}), as in {23.14.12} the language goes beyond the king of Tyre to Satan, inspirer and unseen ruler of all such pomp and pride as that of Tyre. Instances of thus indirectly addressing Satan are:; {1.3.14}; {1.3.15}; {40.16.23}. The unfallen state of Satan is here described; his fall in {23.14.12-14}. (See Scofield on {66.20.10}). But there is more. The vision is not of Satan in his own person, but of Satan fulfilling himself in and through an earthly king who arrogates to himself divine honours, so that the prince of Tyrus foreshadows the Beast.; {27.7.8}; {66.19.20}.
from the tower Or, from Migdol to Syene. {2.14.2}; {24.44.1}.
the day of the Lord Day (of Jehovah) (See Scofield on {23.2.12}).
So thou The nation having failed in corporate responsibility, the appeal is now to individual loyalty. Cf. {55.2.1-26}.

prey to the heathen The whole passage ({26.34.23-30}) speaks of a restoration yet future, for the remnant which returned after the 70 years, and their posterity, were continually under the Gentile yoke, until, in A.D. 70, they were finally driven from the land into a dispersion which still continues.

A beautiful order is discernible in this and the succeeding prophecies:
(1) Restoration of the land {26.36.1-15}.
(2) of the people {26.36.16} to {26.37.28}.
(3) judgment on Israel’s enemies. {26.38.1} to {26.39.24}. Afterward follows that which concerns the worship of Jehovah that He may dwell amongst His people.

bones Having announced {26.36.24-38} the restoration of the nation, Jehovah now gives in vision and symbol the method of its accomplishment. {26.37.11} gives the clue. The "bones" are the whole house of Israel who shall then be living. The "graves" are the nations where they dwell. The order of procedure is: (1) the bringing of the people out {26.37.12-14}; {26.37.19-27} (2) the bringing of them in ({26.37.12}); (3) their conversion ({26.37.13}) (4) the filling with the Spirit ({26.37.14}). The symbol follows. The two sticks are Judah and the ten tribes; united, they are one nation ({26.37.19-21}). Then follows ({26.37.21-27}) the plain declaration as to Jehovah’s purpose, and {26.37.28} implies that then Jehovah will become known to the Gentiles in a marked way. This is also the order of {44.15.16}; {44.15.17} and the two passages strongly indicate the time of full Gentile conversion. See also {23.11.10}.

Gog That the primary reference is to the northern (European) powers, headed up by Russia, all agree. The whole passage should be read in connection with {38.12.1-4}; {38.14.1-9}; {40.24.14-30}; {66.14.14-20}; {66.19.17-21}, "gog" is the prince, "Magog," his land. The reference to Meshech and Tubal (Moscow and Tobolsk) is a clear mark of identification. Russia and the northern powers have been the latest persecutors of dispersed Israel, and it is congruous both with divine justice and with the covenants (e.g. (See Scofield on {1.15.18}; {5.30.3}) that destruction should fall at the climax of the last mad attempt to exterminate the remnant of Israel in Jerusalem. The whole prophecy belongs to the yet future "day of Jehovah"; {23.2.10-22}; {66.19.11-21} and to the battle of Armageddon {66.16.14} (See Scofield on {66.19.19}) but includes also the final revolt of the nations at the close of the kingdom-age. {66.20.7-9}.
speak unto See Armageddon note, (See Scofield on {66.19.17}).
hooks Or, endirons, or, the two hearthstones.

and thou shalt Doubtless these offerings will be memorial, looking back to the cross, as the offerings under the old covenant were anticipatory, looking forward to the cross. In neither case have animal sacrifices power to put away sin. {58.10.4}; {45.3.25}. For Another Point of View: See Topic 301246

records.o: Book Introduction - Daniel Daniel, like Ezekiel was a Jewish captive in Babylon. He was of royal or princely descent ({27.1.3}). For his rank and comeliness he was trained for palace service. In the polluted atmosphere of an oriental court he lived a life of singular piety and usefulness. His long life extended from Nebuchadnezzar to Cyrus. He was a contemporary of Jeremiah, Ezekiel ({26.14.20}), Joshua, the high priest of the restoration, Ezra, and Zerubbabel. Daniel is the indispensable introduction to New Testament prophecy, the themes of which are, the apostasy of the Church, the manifestation of the man of sin, the great tribulation, the return of the Lord, the resurrections and the judgments. These, except the first, are Daniel’s themes also. But Daniel is distinctively the prophet of the "times of the Gentiles" ({42.21.24}), (See Scofield on {42.21.24}). His vision sweeps the whole course of Gentile world-rule to its end in catastrophe, and to the setting up of the Messianic kingdom. Daniel is in four broad divisions: 1. Introduction. 2. The personal history of Daniel from the conquest of Jerusalem to the second year of Nebuchadnezzar, {27.1.1-21}. 3. The visions of Nebuchadnezzar and their results, {27.2.1} to {27.4.37}. 4. The personal history of Daniel under Belshazzar and Darius, {27.5.1} to {27.6.28}. The visions of {27.7.1} to {27.12.13}. The events recorded in Daniel cover a period of 73 years (Ussher).

v: Belteshazzar i.e. the king’s leader, or attendant. {27.2.26}; {27.4.8}; {27.4.9}; {27.4.18}; {27.4.19}; {27.5.12}. Identical in meaning with Belshazzar.
continued i.e. to see the return of the remnant of Judah at the end of the 70 years, {24.25.11}; {24.25.12}; {24.29.10}. Daniel actually lived beyond the first year of Cyrus. {27.10.1}.
continued i.e. to see the return of the remnant of Judah at the end of the 70 years, {24.25.11}; {24.25.12}; {24.29.10}. Daniel actually lived beyond the first year of Cyrus. {27.10.1}.
Chaldeans i.e. the men having the ancient wisdom; the learned; Chaldeans par excellence ({27.2.13}). "wise"

Syriack From {27.2.4} to {27.7.28} the Book of Daniel is written in Aramaic the ancient language of Syria, and substantially identical with Chaldaic, the language of ancient Babylonia. Upon this fact, together with the occurrence of fifteen Persian, and three Greek words has been based an argument against the historicity of Daniel, and in favour of a date after the conquest of Palestine by Alexander (B.C. 332). It has, however, seemed, with some modern exceptions, to the Hebrew and Christian scholarship of the ages an unanswerable proof rather of the Danielic authorship of the book that, living from boyhood in a land the language of which was Chaldaic, a great part of his writing should be in that tongue. It has often been pointed out that the Chaldaic of Daniel is of high antiquity, as is shown by comparison with that of the Targums. The few words of Persian and Greek in like manner confirm the writer’s residence at a court constantly visited by emissaries from those peoples. It is noteworthy that the Aramaic section is precisely that part of Daniel which most concerned the peoples amongst whom he lived, and to whom a prophecy written in Hebrew would have been unintelligible. The language returns to Hebrew in the predictive portions which have to do with the future of Israel. "The Hebrew of Daniel is closely related to that of Ezekiel."--Delitzsch.

great image The monarchy-vision. Nebuchadnezzar’s dream, as interpreted by Daniel, gives the course and end of "the times of the Gentiles" {42.21.24}. (See Scofield on {66.16.19}) that is, of Gentile world-empire. The four metals composing the image are explained as symbolizing {27.2.38-40} four empires, not necessarily possessing the inhabited earth, but able to do so ({27.2.38}), and fulfilled in Babylon, Media-Persia, Greece (under Alexander), and Rome. The latter power is seen divided, first into two (the legs), fulfilled in the Eastern and Western Roman empires, and then into ten (the toes) (See Scofield on {27.7.26}). As a whole, the image gives the imposing outward greatness and splendour of the Gentile world-power. The smiting Stone {27.2.34}; {27.2.35} destroys the Gentile world-system (in its final form) by a sudden and irremediable blow, not by the gradual processes of conversion and assimilation; and then, and not before, does the Stone become a mountain which fills "the whole earth." (Cf. {27.7.26}; {27.7.27}). Such a destruction of the Gentile monarchy-system did not occur at the first advent of Christ. On the contrary, He was put to death by the sentence of an officer of the fourth empire, which was then at the zenith of its power. Since the crucifixion the Roman empire has followed the course marked out in the vision, but Gentile world dominion still continues, and the crushing blow is still suspended. The detail of the end-time is given in {27.7.1-28}, and Revelation 13-19. It is important to see (1) that Gentile world-power is to end in a sudden catastrophic judgment (see "Armageddon," {66.16.14}; {66.19.21}). (2) that it is immediately followed by the kingdom of heaven, and that the God of the heavens does not set up His kingdom till after the destruction of the Gentile world- system. It is noteworthy that Gentile world-dominion begins and ends with a great image. {27.2.31}; {66.13.14}; {66.13.15}.
mountain A mountain is one of the bibical symbols of a kingdom. (See Scofield on {23.2.2}).
wheresoever the children This is universal dominion. It was never fully realized, but power was given for it.

but there shall be From the "head of gold" ({27.2.38}) to the "iron" of the "fourth kingdom" (Rome) there is deterioration in fineness, but increase of strength ({27.2.40}). Then comes the deterioration of the "fourth kingdom" in that very quality, strength. (1) Deterioration by division: The kingdom is divided into two, the legs (Eastern and Western empires), and these are again divided into kingdoms, the number of which when the Stone smites the image will be ten toes, {27.2.42}; cf. {27.7.23}; {27.7.24}. (2) Deterioration by admixture; the iron of the Roman imperium mixed with the clay of the popular will, fickle and easily moulded. This is precisely what has come to pass in the constitutional monarchies which, the Republic of France and the despotism of Turkey, cover the sphere of ancient Roman rule.

and in the days The passage fixes authoritatively the time relative to other predicted events, when the kingdom of the heavens will be set up. It will be "in the days of those kings," i.e. the days of the ten kings (cf. {27.7.24-27} symbolized by the toes of the image. That condition did not exist at the advent of Messiah, nor was it even possible until the dissolution of the Roman empire, and the rise of the present national world system. See "Kingdom (O.T.)"; {1.1.26}; {38.12.8} "Kingdom (N.T.)"; {42.1.31-33}; {46.15.28}, (See Scofield on {40.3.2}) note (defining "kingdom of heaven"). {27.2.45} repeats the method by which the kingdom will be set up. (Cf) (See Scofield on {27.2.31}); {19.2.5}; {19.2.6}; {38.14.1-8}; {38.14.9}.
Daniel Cf. {1.19.1}. Lot the compromiser with Daniel the inflexible.

an image of gold The attempt of this great king of Babylon to unify the religions of his empire by self- deification will be repeated by the beast, the last head of the Gentile world-dominion {66.13.11-15} See note on "Beast, the" (See Scofield on {27.7.8}; {66.19.20}). It has repeatedly characterized Gentile authority in the earth, e.g.; {27.6.7}; {44.12.22} and the later Roman emperors.

and he will deliver us The three Jews, faithful to God while the nation of Israel far from their land bear no testimony, are a fit type of the Jewish remnant in the last days {23.1.9}; {45.11.5} who will be faithful in the furnace of the great tribulation; {19.2.5}; {66.7.14}.

dwell Nebuchadnezzar, first of the Gentile world-kings in whom the times of the Gentiles {42.21.24}; {66.16.14} began, perfectly comprehended the universality of the sway committed to him {27.2.37}; {27.2.38} as also did Cyrus {15.1.2}. That they did not actually subject the known earth to their sway is true, but they might have done so. The earth lay in their power.
till thou know The discipline was effective. Cf. {27.4.30}; {27.4.37}.

I blessed the most High A progress may be traced in Nebuchadnezzar’s apprehension of the true God. (1) "God is a God of gods one amongst the national or tribal gods, but greater than they], and a Lord Adonai=Master of kings, and a revealer of secrets" {27.2.47}. (2) He is still a Hebrew deity, but Master of angels, and a God who responds to faith {27.3.28}. (3) Here {27.4.34}; {27.4.35} the king rises into a true apprehension of God. Cf. Darius, {27.6.25-27}.
father Nebuchadnezzar was "father" of Belshazzar in the biblical sense that David is called "father" of Jesus, {42.1.32}. Belshazzar was probably a grandson.
thy father Or, grandfather. See note 2, (See Scofield on {27.5.2}).

Darius the Median The biblical order of the monarchs of Daniel’s time, and of the period of the captivity and restoration of Judah, is as follows: (1) Nebuchadnezzar (B.C. 604-561) with whom the captivity of Judah and the "times of the Gentiles" (See Scofield on {42.21.24}; {66.16.19}), began, and who established the first of the four world monarchies.; {27.2.37}; {27.2.38}; {27.7.4}. (2) Belshazzar (prob B.C. 556), the Bel-shar-uzzar of the inscriptions, grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, and son of the victorious general Nabonidus. Belshazzar seems to have reigned as viceroy. (3) Darius the Mede {27.5.31}; {27.6.1-27}; {27.9.1}. Concerning this Darius secular history awaits further discoveries, as formerly in the case of Belshazzar. He has been conjectured to be identical with Gobryas, a Persian general. This Darius was "the son of Ahasuerus, of the seed of the Medes, which was made king over the realm of the Chaldeans" {27.9.1} "Ahasuerus," more a title than a name, the equivalent of the modern "Majesty," is used in Scripture of at least four personages, and is Persian rather than Median. That Darius the Mede was the "son" (or grandson) of an Ahasuerus proves no more than that he was, probably, through the seed of his mother, of the seed royal not only of Media, but also of Persia. There is but one Darius in Daniel. (See {27.9.1}.) (4) Cyrus, with whose rise to power came fully into existence the Medo-Persian, second of the world-empires {27.2.39}; {27.7.5} In Daniel’s vision of this empire in "the third year of the reign of King Belshazzar" {27.8.1-4} the Median power of Darius is seen as the lesser of the two horns of the ram; the Persian power of Cyrus, under whom the Medo-Persian power was consolidated, as the "higher" horn which "came up last." Under Cyrus, who was prophetically named more than a century before his birth. {23.44.28} to {23.45.4}, the return to Palestine of the Jewish remnant began. {15.1.1-4}. See {27.11.2}, marg. ref. (See Scofield on {27.11.2}).

great sea The "sea" in Scripture imagery stands for the populace, the mere unorganized mass of mankind {40.13.47}; {66.13.1}.
three ribs A reference to the three-fold dominion of the second empire, Media, Persia, Babylonia. devour i.e. Lydia, Babylonia, Egypt, etc.
horns A horn symbolizes a king. Cf. {66.17.12}.

little horn The vision is of the end of Gentile world-dominion. The former Roman empire (the iron kingdom of {27.2.33-35}; {27.2.40-44}; {27.7.7} will have ten horns (i.e. kings, {66.17.12} corresponding to the ten toes of the image. As Daniel considers this vision of the ten kings, there rises up amongst them a "little horn" (king), who subdues three of the ten kings so completely that the separate identity of their kingdoms is destroyed. Seven kings of the ten are left, and the "little horn." He is the "king of fierce countenance" typified by that other "king of fierce countenance," Antiochus Epiphanes, {27.8.23-25} the "prince that shall come" of {27.9.26}; {27.9.27} the "king" of {27.11.36-45} the "abomination" of; {27.12.11}; {40.24.15} the "man of sin" of {53.2.4-8} and the "Beast" of {66.13.4-10}. See "Beast"; {27.7.8}; {66.19.20}.

and they This scene is identical with that of {66.5.6-10}. There the ascription of praise of the "kings and priests" (cf. {27.7.18}; {27.7.18} ref. a) ends with the words, "and we shall reign on the earth." Revelation 6. opens the "vexing" of {19.2.5} introductory to setting the king on Zion; {19.2.6}; {66.20.4}. The vision {27.7.9-14} reverses the order of events as they will be fulfilled. {27.7.13} describes the scene in heaven (cf) {66.5.6-10} which, in fulfilment, precedes the events which Daniel sees in vision in {27.7.9-12}. The historic order will be: (1) The investiture of the Son of Man with the kingdom {27.7.13}; {27.7.14}; {66.5.6-10} (2) the "vexing" of {19.2.5}, fully described in {40.24.21}; {40.24.22} Revelation 6-18. (3) The return of the Son of Man in glory to deliver the "smiting" blow of {27.2.45}; {27.7.9-11} {66.19.11-21}. (4) The judgement of the nations and the setting up of the kingdom {27.7.10}; {27.7.26}; {27.7.27}; {40.25.31-46}; {66.20.1-6}.

him {27.7.13}; {27.7.14} is identical with {66.5.1-7} and antedates the fulfilment of {27.2.34}; {27.2.35}.; {27.7.13}; {27.7.14}; {66.5.1-7} describe the investiture of the Son of Man and Son of David with the kingdom authority, while {27.2.34}; {27.2.35} describes the crushing blow (Armageddon, {66.16.14} which destroys Gentile world-power, thus clearing the way for the actual setting up of the kingdom of heaven.; {27.2.34}; {27.2.35}; {66.19.19-21} are the same event.

beasts The monarch vision of Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 2) covers the same historic order as the beast vision of Daniel, but with this difference: Nebuchadnezzar saw the imposing outward power and splendour of the "times of the Gentiles" {42.21.24}; {66.16.19} while Daniel saw the true character of Gentile world-government as rapacious and warlike, established and maintained by force. It is remarkable that the heraldic insignia of the Gentile nations are all beasts or birds of prey.
know the truth of the fourth beast See note 4, (See Scofield on {27.7.17}).

and they shall The end of Gentile world-power. (1) In the beast vision of Daniel 7. the fourth beast is declared to be "the fourth kingdom," i.e. the Roman empire, the "iron" kingdom of Daniel 2. The "ten horns" upon the fourth beast (Roman empire), {27.7.7} are declared to be "ten kings that shall arise" ({27.7.24}) answering to the ten toes of the image vision of Daniel 2. The ten kingdoms, covering the regions formerly ruled by Rome, will constitute, therefore, the form in which the fourth or Roman empire will exist when the whole fabric of Gentile world-domination is smitten by the "stone cut out without hands" == Christ; {27.2.44}; {27.2.45}; {27.7.9}. (2) But Daniel sees a "little horn" rise up and subdue three of the ten kings {27.7.24-26}. His distinguishing mark is hatred of God and of the Saints. He is not to be confounded with the "little horn" of Daniel 8 --a prophecy fulfilled in Antiochus Epiphanes. (See Scofield on {27.8.9}). In Revelation 13, additional particulars of the "little horn" of Daniel 7. are given. (See Scofield on {66.13.1}).

vision The eighth chapter gives details concerning the second and third world-kingdoms: the silver and brass kingdoms of Daniel 2; the bear and leopard kingdoms of Daniel 7, viz., the Medo-Persian and Macedonian kingdoms of history. At the time of this vision ({27.8.1}) the first monarchy was nearing its end. Belshazzar was the last king of that monarchy. third year About B.C. 530.

little horn The "little horn" here is a prophecy fulfilled in Antiochus Epiphanes, B.C. 175, who profaned the temple and terribly persecuted the Jews. He is not to be confounded with the "little horn" of Daniel 7. who is yet to come, and who will dominate the earth during the great tribulation. (See Scofield on {27.7.8}) concerning "The Beast". (See Scofield on {66.19.20}) and "The great tribulation," {19.2.5}. (See Scofield on {66.7.14}). But Antiochus is a remarkable type of the Beast, the terrible "little horn" of the last days. {27.8.24-25} go beyond Antiochus and evidently refer to the "little horn" of Daniel 7. Both Antiochus and the Beast, but the Beast pre-eminently, are in view in {27.8.24-25}. That the "little horn" of Daniel 7. cannot be the little horn of {27.8.9-13}; {27.8.23} is evident. The former comes up among the ten horns into which the fourth empire (Roman) is to be divided; the little horn of Daniel 8. comes out of one of the four kingdoms into which the third (Grecian) empire was divided ({27.8.23}), and in "the latter time" of the four kingdoms {27.8.22}; {27.8.23}). This was historically true of Antiochus Epiphanes. They are alike in hatred of the Jews and of God, and in profaning the temple. Cf. {27.7.25} (the Beast) with {27.8.10-12} (Antiochus): one of them Anticohus Epiphanes came out of Syria, one of the "four notable" kingdoms into which Alexander’s empire was divided.

And it waxed great This passage ({27.8.10-14}) is confessedly the most difficult in prophecy, a difficulty increased by the present state of the text. Historically this was fulfilled in and by Antiochus Epiphanes, but in a more intense and final sense Antiochus but adumbrates the awful blasphemy of the "little horn" of; {27.7.8}; {27.7.24}; {27.7.25}; {27.9.27}; {27.11.36-45}; {27.12.11}. In Daniel {27.8.10-14} the actions of both "little horns" blend.
daily sacrifice Cf. {27.9.27} where the Beast comes into view:

desolation Seven times in Daniel the "desolation" is spoken of: (1) Of the sanctuary, {27.8.13} fulfilled by Antiochus Epiphanes, B.C. 175-170. (2) Of the sanctuary, {27.9.17} the condition in Daniel’s time, when the Jews were in exile and the sanctuary desolate. (3) Generally, of the land, {27.9.18} also referring to Daniel’s time. (4) Of the sanctuary, {27.9.26} fulfilled A.D. 70, in the destruction of city and temple after the cutting off of Messiah. {42.21.20}. (5,6,7) Of the sanctuary, by the Beast, {27.9.27}; {27.11.31}; {27.12.11} Cf; {40.24.15}; {41.13.14}; {53.2.3}; {53.2.8-12}; {66.13.14}; {66.13.15}. one saint Or, holy one, idem. {27.4.13}; {27.4.17}.

end Two "ends" are in view here: (1) historically, the end of the third, or Grecian empire of Alexander out of one of the divisions of which the little horn of {27.8.9} (Antiochus) arose; (2) prophetically, the end of the times of the Gentiles {42.21.24}; {66.16.14} when the "little horn" of {27.7.8}; {27.7.24-26} the Beast, will arise--Daniel’s final time of the end. (See Scofield on {27.12.4}).
ram vs. {27.8.3}; {27.8.4}. The "higher" horn which "came up last" is Cyrus, the other "Darius the Mede."
four kingdoms The four empires into which Alexander’s empire was divided about B.C. 300; Greece, Asia Minor, including Syria, Egypt, the East.
king of fierce countenance i.e. Antiochus Epiphanes who arose out of Syria, one of the "four kingdoms," B.C. 170.

Seventy weeks These are "weeks" or more accurately, sevens of years; seventy weeks of seven years each. Within these "weeks" the national chastisement must be ended and the nation re- established in everlasting righteousness ({27.9.24}). The seventy weeks are divided into seven = 49 years; sixty-two = 434 years; one = 7 years ({27.9.25-27}). In the seven weeks = 49 years, Jerusalem was to be rebuilt in "troublous times." This was fulfilled, as Ezra and Nehemiah record. Sixty-two weeks = 434 years, thereafter Messiah was to come ({27.9.25}). This was fulfilled in the birth and manifestation of Christ ({27.9.26}). {27.9.26} is obviously an indeterminate period. The date of the crucifixion is not fixed. It is only said to be "after" the threescore and two weeks. It is the first event in {27.9.26}. The second event is the destruction of the city, fulfilled A.D. 70. Then, "unto the end," a period not fixed, but which has already lasted nearly 2000 years. To Daniel was revealed only that wars and desolations should continue (cf. {40.24.6-14}.) The N.T. reveals, that which was hidden from the O.T. prophets; {40.13.11-17}; {49.3.1-10} that during this period should be accomplished the mysteries of the kingdom of Heaven {40.13.1-50} and the out-calling of the Church; {40.16.18}; {45.11.25}. When the Church- age will end, and the seventieth week begin, is nowhere revealed. Its duration can be but seven years. To make it more violates the principle of interpretation already confirmed by fulfilment. {27.9.27} deals with the last week. The "he" of {27.9.27} is the "prince that shall come" of {27.9.26}, whose people (Rome) destroyed the temple, A.D. 70. He is the same with the "little horn" of chapter 7. He will covenant with the Jews to restore their temple sacrifices for one week (seven years), but in the middle of that time he will break the covenant and fulfil; {27.12.11}; {53.2.3}; {53.2.4}. Between the sixty-ninth week, after which Messiah was cut off, and the seventieth week, within which the "little horn" of Daniel 7. will run his awful course, intervenes this entire Church-age. {27.9.27} deals with the last three and a half years of the seven, which are identical with the "great tribulation." {40.24.15-28} "time of trouble" {27.12.1} hour of temptation" {66.3.10}. (see "Tribulation,"; {19.2.5}; {66.7.14}). (See Scofield on {19.2.5}). make reconciliation There is no word in the O.T. properly rendered reconcile. In the A.V. the English word is found {9.29.4}; {14.29.24}; {3.6.30}; {3.8.15}; {3.16.20}; {26.45.15}; {26.45.17}; {26.45.20}; {27.9.24} but always improperly; atonement is invariably the meaning. Reconciliation is a N.T. doctrine {45.5.10} (See Scofield on {51.1.21}). thy people Cf. {28.1.9} The Jews, rejected, are "thy people," i.e. Daniel’s, not Jehovah’s though yet to be restored. reconciliation Heb. kaphar, atonement. See this verse note 1, and see note, {2.29.33} (See Scofield on {2.29.33}).

from the going forth of the commandment Three decrees concerning Jerusalem are recorded, that of Cyrus, B.C. 536 (Ussher), for the restoration of the "house of the Lord God of Israel" {14.36.22}; {14.36.23}; {15.1.1-3} that of Darius {26.6.3-8} B.C. 521-486), and that of Artaxerxes in his seventh year. {26.7.7} say, B.C. 458). Artaxerxes in his twentieth year, B.C. 444 (Hales, Jahn), 446 (A.V.), 454 (Ussher, Hengstenberg), gave permission for the rebuilding of the "city," i.e., "Jerusalem" {16.2.1-8}. The latter decree is, obviously, that from which the "seven weeks" (49 years) run, unless by "the commandment to restore," etc. is meant the divine decree {27.9.23}. In the present state of biblical chronology the date of the decree of Artaxerxes cannot be unanswerably fixed farther than to say that it was issued between 454 and 444 B.C. In either case we are brought to the time of Christ. Prophetic time is invariably so near as to give full warning, so indeterminate as to give no satisfaction to mere curiosity. (cf); {40.24.36}; {44.1.7}. The 434 years reckon, of course, from the end of the seven weeks so that the whole time from "the going forth of the commandment to restore," etc., "unto the Messiah" is sixty-nine weeks of years, or 483 years.

abominations (Cf) {40.24.15}. The expression occurs three times in Daniel. In; {27.9.27}; {27.12.11} the reference is to the "Beast," "man of sin"; {53.2.3}; {53.2.4} and is identical with {40.24.15}. In {27.11.31} the reference is to the act of Antiochus Epiphanes, the prototype of the man of sin, who sacrificed a sow upon the altar, and entered the holy of holies.

abominations (Cf) {40.24.15}. The expression occurs three times in Daniel. In; {27.9.27}; {27.12.11} the reference is to the "Beast," "man of sin"; {53.2.3}; {53.2.4} and is identical with {40.24.15}. In {27.11.31} the reference is to the act of Antiochus Epiphanes, the prototype of the man of sin, who sacrificed a sow upon the altar, and entered the holy of holies.
And, behold vs. {27.10.10-15}, introduce an angel. The theophany begins again at {27.10.16}.

prince of {27.10.20}. The intimation is clear that as the holy angels are sent forth in behalf of the heirs of salvation, so demons are concerned in behalf of the world-system of Satan. {43.7.7}; {66.13.8}.

The spirit of prophecy here returns to that which more immediately concerned Daniel and his royal masters--the near future of the empire in which he was so great a personage. Four kings were yet to follow in Media-Persia. Then will come Alexander the "mighty king" of Grecia ({27.11.3}). The division of Alexander’s empire into four parts ({27.11.4}) as already predicted {27.8.22} is foretold. The troublous course of affairs in two parts of the disintegrated Alexandrian empire, Syria and Egypt, is then traced down to {27.11.20}. Here Antiochus Epiphanes, the "little horn" of Daniel 8, occupies the vision down to {27.11.36}. His pollution of the sanctuary is again mentioned. (Cf) (See Scofield on {27.8.9}). From {27.11.36} the interpretation is of the final "little horn" {27.7.8}; {27.7.24-26} (See Scofield on {27.11.35}). three kings Ahasuerus, {15.4.6}, Artaxerxes, {15.4.7}, and Darius called "Hystaspes" {15.4.24}. fourth Xerxes, who invaded Greece BC 483-480.

south i.e. "south" of Palestine. Egypt is meant. his princes i.e. One of Alexander’s princes; historically Ptolemy Lagidae. he shall Not the "king of the south" (Ptolemy Lagidae, to whom Egypt was given), but the "king of the north" {27.11.6}, Seleucus, to whom Syria was given:

they shall i.e. the descendants and successors of Ptolemy Lagidae and Seleucus, not those very personages. The prediction was fulfilled in the marriage of Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy Philadelphus, to Antiochus Theos, third king of Syria, B.C. 285-247.
branch of her roots Ptolemy Euergetes, brother of Berenice, who invaded Syria as described in {27.11.7-9}.
but his sons {40.11.10-19}, prophetic foreview of the wars of Egypt and Syria, Palestine, {27.11.17}, the battleground, B.C. 284-175.
king of the north Antiochus the Great, B.C. 198.
daughter of women Probably a reference to the marriage of Cleopatra to an Egyptian king, Ptolemy Philometor.
isles i.e. of Greece. prince for his own i.e. Historically on of the Scipios: the power of Rome felt in the East for the first time.
a raiser of taxes A reference to the tribute exacted of the son of Antiochus the Great by the Romans.
come toward the south Antiochus Epiphanes’ second expedition against Egypt. Stopped by the mandate of Rome, {27.11.30}, he turns against the Jews:
abomination This is historic -- the act of Antiochus Epiphanes. {40.24.15} refers to {27.12.11}, (See Scofield on {27.9.27}).
strong e.g. the Maccabees. B.C. 168 and following.
