JESUS The Greek form of the Hebrew Jehoshua meaning saviour.

Herod the king Called Herod the Great, son of Antipater, an Idumean {1.36.1} (See Scofield on {1.36.1}) and Cypros, an Arabian woman. Antipater was appointed procurator of Judea by Julius Caesar, B.C. 47. At the age of fifteen Herod was appointed to the government of Galilee. B.C. 40 the Roman senate made him king of Judea. An able, strong, and cruel man, he increased greatly the splendour of Jerusalem, erecting the temple which was the centre of Jewish worship in the time of our Lord.

King "The King" is one of the divine titles {19.10.16} and so used in the worship of the Church {54.1.17} but Christ is never called "King of the Church." He is "King of the Jews" {40.2.2} and Lord and "Head of the Church" {49.1.22}; {49.1.23} (See Scofield on {40.16.18}; {58.12.23}); {40.16.18}; {58.12.23}

Scribes (Greek - "ἀπόλλυμι" = "writer") Heb. "spherim," "to write," "set in order," "count." The scribes were so called because it was their office to make copies of the Scriptures; to classify and teach the precepts of oral law (See Scofield on {40.3.7}) and to keep careful count of every letter in the O.T. writings. Such an office was necessary in a religion of law and precept, and was an O.T. function {10.8.17}; {10.20.25}; {11.4.3}; {24.8.8}; {24.36.10}; {24.36.12}; {24.36.26}. To this legitimate work the scribes added a record of rabbinical decisions on questions of ritual (Halachoth); the new code resulting from those decisions (Mishna); the Hebrew sacred legends (Gemara, forming with the Mishna the Talmud); commentaries on the O.T. (Midrashim); reasonings upon these (Hagada); and finally, mystical interpretations which found in Scripture meanings other than the grammatical, lexical, and obvious ones (the Kabbala); not unlike the allegorical method of Origen, or the modern Protestant "spiritualizing" interpretation. In our Lord’s time, to receive this mass of writing superposed upon the Scriptures was to be orthodox; to return to the Scriptures themselves was heterodoxy--our Lord’s most serious offence.

Out of Egypt The words quoted are in {28.11.1} and the passage illustrates the truth that prophetic utterances often have a latent and deeper meaning than at first appears. Pharisees So called from a Heb. word meaning "separate." After the ministry of the post-exilic prophets ceased, godly men called "Chasidim" (saints) arose who sought to keep alive reverence for the law amongst the descendants of the Jews who returned from the Babylonian captivity. This movement degenerated into the Pharisaism of our Lord’s day-- a letter-strictness which overlaid the law with traditional interpretations held to have been communicated by Jehovah to Moses as oral explanations of equal authority with the law itself. (cf. {40.15.2}; {40.15.3}; {41.7.8-13}; {48.1.14}). The Pharisees were strictly a sect. A member was "chaber" (i.e. "knit together,") {7.20.11} and took an obligation to remain true to the principles of Pharisaism. They were correct, moral, zealous, and self-denying, but self-righteous {42.18.9} and destitute of the sense of sin and need {42.7.39}. They were the foremost prosecutors of Jesus Christ and the objects of His unsparing denunciation (e.g.); {40.23.13-29}; {42.11.42}; {42.11.43} Sadducees Not strictly a sect, but rather those amongst the Jews who denied the existence of angels or other spirits, and all miracles, especially the resurrection. They were the religious rationalists of the time {41.12.18-23}; {44.5.15-17}; {44.23.8} and strongly entrenched in the Sanhedrin and priesthood; {44.4.1}; {44.5.17}. They are identified with no affirmative doctrine, but were mere deniers of the supernatural.

Suffer it to be so Why one who needed no repentance should insist upon receiving a rite which signified confession ({40.3.6}) and repentance ({40.3.11}) is nowhere directly explained. It may be suggested: (1) That Jesus was now to receive His anointing with the Holy Spirit ({40.3.16}) unto His threefold office of Prophet, Priest, and King. In the Levitical order {2.29.4-7} the high priest was first washed, then anointed. While Christ’s priestly work did not begin till He "offered Himself without spot to God" {58.9.14} and His full manifestation as the King- Priest after the order of Melchizedek awaits the kingdom (See Scofield on {1.14.18}) yet He was then anointed, once for all. (2) But John’s baptism was the voice of God to Israel, and the believing remnant responded ({40.3.5}). It was an act of righteousness on the part of Him who had become, as to the flesh, an Israelite, to take His place with this believing remnant. righteousness (See Scofield on {62.3.7}).
Jesus For the first time the Trinity, foreshadowed in many ways in the O.T., is fully manifested. The Spirit descends upon the Son, and at the same moment the Father’s voice is heard from heaven.

Then was Jesus The temptation of Christ, the "last Adam" {46.15.45} is best understood when contrasted with that of the "first man Adam." Adam was tempted in his place of lord of creation, a lordship with but one reservation, the knowledge of good and evil; {1.1.26}; {1.2.16}; {1.2.17}. Through the woman he was tempted to add that also to his dominion. Falling, he lost all. But Christ had taken the place of a lowly Servant, acting only from and in obedience to the Father.; {50.2.5-8}; {43.5.19}; {43.6.57}; {43.8.28}; {43.8.54} (See Scofield on {23.41.8}) that He might redeem a fallen race and a creation under the curse; {1.3.17-19}; {45.8.19-23}. Satan’s one object in the threefold temptation was to induce Christ to act from Himself, in independency of His Father. The first two temptations were a challenge to Christ from the god of this world to prove Himself indeed the Son of God ({40.4.3}; {40.4.6}). The third was the offer of the usurping prince of this world to divest himself of that which rightfully belonged to Christ as Son of man and Son of David, on the condition that He accept the sceptre on Satan’s world-principles (cf. {43.18.36}). (See Scofield on {66.13.8}). Christ defeated Satan by a means open to His humblest follower, the intelligent use of the word of God ({40.4.4}; {40.4.7}). In his second temptation Satan also used Scripture, but a promise available only to one in the path of obedience. The scene give emphasis to the vital importance of "rightly dividing the word of truth" {55.2.15}.

holy city In the N.T. one Greek word, hagios, in its various forms, is rendered, "holy," "holiness," "sanctify," "sanctified," "sanctification." Like the heb. qodesh, it signifies "set apart for God." The important references follow {40.4.5}, marg. (See Scofield on {40.4.5}).

world The Greek word kosmos means "order," "arrangement," and so, with the Greeks, "beauty"; for order and arrangement in the sense of system are at the bottom of the Greek conception of beauty. When used in the N.T. of humanity, the "world" of men, it is organized humanity-- humanity in families, tribes, nations--which is meant. The word for chaotic, unorganized humanity--the mere mass of man is thalassa, the "sea" of men (e.g.) {66.13.1} (See Scofield on {66.13.8}). For "world" (kosmos) in the bad ethical sense, "world system" {43.7.7}.

at hand "At hand" is never a positive affirmation that the person or thing said to be "at hand" will immediately appear, but only that no known or predicted event must intervene. When Christ appeared to the Jewish people, the next thing in the order of revelation as it then stood, should have been the setting up of the Davidic kingdom. In the knowledge of God, not yet disclosed, lay the rejection of the kingdom (and King), the long period of the mystery-form of the kingdom, the world-wide preaching of the cross, and the out-calling of the Church. But this was as yet locked up in the secret counsels of God. {40.13.11}; {40.13.17}; {49.3.3-10}. kingdom See note 2, (See Scofield on {40.5.2}). is at hand (See Scofield on {40.3.2}). For Another Point of View: See Topic 301207
two brethren Peter and John were already disciples, {43.1.35-42}. This is a call to service.

James Two persons are called by this name in the N.T. (1) James the son of Zebedee, an apostle {40.10.2} and the brother of the apostle John, apart from whom he is never mentioned, and with whom, together with Peter, he was admitted to the especial intimacy of our Lord.; {40.17.1}; {41.5.37}; {41.9.2}; {41.14.33} He was martyred by Herod. {44.12.2} (2) A son of Alphaeus (or Cleopas) and Mary the sister of Mary the mother of Jesus. (See Scofield on {40.1.16}) and brother of Joses. {41.15.40}. He was, therefore, a cousin of the Lord Jesus. He is called James "the less" {41.15.40} lit. little, i.e. of shorter stature than James the son of Zebedee). He was an apostle. {40.10.3} It has been conjectured that "Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus" {40.10.3} was identical with the Juda of {42.6.16} who is there called "of i.e. ’son’ or ’brother’ as is has been variously translated] James." A Juda is mentioned with a James and Joses and Simon in {41.6.3} as "brother" of our Lord (See Scofield on {40.13.55}, marg.). The Gospels mention no other James who could be called the brother of the Lord Jesus, but James the less was certainly the son of Alphaeus and Mary the sister of our Lord’s mother. The conclusion seems, therefore most probable that; {40.10.3}; {40.13.55}; {41.3.18}; {41.6.3}; {42.6.15}; {44.1.13}; {44.12.17}; {41.15.13}; {48.1.19}; {48.2.9}; {48.2.12}; {59.1.1} refer to James the less, son of Alphaeus and Mary, and cousin, or, according to Jewish usage, "brother" of the Lord Jesus. He was the author of the Epistle of James.

And he opened his mouth Having announced the kingdom of heaven as "at hand," the King, in Matthew 5-7, declares the principles of the kingdom. The Sermon on the Mount has a twofold application: (1) literally to the kingdom. In this sense it gives the divine constitution for the righteous government of the earth. Whenever the kingdom of heaven is established on earth it will be according to that constitution, which may be regarded as an explanation of the word "righteousness" as used by the prophets in describing the kingdom (e.g.) {23.11.4}; {23.11.5}; {23.32.1}; {27.9.24} In this sense the Sermon on the Mount is pure law, and transfers the offence from the overt act to the motive. {40.5.21}; {40.5.22}; {40.5.27}; {40.5.28}. Here lies the deeper reason why the Jews rejected the kingdom. They had reduced "righteousness" to mere ceremonialism, and the Old Testament idea of the kingdom to a mere affair of outward splendour and power. They were never rebuked for expecting a visible and powerful kingdom, but the words of the prophets should have prepared them to expect also that only the poor in spirit and the meek could share in it (e.g.) {23.11.4}. The seventy-second Psalm, which was universally received by them as a description of the kingdom, was full of this. For these reasons, the Sermon on the Mount in its primary application gives neither the privilege nor the duty of the Church. These are found in the Epistles. Under the law of the kingdom, for example, no one may hope for forgiveness who has not first forgiven. {40.6.12}; {40.6.14}; {40.6.15}. Under grace the Christian is exhorted to forgive because he is already forgiven. {49.4.30-32}. (2) But there is a beautiful moral application to the Christian. It always remains true that the poor in spirit, rather than the proud, are blessed, and those who mourn because of their sins, and who are meek in the consciousness of them, will hunger and thirst after righteousness, and hungering, will be filled. The merciful are "blessed," the pure in heart do "see God." These principles fundamentally reappear in the teaching of the Epistles. saying The beatific character, unattainable by effort, is wrought in the believer by the Spirit, {48.5.22}; {48.5.23}. For Another Point of View: See Topic 301232

I am not come to destroy Christ’s relation to the law of Moses may be thus summarized: (1) He was made under the law {48.4.4}. (2) He lived in perfect obedience to the law {43.8.46}; {40.17.5}; {60.2.21-23}. (3) he was a minister of the law to the Jews, clearing it from rabbinical sophistries, enforcing it in all its pitiless severity upon those who professed to obey it (e.g.) {42.10.25-37} but confirming the promises made to the fathers under the Mosaic Covenant {45.15.8}. (4) He fulfilled the types of the law by His holy life and sacrificial death {58.9.11-26}. (5) He bore, vicariously, the curse of the law that the Abrahamic Covenant might avail all who believe {48.3.13}; {48.3.14}. (6) He brought out by His redemption all who believe from the place of servants under the law into the place of sons {48.4.1-7}. (7) He mediated by His blood the New Covenant of assurance and grace in which all believers stand {45.5.2}; {58.8.6-13} so establishing the "law of Christ" {48.6.2} with its precepts of higher exaltation made possible by the indwelling Spirit.

hell fire Gr. "Geenna" = Gehenna, the place in the valley of Hinnom where, anciently, human sacrifices were offered. {14.33.6}; {24.7.31} The word occurs,; {40.5.22}; {40.5.29}; {40.5.30}; {40.10.28}; {40.18.9}; {40.23.15}; {40.23.33}; {41.9.43}; {41.9.45}; {41.9.47}; {42.12.5}; {59.3.6}. In every instance except the last the word comes from the lips of Jesus Christ in most solemn warning of the consequences of sin. He describes it as the place where "their" worm never dies and of fire never to be quenched. The expression is identical in meaning with "lake of fire".; {66.19.20}; {66.20.10}; {66.20.14}; {66.20.15}. See "Death, the second" ({43.8.24}; {66.21.8}); also (See Scofield on {66.21.8}; {42.16.23}).

perfect The word implies full development, growth into maturity of godliness, not sinless perfection. {49.4.12}; {49.4.13}. In this passage the Father’s kindness, not His sinlessness, is the point in question. {42.6.35}; {42.6.36}
alms Or, righteous acts. The word refers to religious externalities. These may be seen of men, but that must not be the motive.
reward i.e. the reward they have sought.

we forgive our debtors This is legal ground. Cf. {49.4.32} which is grace. Under law forgiveness is conditioned upon a like spirit in us; under grace we are forgiven for Christ’s sake, and exhorted to forgive because we have been forgiven.; {40.18.32}; {40.26.28}. (See Scofield on {40.26.28}). For Another Point of View: See Topic 301235 debts sin (See Scofield on {45.3.23}).
take no thought Or, have no anxiety. {40.6.34}.

kingdom of God The kingdom of God is to be distinguished from the kingdom of heaven (See Scofield on {40.3.2}), in five respects: (1) The kingdom of God is universal, including all moral intelligences willingly subject to the will of God, whether angels, the Church, or saints of past or future dispensations {42.13.28}; {42.13.29}; {58.12.22}; {58.12.23} while the kingdom of heaven is Messianic, mediatorial, and Davidic, and has for its object the establishment of the kingdom of God in the earth (See Scofield on {40.3.2}) {46.15.24}; {46.15.25}. (2) The kingdom of God is entered only by the new birth {43.3.3}; {43.3.5-7} the kingdom of heaven, during this age, is the sphere of a profession which may be real or false. (See Scofield on {40.13.3}) {40.25.1}; {40.25.11}; {40.25.12} (3) Since the kingdom of heaven is the earthly sphere of the universal kingdom of God, the two have almost all things in common. For this reason many parables and other teachings are spoken of the kingdom of heaven in Matthew, and of the kingdom of God in Mark and Luke. It is the omissions which are significant. The parables of the wheat and tares, and of the net {40.13.24-30}; {40.13.36-43}; {40.13.47-50} are not spoken of the kingdom of God. In that kingdom there are neither tares nor bad fish. But the parable of the leaven {40.13.33} is spoken of the kingdom of God also, for, alas, even the true doctrines of the kingdom are leavened with the errors of which the Pharisees, Sadducees, and the Herodians were the representatives. (See Scofield on {40.13.33}). (4) The kingdom of God "comes not with outward show" {42.17.20} but is chiefly that which is inward and spiritual {45.14.17} while the kingdom of heaven is organic, and is to be manifested in glory on the earth. (See "Kingdom (O.T.)," {38.12.8}, note; (N.T.),; {42.1.31-33}; {46.15.24}, note; {40.17.2}, note.) (See Scofield on {38.12.8}), {42.1.31-33} (See Scofield on {46.15.24}; {40.17.2}). (5) The kingdom of heaven merges into the kingdom of God when Christ, having put all enemies under his feet, "shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father" {46.15.24-28} (See Scofield on {40.3.2}).
judge not In the sense of condemnation.

Devils Devils, lit demons. To the reality and personality of demons the N.T. scriptures bear abundant testimony. As to their origin nothing is clearly revealed, but they are not to be confounded with the angels mentioned in {61.2.4}; {65.1.6}. Summary: Demons are spirits {40.12.43}; {40.12.45} are Satan’s emissaries; {40.12.26}; {40.12.27}; {40.25.41} and so numerous as to make Satan’s power practically ubiquitous. {41.5.9}. They are capable of entering and controlling both men and beasts {41.5.8}; {41.5.11-13} and earnestly seek embodiment, without which, apparently, they are powerless for evil.; {40.12.43}; {40.12.44}; {41.5.10-12}. Demon influence and demon possession are discriminated in the N. T. Instances of the latter are; {40.4.24}; {40.8.16}; {40.8.28}; {40.8.33}; {40.9.32}; {40.12.22}; {41.1.32}; {41.5.15}; {41.5.16}; {41.5.18}; {42.8.35}; {44.8.7}; {44.16.16}. They are unclean, sullen, violent, and malicious; {40.8.28}; {40.9.23}; {40.10.1}; {40.12.43}; {41.1.23}; {41.5.3-5}; {41.9.17}; {41.9.20}; {42.6.18}; {42.9.39}. They know Jesus Christ as Most High God, and recognize His supreme authority; {40.8.31}; {40.8.32}; {41.1.24}; {44.19.15}; {59.2.19}. They know their eternal fate to be one of torment; {40.8.29}; {42.8.31}. They inflict physical maladies; {40.12.22}; {40.17.15-18}; {42.13.16} but mental disease is to be distinguished from the disorder of mind due to demonical control. Demon influence may manifest itself in religion asceticism and formalism {54.4.1-3} degenerating into uncleanness {61.2.10-12}. The sign of demon influence in religion is departing from the faith, i.e. the body of revealed truth in the Scriptures. {54.4.1}. The demons maintain especially a conflict with believers who would be spiritual.; {49.6.12}; {54.4.1-3}. All unbelievers are open to demon possession {49.2.2}. The believer’s resources, prayer and bodily control {40.17.21} "the whole armour of God" {49.6.13-18}. Exorcism in the name of Jesus Christ {44.16.18} was practised for demon possession. One of the awful features of the apocalyptic judgments in which this age will end is an irruption of demons out the abyss. {66.9.1-11}.

behold, there came a leper The King, having in Matthew 5-7. declared the principles of the kingdom, makes proof, in Matthew 8, 9, of His power to banish from the earth the consequences of sin, and to control the elements of nature. Lord Gr. Kurios. The first occurrence of the word is applied to Jesus with His evident sanction. In itself the word means "master," and is so used of mere human relationships in, e.g. {40.6.24}; {40.15.27}; {41.13.35}; {49.6.9} Both uses, divine and human, are brought together in {51.4.1}. It is the (Greek - ἀθέμιτος Heb). "Adonai." (See Scofield on {1.15.2}), and is so used by Jesus Christ in {40.22.43-45}. In the N.T. the distinctive uses of Kurios (Lord) are: (1) As the N.T. translation of the Heb. Jehovah (Lord), e.g. {40.1.20}; {40.1.22}; {40.2.15}; {40.3.3}; {40.4.7}; {40.4.10}; {40.11.25}; {40.21.9}; {41.12.29}; {41.12.30}; {42.1.68}; {42.2.9} (2) Jesus Himself so uses Kurios, e.g. {40.4.7}; {40.4.10}; {40.11.25}; {41.12.11}. (3) But the great use of Kurios is as the divine title of Jesus, the Christ. In this sense it occurs in the N.T. 663 times. That the intent is to identify Jesus Christ with the O.T. Deity is evident from {40.3.3}; {40.12.8}; {40.21.9}; {19.118.26}; {40.22.43-45}; {42.1.43}; {43.8.58}; {43.14.8-10}; {43.20.28}; {44.9.5}; {44.13.33}. (Psalms 2.). (See Scofield on {43.20.28}).

Son of man (See Scofield on {26.2.1}). Our Lord thus designates Himself about eighty times. It is His racial name as the representative Man, in the sense of {46.15.45-47} as Son of David is distinctly his Jewish name, and Son of God His divine name. Our Lord constantly uses this term as implying that his mission (e.g.); {40.11.19}; {42.19.10}. His death and resurrection (e.g.); {40.12.40}; {40.20.18}; {40.26.2} and His second coming (e.g.); {40.24.37-44}; {42.12.40} transcended in scope and result all merely Jewish imitations. When Nathanael confesses him as "King of Israel," our Lord’s answer is, "Thou shalt see greater things.. . the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man." When His messengers are cast out by the Jews, His thought leaps forward to the time when the Son of man shall come, not then to Israel only but to the race; {40.10.5}; {40.10.6}; {40.8.23}. It is in this name, also, that universal judgment is committed to Him {43.5.22}; {43.5.27}. It is also a name indicating that in Him is fulfilled the O.T. foreview of blessing through a coming man. (See Scofield on {1.1.26}); {1.3.15}; {1.12.3}; {19.8.4}; {19.80.17}; {23.7.14}; {23.9.6}; {23.9.7}; {23.32.2}; {38.13.7}; {23.32.2}; {38.13.7}.
Son of man (See Scofield on {40.8.20}). sins Sin. (See Scofield on {45.3.23}).

apostles The word apostle, = "one sent forth," is used of our Lord {58.3.1}. Elsewhere it is used for the twelve who were called to that office by our Lord during His earth ministry; of Paul, called to the apostleship by the risen and ascended Lord, and of Barnabas {44.14.14} specially designated by the Holy Spirit {44.13.2}. Of Matthias, chosen by lot by the eleven to take the place of Judas Iscariot, {44.1.16-26} it is said: "And he was numbered with the eleven." {44.1.26}. The "signs" of an apostle were (1) They were chosen directly by the Lord Himself, or, as in the case of Barnabas, by the Holy Spirit {40.10.1}; {40.10.2}; {41.3.13}; {41.3.14}; {42.6.13}; {44.9.6}; {44.9.15}; {44.13.2}; {44.22.10}; {44.22.14}; {44.22.15}; {45.1.1} (2) They were endued with sign gifts, miraculous powers which were the divine credentials of their office {40.10.1}; {44.5.15}; {44.5.16}; {44.16.16-18}; {40.28.8}; {40.28.9}. (3) Their relation to the kingdom was that of heralds, announcing to Israel only {40.10.5}; {40.10.6} the kingdom as at hand. (See Scofield on {40.4.17}) and manifesting kingdom powers {40.10.7}; {40.10.8}. (4) To one of them, Peter, the keys of the kingdom of heaven, viewed as the sphere of Christian profession, as in Matthew 13, were given {40.16.19}. (5) Their future relation to the king will be that of judges over the twelve tribes {40.19.28}. (6) Consequent upon the rejection of the kingdom, and the revelation of the mystery hid in God {40.16.18}; {49.3.1-12} the Church, the apostolic office was invested with a new enduement, the baptism with the Holy Spirit {44.2.1-4} a new power, that of imparting the Spirit to Jewish-Christian believers; a new relation, that of foundation stones of the new temple {49.2.20-22} and a new function, that of preaching the glad tidings of salvation through a crucified and risen Lord to Jew and gentile alike. (7) The indispensable qualification of an apostle was that he should have been an eye- witness of the resurrection {44.1.22}; {46.9.1}. James son of Zebedee (See Scofield on {40.4.21}).
Gentiles The kingdom was promised to the Jews. Gentiles could be blessed only through Christ crucified and risen. Cf. {43.12.20-24}.

Provide neither gold (Cf) {41.6.8}; {41.6.9}; {42.9.3}. The central thought here, urgency, must be kept in mind. The emphasis is upon "provide." Time is not to be taken to search for additional staves or shoes. The disciples were to go in their ordinary sandals, with such staff as they might have, or with none. Cf. Paul, {45.1.15}.

send The scope of {40.10.16-23} reaches beyond the personal ministry of the twelve, covering in a general sense the sphere of service during the present age. {40.10.23} has in view the preaching of the remnant. {23.1.9}. (See Scofield on {45.11.5}) in the tribulation {19.2.5}. (See Scofield on {66.7.14}). and immediately preceding the return of Christ in glory; {5.30.3}; {44.1.9-11}. (See Scofield on {44.1.11}). The remnant then will not have gone over the cities of Israel till the Lord comes.
for it shall be given An instruction to martyrs, not to preachers.
Beelzebub Beelzebul, title of a heathen deity.

peace Cf. {43.14.27}. Peace is spoken of in Scripture in three ways: (1) "Peace with God" {45.5.1} this is the work of Christ into which the individual enters by faith; {49.2.14-17}; {45.5.1}. (2) "The peace of God" {50.4.7} inward peace, the state of soul of that believer who, having entered into peace with God through faith in Christ, has also committed to God through prayer and supplication with thanksgiving all his anxieties; {42.7.50}; {50.4.6}. (3) Peace "on earth" {42.2.14}; {19.72.7}; {19.85.10}; {23.9.6}; {23.9.7}; {23.11.1-12} the universal prevalency of peace in the earth under the kingdom. {40.10.34} was Christ’s warning that the truth which He was proclaiming would not bring in the kingdom age of peace, but conflict rather. {43.14.27}.
blessed In prison, the King rejected, John’s faith wavers; the Lord exhorts and encourages His servant. Cf. {43.15.20}; {23.42.3}.

greater Positionally greater, not morally. John the Baptist was as great morally, as any man "born of woman," but as to the kingdom he but announced it at hand. The kingdom did not then come, but was rejected, and John was martyred, and the King presently crucified. The least in the kingdom when it is set up in glory (see "Kingdom (N.T.)") {42.1.31-33}; {46.15.24} will be in the fullness of power and glory. It is not heaven which is in question, but Messiah’s kingdom. (See Scofield on {40.3.2}; {40.6.33}). kingdom (See Scofield on {40.3.2}).

suffereth violence It has been much disputed whether the "violence" here is external, as against the kingdom in the persons of John the Baptist and Jesus; or that, considering the opposition of the scribes and Pharisees, only the violently resolute would press into it. Both things are true. The King and His herald suffered violence, and this is the primary and greater meaning, but also, some were resolutely becoming disciples. CF {42.16.16}.

Then The kingdom of heaven announced as "at hand" by John the Baptist, by the King Himself, and by the twelve, and attested by mighty works, has been morally rejected. The places chosen for the testing of the nation, Chorazin, Bethsaida, etc. having rejected both John and Jesus, the rejected King now speaks of judgment. The final official rejection is later. {40.27.31-37}. For Another Point of View: See Topic 301190 For Additional Factors See Topic 301199

Come The new message of Jesus. The rejected King now turns from the rejecting nation and offers, not the kingdom, but rest and service to such in the nation as are conscious of the need. It is a pivotal point in the ministry of Jesus.

sabbath (1) The sabbath ("cessation") appears in Scripture as the day of God’s rest in the finished work of creation. {1.2.2}; {1.2.3}. For 2500 years of human life absolutely no mention is made of it. Then the sabbath was revealed; {2.16.23}; {16.9.13}; {16.9.14} made a part of the law {2.20.8-11} and invested with the character of a "sign" between Jehovah and Israel, and a perpetual reminder to Israel of their separation to God {2.31.13-17}. It was observed by complete rest {2.35.2}; {2.35.3} and by Jehovah’s express order a man was put to death for gathering sticks on the sabbath day. {4.15.32-36}. Apart from maintaining the continued burnt-offering {4.28.9}, and its connection with the annual feasts; {2.12.16}; {3.23.3}; {3.23.8}; {4.28.25} the seventh day sabbath was never made a day of sacrifice, worship, or any manner of religious service. It was simply and only a day of complete rest for man and beast, a humane provision for man’s needs. In Christ’s words, "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." {41.2.27}. (2) Our Lord found the observance of the day encrusted with rabbinical evasions {40.12.2} and restrictions, wholly unknown to the law, so that He was Himself held to be a sabbath breaker by the religious authorities of the time. The sabbath will be again observed during the kingdom age {23.66.23}. (3) The Christian first day perpetuates in the dispensation of grace the principle that one-seventh of the time is especially sacred, but in all other respects is in contrast with the sabbath. One is the seventh day, the other the first. The sabbath commemorates God’s creation rest, the first day Christ’s resurrection. On the seventh day God rested, on the first day Christ was ceaselessly active. The sabbath commemorates a finished creation, the first day a finished redemption. The sabbath was a day of legal obligation, the first day one of voluntary worship and service. The sabbath is mentioned in the Acts only in connection with the Jews, and in the rest of the N.T. but twice. {51.2.16}; {58.4.4}. In these passages the seventh day sabbath is explained to be to the Christian not a day to be observed, but a type of the present rest into which he enters when "he also ceases from his own works" and trusts Christ.

what David did Jesus’ action {40.12.1-7} is highly significant. "What David did" refers to the time of his rejection and persecution by Saul. {9.21.6}. Jesus here is not so much the rejected Saviour as the rejected King; hence the reference to David.

Gentiles This too is most significant. The rejected King of Israel will turn to the Gentiles (cf.) {40.10.5}; {40.10.6}. In fulfilment this awaited the official rejection, crucifixion, and resurrection of Christ, and the final rejection of the risen Christ.; {42.24.46}; {42.24.47}; {44.9.15}; {44.13.46}; {44.28.25-28}; {45.11.11}.
sin Sin. (See Scofield on {45.3.23}). blasphemy Ascribing to Satan the work of the Holy Spirit. Cf. {40.12.24}; {40.12.32}; {40.12.40}.

The men of Nineveh Again the rejected King announces judgment (cf) {40.11.20-24} Israel, in the midst of the Pharisaic revival of outward religious strictness, was like a man out of whom a demon had "gone," i.e, of his own volition. He would come back and find an empty house, etc. The personal application is to a mere self-cleansed moralist. Nineveh vs. {32.3.5-9}; {42.11.32} (See Scofield on {34.1.1}).

While Rejected by Israel, His "kinsmen according to the flesh" (cf) {45.9.3} our Lord intimates the formation of the new family of faith which, overstepping mere racial claims, receives "whosoever" will be His disciple.; {40.12.49}; {40.12.50}; {43.6.28}; {43.6.29}. The seven parables of Matthew 13, called by our Lord, "mysteries of the kingdom of heaven" ({40.13.11}), taken together, describe the result of the presence of the Gospel in the world during the present age, that is, the time of seed sowing which began with our Lord’s personal ministry, and ends with the "harvest" {40.13.40-43}. Briefly, the result is mingled tares and wheat, good fish and bad, in the sphere of Christian profession. It is Christendom. sower The figure marks a new beginning. To labour in God’s vineyard Israel, {23.5.1-7} is one thing, to go forth sowing the seed of the word in a field which is the world, quite another (cf) {40.10.5}. One fourth of the seed takes permanent root, but the result is "wheat"; {40.13.25}; {60.1.23} or "children of the kingdom" {40.13.38}. This parable {40.13.3-9}; {40.13.18-23} is treated throughout as foundational to the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. It is interpreted by our Lord Himself.

mysteries A "mystery" in Scripture is a previously hidden truth, now divinely revealed; but in which a supernatural element still remains despite the revelation. The greater mysteries are: (1) The mysteries of the kingdom of heaven {40.13.3-50}. (2) the mystery of Israel’s blindness during this age {45.11.25} (with context); (3) the mystery of the translation of living saints at the end of this age {46.15.51}; {46.15.52}; {52.4.14-17}. (4) the mystery of N.T. church as one body composed of Jew and Gentile {49.3.1-11}; {45.16.25}; {49.6.19}; {51.4.3}. (5) the mystery of the church as the bride of Christ {49.5.28-32}. (6) the mystery of the inliving Christ {48.2.20}; {51.1.26}; {51.1.27}. (7) the "mystery of God even Christ," i.e. Christ as the incarnate fullness of the Godhead embodied, in whom all the divine wisdom for man subsists {51.2.2}; {51.2.9}; {46.2.7}. (8) the mystery of the processes by which godlikeness is restored to man {54.3.16}. (9) the mystery of iniquity {53.2.7}; {40.13.33}. (10) the mystery of the seven stars {66.1.20}. (11) the mystery of Babylon {66.17.5}; {66.17.7}. kingdom (See Scofield on {40.3.2}).

prophets The O.T. prophets saw in blended vision the rejection and crucifixion of the King (see "Christ, sacrifice,) {1.4.4}, (See Scofield on {58.10.18}) and also His glory as David’s Son. (See Scofield on {38.12.8}), but "what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ and the glory that should follow," was not revealed to them--only that the vision was not for themselves. {60.1.10-12}. That revelation Christ makes in these parables. A period of time is to intervene between His sufferings and His glory. That interval is occupied with the "mysteries of the kingdom of heaven" here described. righteous Righteousness. (See Scofield on {45.10.10}).

parable This parable {40.13.24-30} is also interpreted by our Lord {40.13.36-43}. Here the "good seed" is not the "word," as in the first parable {40.13.19}; {40.13.23} but rather that which the word has produced. {60.1.23}, viz.: the children of the kingdom. These are, providentially {40.13.37} "sown," i.e. scattered, here and there in the "field" of the "world" {40.13.38}. The "world" here is both geographical and ethnic--the earth-world, and also the world of men. The wheat of God at once becomes the scene of Satan’s activity. Where children of the kingdom are gathered, there "among the wheat" {40.13.25}; {40.13.38}; {40.13.39}. Satan "sows" "children of the wicked one," who profess to be children of the kingdom, and in outward ways are so like the true children that only the angels may, in the end, be trusted to separate them {40.13.28-30}; {40.13.40-43}. So great is Satan’s power of deception that the tares often really suppose themselves to be children of the kingdom {40.7.21-23}. Many other parables and exhortations have this mingled condition in view (e.g.) {40.22.11-14}; {40.25.1-13}; {40.25.14-30}; {42.18.10-14}; {58.6.4-9} Indeed, it characterizes Matthew from Chapter 13 to the end. The parable of the wheat and tares is not a description of the world, but of that which professes to be the kingdom. Mere unbelievers are never the children of the devil, but only religious unbelievers are so called (cf) {40.13.38}; {43.8.38-44}; {40.23.15}. The kingdom (See Scofield on {40.3.2}).

1 Gather
The gathering of the tares into bundles for burning does not imply immediate judgment. At the end of this age ({40.13.40}) the tares are set apart for burning, but first the wheat is gathered into the barn.; {43.14.3}; {52.4.14-17}.

kingdom 2 Another parable The parable of the Mustard Seed prefigures the rapid but unsubstantial growth of the mystery form of the kingdom from an insignificant beginning {44.1.15}; {44.2.41}; {46.1.26} to a great place in the earth. The figure of the fowls finding shelter in the branches is drawn from {27.4.20-22}. How insecure was such a refuge the context in Daniel shows. kingdom (See Scofield on {40.3.2}).

Another parable That interpretation of the parable of the Leaven ({40.13.33}) which makes (with variation as to details) the leaven to be the Gospel, introduced into the world ("three measures of meal") by the church, and working subtly until the world is converted ("till the whole was leavened") is open to fatal objection: (1) it does violence to the unvarying symbolical meaning of leaven, and especially to the meaning fixed by our Lord Himself. {40.16.6-12}; {41.8.15} See "Leaven," {1.19.3}. (See Scofield on {40.13.33}). (2) The implication of a converted world in this age ("till the whole was leavened"), is explicitly contradicted by our Lord’s interpretation of the parables of the Wheat and Tares, and of the Net. Our Lord presents a picture of a partly converted kingdom in an unconverted world; of good fish and bad in the very kingdom-net itself. (3) The method of the extension of the kingdom is given in the first parable. It is by sowing seed, not by mingling leaven. The symbols have, in Scripture, a meaning fixed by inspired usage. Leaven is the principle of corruption working subtly; is invariably used in a bad sense (see "Leaven," (See Scofield on {1.19.3}), and is defined by our Lord as evil doctrine. {40.16.11}; {40.16.12}; {41.8.15}. Meal, on the contrary, was used in one of the sweet- savour offerings {3.2.1-3}. and was food for the priests {3.6.15-17}. A woman, in the bad ethical sense, always symbolizes something out of place, religiously, (See Scofield on {38.5.6}). In Thyatira it was a woman teaching (cf).; {66.2.20}; {66.17.1-6}. Interpreting the parable by these familiar symbols, it constitutes a warning that the true doctrine, given for nourishment of the children of the kingdom; {40.4.4}; {54.4.6}; {60.2.2} would be mingled with corrupt and corrupting false doctrine, and that officially, by the apostate church itself; {54.4.1-3}; {55.2.17}; {55.2.18}; {55.4.3}; {55.4.4}; {61.2.1-3}. 4 Leaven Summary: (1) Leaven, as a symbolic or typical substance, is always mentioned in the O.T. in an evil sense {1.19.3}, (See Scofield on {1.19.3}). (2) The use of the word in the N.T. explains its symbolic meaning. It is "malice and wickedness," as contrasted with "sincerity and truth" {46.5.6-8}, it is evil doctrine {40.16.12} in its three-fold form of Pharisasism, Sadduceeism, Herodianism; {40.16.6}; {41.8.15}. The leaven of the Pharisees was externalism in religion. {40.23.14}; {40.23.16}; {40.23.23-28} of the Sadducees, scepticism as to the supernatural and as to the Scriptures {40.22.23}; {40.22.29} of the Herodians, worldliness--a Herod party amongst the Jews; {40.22.16-21}; {41.3.6}. (3) The use of the word in {40.13.33} is congruous with its universal meaning.
world kosmos = mankind. (See Scofield on {40.4.8}). kingdom (See Scofield on {40.3.2}).
devil Satan. Br. diabolos, accuser. See note, {40.16.23}; {1.3.1}; {66.20.10}. (See Scofield on {66.20.10}). angels (See Scofield on {58.1.4}).
Son of man (See Scofield on {40.8.20}). angels (See Scofield on {58.1.4}). kingdom (See Scofield on {40.3.2}). them which do Sin. (See Scofield on {45.3.23}).

Then The kingdom does not become the kingdom of the "Father" until Christ, having "put all enemies under his feet," including the last enemy, death, has "delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father" {46.15.24-28}; {66.20.2}. There is triumph over death at the first resurrection {46.15.54}; {46.15.55} but death, "the last enemy," is not destroyed till the end of the millennium. {66.20.14}. righteous (See Scofield on {45.10.10}), Also, {51.3.4}; {53.1.5-10}

kingdom The interpretation of the parable of the treasure, which makes the buyer of the field to be a sinner who is seeking Christ, has no warrant in the parable itself. The field is defined ({40.13.38}) to be the world. The seeking sinner does not buy, but forsakes, the world to win Christ. Furthermore, the sinner has nothing to sell, nor is Christ for sale, nor is He hidden in a field, nor, having found Christ, does the sinner hide Him again (cf) {41.7.24}; {44.4.20}. At every point the interpretation breaks down. Our Lord is the buyer at the awful cost of His blood {60.1.18}, and Israel, especially Ephraim {24.31.5-12}; {24.31.18-20} the lost tribes hidden in "the field," the world ({40.13.38}), is the treasure; {2.19.5}; {19.135.4}. Again, as in the separation of tares and wheat, the angels are used; {40.24.31}; {24.16.16}. The divine Merchantman buys the field (world) for the sake of the treasure ({40.13.44}) {45.11.28}, beloved for the fathers’ sakes, and yet to be restored and saved. The note of joy ({40.13.44}) is also that of the prophets in view of Israel’s restoration. {5.30.9}; {23.49.13}; {23.52.1-3}; {23.62.4-7} {23.65.18}; {23.65.19}. (See "Israel,") {1.11.10}; {45.11.26}. kingdom (See Scofield on {40.3.2}).

pearls The true Church, "one body" formed by the Holy Spirit {46.12.12}; {46.12.13}. As Israel is the hid treasure, so the Church is the pearl of great cost. Covering the same period of time as the mysteries of the kingdom, is the mystery of the Church; {45.16.25}; {45.16.26}; {49.3.3-10}; {49.5.32}. Of the true Church a pearl is a perfect symbol: (1) A pearl is one, a perfect symbol of unity {46.10.17}; {46.12.12}; {46.12.13}; {49.4.4-6}. (2) a pearl is formed by the accretion, and that not mechanically, but vitally, through a living one, as Christ adds to the Church {44.2.41}; {44.2.47}; {44.5.14}; {44.11.24}; {49.2.21}; {51.2.19}. (3) Christ, having given Himself for the pearl, is now preparing it for presentation to Himself {49.5.25-27}. The kingdom is not the Church, but the true children of the kingdom during the fulfilment of these mysteries, baptized by one Spirit into one body {46.12.12}; {46.12.13} compose the true Church, the pearl. kingdom (See Scofield on {40.3.2}).

the kingdom of heaven The parable of the Net (Greek - δαιμονίζομαι-net) presents another view from that of the wheat and tares of the mysteries of the kingdom as the sphere of profession, but with this difference: there Satan was the active agent; here the admixture is more the result of the tendency of a movement to gather to itself that which is not really of it). The kingdom of heaven is like a net which, cast into the sea of humanity, gathers of every kind, good and bad, and these remain together in the net ({40.13.49}) and not merely in the sea, until the end of the age. It is not even a converted net, much less a converted sea. Infinite violence has been done to sound exegesis by the notion that the world is to be converted in this age. Against that notion stands our Lord’s own interpretation of the parables of the Sower, the Wheat and Tares, and the Net. Such, then, is the mystery form of the kingdom. (See Scofield on {40.3.2}; {40.6.33}). It is the sphere of Christian profession during this age. It is a mingled body of true and false, wheat and tares, good and bad. It is defiled by formalism, doubt, and worldliness. But within it Christ sees the true children of the true kingdom who, at the end, are to "shine forth as the sun." In the great field, the world, He sees the redeemed of all ages, but especially His hidden Israel, yet to be restored and blessed, Also, in this form of the kingdom, so unlike that which is to be, He sees the Church, His body and bride, and for joy He sells all that He has {47.8.9} and buys the field, the treasure, and the pearl. heaven (See Scofield on {40.3.2}).

Peter There is the Greek a play upon the words, "thou art Peter petros-- literally ’a little rock’, and upon this rock Petra I will build my church." He does not promise to build His church upon Peter, but upon Himself, as Peter is careful to tell us ({60.2.4-9}) church 2 (Greek - ἀπόλλυμι (ek="out of," kaleo ="to call"), an assembly of called out ones). The word is used of any assembly; the word itself implies no more, as, e.g., the town-meeting at Ephesus {44.19.39} and Israel, called out of Egypt and assembled in the wilderness {44.7.38}. Israel was a true "church," but not in any sense the N.T. church--the only point of similarity being that both were "called out" and by the same God. All else is contrast. A key is a badge of power or authority (cf) {23.22.22}; {66.3.7}. The apostolic history explains and limits this trust, for it was Peter who opened the door of Christian opportunity to Israel on the day of Pentecost {44.2.38-42} and to Gentiles in the house of Cornelius. {44.10.34-46}. There was no assumption by Peter of any other authority {44.15.7-11}. In the council James, not Peter, seems to have presided; {44.15.19}; {48.2.11-15}. Peter claimed no more for himself than to be an apostle by gift {60.1.1} and an elder by office {60.5.1}. The power of binding and loosing was shared {40.18.18}; {43.20.23} by the other disciples. That it did not involve the determination of the eternal destiny of souls is clear from {66.1.18}. The keys of death and the place of departed spirits are held by Christ alone. kingdom (See Scofield on {40.3.2}).

was transfigured
The transfiguration scene contains, in miniature, all the elements of the future kingdom in manifestation:
(1) the Lord, not in humiliation, but in glory ({40.17.2}).
(2) Moses, glorified, representative of the redeemed who have passed through death into the kingdom. {40.13.43}; {42.9.30}; {42.9.31}.
(3) Elijah, glorified, representative of the redeemed who have entered the kingdom by translation. {46.15.50-53}; {52.4.14-17}.
(4) Peter, James, and John, not glorified, representatives (for the moment) of Israel in the flesh in the future kingdom {26.37.21-27}.
(5) The multitude at the foot of the mountain {40.17.2}, representative of the nations who are to be brought into the kingdom after it is established over Israel {23.11.10-12}, etc.

(2) But John the Baptist had come already, and with a ministry so completely in the spirit and power of Elijah’s future ministry {42.1.17} that in an adumbrative and typical sense it could be said: "Elias is come already." Cf; {40.10.40}; {57.1.12}; {57.1.17} where the same thought of identification, while yet preserving personal distinction, occurs. {43.1.27}

Tell us The beginning of the Olivet Discourse Matthew 24 with {42.21.20-24} answers the threefold question. The order is as follows: "when shall these things be?"--i.e. destruction of the temple and city. Answer: {42.21.20-24}. Second and third questions: "And what shall be the sign of thy coming, and of the end of the age?" Answer: {40.24.4-33}. {40.24.4-14} have a double interpretation: They give: (1) the character of the age--wars, international conflicts, famines, pestilences, persecutions, and false Christs (cf) {27.9.26}. This is not the description of a converted world. (2) But the same answer ({40.24.4-14}) applies in a specific way to the end of the age, viz. Daniel’s seventieth week. {27.9.24-27}. (See Scofield on {27.9.24}). All that has characterized the age gathers into awful intensity at the end. {40.24.14} has specific reference to the proclamation of the good news that the kingdom is again "at hand" by the Jewish remnant {23.1.9}; {66.14.6}; {66.14.7}. (See Scofield on {45.11.5}). {40.24.15} gives the sign of the abomination, (See Scofield on {27.9.27}), the "man of sin," or "Beast" {53.2.3-8}; {27.9.27}; {27.12.11}; {66.13.4-7}. This introduces the great tribulation {19.2.5}. (See Scofield on {66.7.14}), which runs its awful course of three and a half years, culminating in the battle of (See Scofield on {66.19.19}) at which time Christ becomes the smiting Stone of {27.2.34}. The detail of this period ({40.24.15-28}) is: (1) The abomination in the holy place ({40.24.15}); (2) the warning ({40.24.16-20}) to believing Jews who will then be in Jerusalem; (3) the great tribulation, with renewed warning as to false Christs ({40.24.21-26}); (4) the sudden smiting of the Gentile world-power ({40.24.27}; {40.24.28}); (5) the glorious appearing of the Lord, visible to all nations, and the regathering of Israel ({40.24.29-31}); (6) the sign of the fig-tree ({40.24.32}; {40.24.33}); (7) warnings, applicable to this present age over which these events are ever impending ({40.24.34-51}). {50.4.5}. Careful study of Daniel 2, 7, 9, and Revelation 13 will make the interpretation clear. See, also, "Remnant" ({23.1.9}; {45.11.5}).

remission Forgiveness. Summary: The Greek word translated "remission" in {40.26.28}; {44.10.43}; {58.9.22} is elsewhere rendered "forgiveness." It means, to send off, or away. And this, throughout Scripture, is the one fundamental meaning of forgiveness--to separate the sin from the sinner. Distinction must be made between divine and human forgiveness: (1) Human forgiveness means the remission of penalty. In the Old Testament and the New, in type and fulfilment, the divine forgiveness follows the execution of the penalty. "The priest shall make an atonement for his sin that he had committed, and it shall be forgiven him" {3.4.35}. "This is my blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many for the remission sending away, forgiveness of sins" ({40.25.28}). "Without shedding of blood there is no remission" {58.9.22}. See "Sacrifice" (See Scofield on {1.4.4}); {1.4.4} (See Scofield on {58.10.18}). The sin of the justified believer interrupts his fellowship, and is forgiven upon confession, but always on the ground of Christ’s propitiating sacrifice; {62.1.6-9}; {62.2.2}. (2) Human forgiveness rests upon and results from the divine forgiveness. In many passages this is assumed rather than stated, but the principle is declared in {49.4.32}; {40.18.32}; {40.18.33}. sins Sin. (See Scofield on {45.3.23}).

The three find the stone rolled away, and Mary Magdalene goes to tell the disciples. {42.23.55} to {42.24.9}; {43.20.1}; {43.20.2}. records.o: Book Introduction - Mark WRITER: The writer of the second Gospel, Mark, called also John, was the son of one the New Testament "Marys", and nephew of Barnabas. He was an associate of the apostles, and is mentioned in the writings of Paul and of Luke {44.12.12}; {44.12.25}; {44.15.37}; {44.15.39}; {51.4.10}; {55.4.11}; {57.1.24}. DATE: The date of Mark has been variously placed between A.D. 57 and 63. THEME: The scope and purpose of the book are evident from its contents. In it Jesus is seen as the mighty Worker, rather than as the unique Teacher. It is the Gospel of Jehovah’s "Servant the Branch" {38.3.8} as Matthew is the Gospel of the "Branch.. .unto David" {24.33.15}. Everywhere the servant character of the incarnate Son is manifest. The key verse is {41.10.45}. "For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister." The characteristic word is "straightway," a servant’s word. There is no genealogy, for who gives the genealogy of a servant? The distinctive character of Christ in Mark is that set forth in {50.2.6-8}. But this lowly Servant, who emptied Himself of the "form of God," "and was found in fashion as a man," was, nevertheless, "the mighty God" {23.9.6} as Mark distinctly declares ({41.1.1}) and therefore mighty works accompanied and authenticated His ministry. As befits a Servant-Gospel, Mark is characteristically a Gospel of deeds, rather than on words. The best preparation of the heart for the study of Mark is the prayerful reading of {23.42.1-21}; {23.50.4-11}; {23.52.13} to {23.53.12}; {38.3.8}; {50.2.5-8}. Mark is in five principal divisions: 1. The manifestation of the Servant-Son, {41.1.1-11}. 2. The Servant-Son tested as to His fidelity, {41.1.12-13}. 3. The Servant-Son at work, {41.1.14} to {41.13.37}. 4. The Servant-Son "obedient unto death," {41.14.1} to {41.15.47}. 5. The ministry of the risen Servant-Son, now exalted to all authority, {41.16.1-20}. 6. The events recorded in this book cover a period of 7 years.

records.o: Book Introduction - Luke WRITER: The writer of the third Gospel is called by Paul "the beloved physician" {51.4.14} and, as we learn from the Acts, was Paul’s frequent companion. He was of Jewish ancestry, but his correct Greek marks him as a Jew of the dispersion. Tradition says that he was a Jew of Antioch, as Paul was of Tarsus. DATE: The date of Luke falls between A.D. 63 and 68. THEME: Luke is the Gospel of the human-divine One, as John is of the divine-human One. The key-phrase is "Son of man," and the key-verse {42.19.10}. "For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost." In harmony with this intent, Luke relates those things concerning Jesus which demonstrate how entirely human He was. His genealogy is traced to Adam, and the most detailed account is given of His mother, and of His infancy and boyhood. The parables peculiar to Luke have distinctively the human and the seeking note. But Luke is careful to guard the Deity and Kingship of Jesus Christ {42.1.32-35}. Luke, then, is the Gospel of "the man whose name is The BRANCH" {38.6.12}. Luke has seven chief divisions: 1. The Evangelist’s Introduction, {42.1.1-4}. 2. The human relationships of Jesus, {42.1.5} to {42.2.52}. 3. The baptism, ancestry, and testing of Jesus, {42.3.1} to {42.4.13}. 4. The ministry of the Son of man as Prophet-King in Galilee, {42.4.14} to {42.9.50}. 5. The final offer of the Son of man as King to israel, His rejection and sacrifice, {42.19.45} to {42.23.56}. 6. The resurrection, resurrection ministry, and ascension of the Son of man, {42.24.1-53}. The events recorded in this book cover a period of 39 years.

v: from "From the very first": (Greek - ἄνωθεν," "from above)." So translated in {43.3.31}; {43.19.11}; {59.1.17}; {59.3.15}; {59.3.17}. In no other place is ANOTHEN translated "from the very first." The use by Luke of anothen is an affirmation that his knowledge of these things, derived from those who had been eye-witnesses from the beginning {42.1.2} was confirmed by revelation. In like manner Paul had doubtless heard from the eleven the story of the institution of the Lord’s Supper, but he also had it by revelation from the Lord (cf) {46.11.23} and his writing, like Luke’s anothen knowledge, thus became first-hand, not traditional, merely. understanding (Greek - ἄνωθεν," lit). followed alongside of; or, closely traced. in order The words "in order" are emphatic, indicating Luke’s purpose to reduce to order the Gospel story.

just and devout righteousness The O.T. righteousness. Summary: In the O.T. "righteous" and "just" are English words used to translate the Hebrew words yasher, "upright"; tsadiq, "just"; tsidkah, "righteous." In all of these words but one idea inheres: the righteous, or just, man is so called, because he is right with God; and he is right with God because he has walked "in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless" {42.1.6}; {45.10.5}; {50.3.6}. The O.T. righteous man was not sinless {21.7.20}, but one who, for all his sins, resorted to the ordinances, and offered in faith the required sacrifice (e.g.) {3.4.27-35} CF. "Righteousness (N.T.), (See Scofield on {45.10.10}) and Paul’s contrast, {50.3.4-9}.

son of Heli In Matthew, where unquestionably we have the genealogy of Joseph, we are told {40.1.16}, that Joseph was the son of Jacob. In what sense, then, could he be called in Luke "the son of Heli"? He could not be by natural generation the son both of Jacob and of Heli. But in Luke it is not said that Heli begat Joseph, so that the natural explanation is that Joseph was the son-in-law of Heli, who was, like himself, a descendant of David. That he should in that case be called "son of Heli" ("son" is not in the Greek, but rightly supplied by the translators) would be in accord with Jewish usage. (CF) {9.24.16} The conclusion is therefore inevitable that in Luke we have Mary’s genealogy; and Joseph was "son of Heli" because espoused to Heli’s daughter. The genealogy in Luke is Mary’s, whose father, Heli, was descended from David.

teach us to pray This is the central N.T. passage on prayer. In the Sermon on the Mount Christ had announced the new basis of prayer, viz.: relationship {40.6.9}; {40.6.28-32}. The believer is a child of God through the new birth. (See Scofield on {43.3.3}). The clear revelation of this fact at once establishes the reasonableness of prayer; a reasonableness against which the argument from the apparent uniformity of natural law shatters itself. God is more than a Creator, bringing a universe into being, and establishing laws for it; more than a decree- maker determining future events by an eternal fiat. Above all this is the divine family for whom the universe with its laws exists; {51.1.16-20}; {58.1.2}; {58.2.10}; {58.2.11}; {45.8.17}". When ye pray, say, Our Father." What God habitually does in the material universe concerns the reverent investigator of that universe. What He may do in His own family concerns Him, and them, and is matter for divine promise and revelation. Science, which deals only with natural phenomena, cannot intrude there {46.2.9}. Christ’s law of prayer may be thus summarized: (1) He grounds prayer upon relationship, and reveals God as freely charging himself with all the responsibilities, as His heart glows with all the affections of a Father toward all who believe on Jesus Christ {40.6.25}; {40.6.32}; {40.7.9-11}. Prayer, therefore, is a child’s petition to an all-wise, all-loving, and all-powerful, Father-God. (2) In the so-called Lord’s prayer Christ gives an incomparable model for all prayer. It teaches that right prayer begins with worship; puts the interest of the kingdom before merely personal interest; accepts beforehand the Father’s will, whether to grant or withhold; and petitions for present need, leaving the future to the Father’s care and love. Used as a form, the Lord’s prayer is, dispensationally, upon legal, not church ground; it is not a prayer in the name of Christ (cf) {43.14.13}; {43.14.14}; {43.16.24} and it makes human forgiveness, as under the law it must, the condition of divine forgiveness; an order which grace exactly reverses (cf) {49.4.32}. (3) Prayer is to be definite {42.11.5}; {42.11.6} and, (4) importunate, that is undiscouraged by delayed answers.

give It is evident that none of the disciples, with the possible exception of Mary of Bethany, asked for the Spirit in the faith of this promise. It was a new and staggering thing to a Jew that, in advance of the fulfilment of {29.2.28}; {29.2.29} all might receive the Spirit. Mary alone of the disciples understood Christ’s repeated declaration concerning His own death and resurrection {43.12.3-7}. Save Mary, not one of the disciples but Peter, and he only in the great confession {40.16.16} manifested a spark of spiritual intelligence till after the resurrection of Christ and the impartation of the Spirit; {43.20.22}; {44.2.1-4}. To go back to the promise of {42.11.13}, is to forget Pentecost, and to ignore the truth that now every believer has the indwelling Spirit; {45.8.9}; {45.8.15}; {46.6.19}; {48.4.6}; {62.2.20}; {62.2.27}. hell (Greek - ᾅδης, "the unseen world," is revealed as the place of departed human spirits between death and resurrection). The word occurs, {40.11.23}; {40.16.18}; {42.10.15}; {44.2.27}; {44.2.31}; {66.1.18}; {66.6.8}; {66.20.13}; {66.20.14} and is the equivalent of the O.T. "sheol." (See Scofield on {35.2.5}). The Septuagint invariably renders sheol by hades. Summary: (1) Hades before the ascension of Christ. The passages in which the word occurs make it clear that hades was formerly in two divisions, the abodes respectively of the saved and of the lost. The former was called "paradise" and "Abraham’s bosom." Both designations were Talmudic, but adopted by Christ in {42.16.22}; {42.23.43}. The blessed dead were with Abraham, they were conscious and were "comforted" {42.16.25}. The believing malefactor was to be, that day, with Christ in "paradise." The lost were separated from the saved by a "great gulf fixed" {42.16.26}. The representative man of the lost who are now in hades is the rich man of {42.16.19-31}. He was alive, conscious, in the full exercise of his faculties, memory, etc., and in torment. (2) Hades since the ascension of Christ. So far as the unsaved dead are concerned, no change of their place or condition is revealed in Scripture. At the judgment of the great white throne, hades will give them up, they will be judged, and will pass into the lake of fire {66.20.13}; {66.20.14}. But a change has taken place which affects paradise. Paul was "caught up to the third heaven.. .into paradise" {47.12.1-4}. Paradise, therefore, is now in the immediate presence of God. It is believed that {49.4.8-10} indicates the time of the change. "When he ascended up on high he led a multitude of captives." It is immediately added that He had previously "descended first into the lower parts of the earth," i.e. the paradise division of Hades. During the present church-age the saved who died are "absent from the body, at home with the Lord." The wicked dead in hades, and the righteous dead "at home with the Lord," alike await the resurrection; {18.19.25}; {46.15.52}. (See Scofield on {40.5.22}).

(Greek - ἐντός = "in the midst)." It could not be said of a self-righteous, Christ rejecting pharisee, that the kingdom of God, as to its spiritual content, was within him. Our Lord’s whole answer, designedly enigmatic to the Pharisees (cf) {40.13.10-13} had a dispensational meaning. The kingdom in its outward form, as covenanted to David {10.7.8-17} and described by the prophets (See Scofield on {38.12.8}) had been rejected by the Jews; so that, during this present age, it would not "come with observation" (lit. "outward show") but in the hearts of men (cf); {42.19.11}; {42.19.12}; {44.1.6-8}. (See Scofield on {44.1.6}; {45.14.17}). Meantime, the kingdom was actually "in the midst" of the Pharisees in the persons of the King and His disciples. within you in the midst of.

The Jewish age was marked by temporal blessings as the reward of an obedient people. {5.28.1-15}. records.o: Book Introduction - John WRITER: The fourth Gospel was written by the Apostle John {43.21.24}. This has been questioned on critical grounds, but on the same grounds and with equal scholarship, the early date and Johanean authorship have been maintained. DATE: The date of John’s Gospel falls between A.D. 85 and 90. Probably the latter. THEME: This is indicated both in the Prologue ({43.1.1-14}), and in the last verse of the Gospel proper ({43.20.31}), and is: The incarnation of the eternal Word, and Son of life; (2) that as many as believe on Him as "the Christ, the Son of God" ({43.20.31}) may have eternal life. The prominent words are, "believed" and "life." The book is in seven natural divisions: 1. Prologue: The eternal Word incarnate in Jesus the Christ, {43.1.1-14}. 2. The witness of John the Baptist, {43.1.15-34}. 3. The public ministry of Christ, {43.1.35} to {43.12.50}. 4. The private ministry of Christ to His own, {43.13.1} to {43.17.26}. 5. The sacrifice of Christ, {43.18.1} to {43.19.42}. 6. The manifestation of Christ in resurrection, {43.20.1-31}. 7. Epilogue: Christ the Master of life and service, {43.21.1-25}. The events recorded in this book cover a period of 7 years.

v: Word Gr. "Logos" (arm. "Memra," used in the Targums, or Heb. paraphrases, for God). The Greek term means, (1) a thought or concept; (2) the expression or utterance of that thought. As a designation of Christ, therefore, Logos is peculiarly felicitous because, (1) in Him are embodied all the treasures of the divine wisdom, the collective "thought" of God {46.1.24}; {49.3.11}; {51.2.2}; {51.2.3} and, (2) He is from eternity, but especially in His incarnation, the utterance or expression of the Person, and "thought" of Deity {43.1.3-5}; {43.1.9}; {43.1.14-18}; {43.14.9-11}; {51.2.9}. In the Being, Person, and work of Christ, Deity is told out.

grace Grace. Summary: (1) Grace is "the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man.. . not by works of righteousness which we have done" {56.3.4}; {56.3.5}. It is, therefore, constantly set in contrast to law, under which God demands righteousness from man, as, under grace, he gives righteousness to man {45.3.21}; {45.3.22}; {45.8.4}; {50.3.9}. Law is connected with Moses and works; grace with Christ and faith; {43.1.17}; {45.10.4-10}. Law blesses the good; grace saves the bad; {2.19.5}; {49.2.1-9}. Law demands that blessings be earned; grace is a free gift; {5.28.1-6}; {49.2.8}; {45.4.4}; {45.4.5}. (2) As a dispensation, grace begins with the death and resurrection of Christ {45.3.24-26} {45.4.24}; {45.4.25}. The point of testing is no longer legal obedience as the condition of salvation, but acceptance or rejection of Christ, with good works as a fruit of salvation,; {43.1.12}; {43.1.13}; {43.3.36}; {40.21.37}; {40.22.24}; {43.15.22}; {43.15.25}; {58.1.2}; {62.5.10-12}. The immediate result of this testing was the rejection of Christ by the Jews, and His crucifixion by Jew and Gentile {44.4.27}. The predicted end of the testing of man under grace is the apostasy of the professing church: See "Apostasy" (See Scofield on {55.3.1}) {55.3.1-8} and the resultant apocalyptic judgments. (3) Grace has a twofold manifestation: in salvation {45.3.24} and in the walk and service of the saved {45.6.15}. See, for the other six dispensations: Innocence, (See Scofield on {1.1.28}). Conscience, (See Scofield on {1.3.23}). Human Government, (See Scofield on {1.8.21}). Promise, (See Scofield on {1.12.1}). Law, (See Scofield on {2.19.8}). Kingdom, (See Scofield on {49.1.10}).

However gifted, moral, or refined, the natural man is absolutely blind to spiritual truth, and impotent to enter the kingdom; for he can neither obey, understand, nor please God {43.3.3}; {43.3.5}; {43.3.6}; {19.51.5}; {24.17.9}; {41.7.21-23}; {46.2.14}; {45.8.7}; {45.8.8}; {49.2.3} (See Scofield on {40.6.33}). I am the door of the sheep The shepherd work of our Lord has three aspects: (1) As the "Good" Shepherd He gives His life for the sheep {43.10.11} and is, therefore, "the door" by which "if any man enter in he shall be saved." {43.10.9}. This answers to Psalms 22. (2) He is the "Great" Shepherd, "brought again from the dead" {58.13.20} to care for and make perfect the sheep. This answers to Psalms 23. (3) He is the "Chief" Shepherd, who is coming in glory to give crowns of reward to the faithful shepherds {60.5.4}. This answers to Psalms 24.

Except John 12-17 are a progression according to the order of approach to God in the tabernacle types: John 12, in which Christ speaks of His death, answers to the brazen altar of burnt-offering, type of the cross. Passing from the altar toward the holy of holies, the laver is next reached {2.30.17-21}, answering to John 13. With His associate priests, now purified, the High Priest approaches and enters the holy place, in the high communion of John 14-16. Entering alone the holy of holies {43.17.1}, the High Priest intercedes. (Cf) {58.7.24-28}. That intercession is not for the salvation, but the keeping and blessing of those for whom He prays. His death (assumed as accomplished), {43.17.4} has saved them.

needeth The underlying imagery is of an oriental returning from the public baths to his house. His feet would contract defilement and require cleansing, but not his body. So the believer is cleansed as before the law from all sin "once for all" {58.10.1-12} but needs ever to bring his daily sins to the Father in confession, that he may abide in unbroken fellowship with the Father and with the Son {62.1.1-10}. The blood of Christ answers forever to all the law could say as to the believer’s guilt, but he needs constant cleansing from the defilement of sin,; {49.5.25-27}; {62.5.6}. Typically, the order of approach to the presence of God was, first, the brazen altar of sacrifice, and then the laver of cleansing {2.40.6}; {2.40.7}. See, also, the order in {2.30.17-21}. Christ cannot have communion with a defiled saint, but He can and will cleanse him. washed Lit. bathed. The Greek word signifies a complete ablution. "Wash" is another word.

abide To abide in Christ is, on the one hand, to have no known sin unjudged and unconfessed, no interest into which He is not brought, no life which He cannot share. On the other hand, the abiding one takes all burdens to Him, and draws all wisdom, life and strength from Him. It is not unceasing consciousness of these things, and of Him, but that nothing is allowed in the life which separates from Him. See "Fellowship," {62.1.3}. See "Communion," {46.10.16}.

The minor moralities and graces of Christianity are often imitated, but never the ninefold "fruit" of {48.5.22}; {48.5.23}. Where such fruit is the Father glorified. The Pharisees were moral and intensely "religious," but not one of them could say with Christ, "I have glorified thee on the earth" {43.17.4}.

Having accomplished the sacrifice, He was on His way to present the sacred blood in heaven, and that, between the meeting with Mary in the garden and the meeting of {40.28.9}. He had so ascended and returned: a view in harmony with types. (2) That Mary Magdalene, knowing as yet only Christ after the flesh {47.5.15-17} and having found her Beloved, sought only to hold Him so; while He, about to assume a new relation to His disciples in ascension, gently teaches Mary that now she must not seek to hold Him to the earth, but rather become His messenger of the new joy. (3) That He merely meant: "Do not detain me now; I am not yet ascended; you will see me again; run rather to my brethren," etc. Touch me not Or, do not detain me.

records.o: Book Introduction - Acts WRITER: In the Acts of the Apostles Luke continues the account of Christianity begun in the Gospel which bears his name. In the "former treatise" he tells what Jesus "began both to do and teach"; in the Acts, what Jesus continued to do and teach through His Holy Spirit sent down. DATE: The Acts concludes with the account of Paul’s earliest ministry in Rome, A.D. 65, and appears to have been written at or near that time. THEME: This book records the ascension and promised return of the Lord Jesus, the descent of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, Peter’s use of the keys, opening the kingdom (considered as the sphere of profession, as in Matthew 13) to the Jews at Pentecost, and to the Gentiles in the house of Cornelius; the beginning of the Christian church and the conversion and ministry of Paul. The Holy Spirit fills the scene. As the presence of the Son, exalting and revealing the Father, is the great fact of the Gospels, so the presence of the Spirit, exalting and revealing the Son, is the great fact of the Acts. Acts is in two chief parts: 1. In the first section ({44.1.1} to {44.9.43}) Peter is the prominent personage, Jerusalem is the center, and the ministry is to Jews. Already in covenant relations with Jehovah, they had sinned in rejecting Jesus as the Christ. The preaching, therefore, was directed to that point, and repentance (i.e. "a changed mind") was demanded. The apparent failure of the Old Testament promises concerning the Davidic kingdom was explained by the promise that the kingdom would be set up at the return of Christ ({44.2.25-31}; {44.15.14-16}). This ministry to Israel fulfilled {42.19.12-14}. In the persecutions of the apostles and finally in the martyrdom of Stephen, the Jews sent after the king the message, "We will not have this man to reign over us." 2. In the second division ({44.10.1} to {44.28.31}) Paul is prominent, a new center is established at Antioch, and the ministry is chiefly to Gentiles who, as "strangers from the covenants of promise" ({49.2.12}), had but to "believe on the Lord Jesus Christ" to be saved. Acts 11-15 of this section are transitional, establishing finally the distinction, doctrinally, between law and grace. Galatians should be read in this connection. The events recorded in The Acts cover a period of 32 years.

come The two Advents--Summary: (1) The O.T. foreview of the coming Messiah is in two aspects--that of rejection and suffering (as e.g. in Is 53), and that of earthly glory and power (as e.g. In Is 11 Jeremiah 23 Ezekiel 37). Often these two aspects blend in one passage (e.g. Psalms 2). The prophets themselves were perplexed by this seeming contradiction {60.1.10}; {60.1.11}. It was solved by partial fulfilment. In due time the Messiah, born of a virgin according to Isaiah, appeared among men and began His ministry by announcing the predicted kingdom as "at hand." (See Scofield on {40.4.17}). The rejection of King and kingdom followed. (2) Thereupon the rejected King announced His approaching crucifixion, resurrection, departure, and return (Matthew 24, 25). {40.12.38-40}; {40.16.1-4}; {40.16.21}; {40.16.27}; {42.12.35-46}; {42.17.20-36}; {42.18.31-34}; {42.19.12-27}. (3) He uttered predictions concerning the course of events between His departure and return {40.13.1-50}; {40.16.18}; {40.24.4-26} (4) This promised return of Christ becomes a prominent theme in the Acts, Epistles, and Revelation. Taken together, the N.T. teachings concerning the return of Jesus Christ may be summarized as follows: (1) That return is an event, not a process, and is personal and corporeal {40.23.39}; {40.24.30}; {40.25.31}; {41.14.62}; {42.17.24}; {43.14.3}; {44.1.11}; {50.3.20}; {50.3.21}; {52.4.14-17}. (2) His coming has a threefold relation: to the church, to Israel, to the nations. (a) To the church the descent of the Lord into the air to raise the sleeping and change the living saints is set forth as a constant expectation and hope {40.24.36}; {40.24.44}; {40.24.48-51}; {40.25.13}; {46.15.51}; {46.15.52}; {50.3.20}; {52.1.10}; {52.4.14-17}; {54.6.14}; {56.2.13}; {66.22.20}. (b) To Israel, the return of the Lord is predicted to accomplish the yet unfulfilled prophecies of her national regathering, conversion, and establishment in peace and power under the Davidic Covenant {44.15.14-17} with {38.14.1-9}. See "Kingdom (O.T.)" {10.7.8-17}. (See Scofield on {38.13.8}). {42.1.31-33} (See Scofield on {46.15.24}). (c) To the Gentile nations the return of Christ is predicted to bring the destruction of the present political world-system {27.2.34}; {27.2.35}. (See Scofield on {66.19.11}), the judgment of {40.25.31-46} followed by world-wide Gentile conversion and participation in the blessings of the kingdom; {23.2.2-4}; {23.11.10}; {23.60.3}; {38.8.3}; {38.8.20}; {38.8.23}; {38.14.16-21}.

Holy Ghost The Holy Spirit, N.T. Summary (see {39.2.15}, note): (See Scofield on {39.2.15}). (1) The Holy Spirit is revealed as a divine Person. This is expressly declared (e.g.) {43.14.16}; {43.14.17}; {43.14.26}; {43.15.26}; {43.16.7-15}; {40.28.19} and everywhere implied. (2) The revelation concerning Him is progressive (a) In the O.T. (See Scofield on {39.2.15}). He comes upon whom He will, apparently without reference to conditions in them (b) During His earth-life, Christ taught His disciples {42.11.13} that they might receive the Spirit through prayer to the Father. (c) At the close of His ministry He promised that He would Himself pray the Father, and that in answer to prayer the Comforter would come to abide {43.14.16}; {43.14.17}. (d) On the evening of His resurrection He came to the disciples in the upper room, and breathed on them saying, "Receive ye the Holy Ghost" {43.20.22} but instructed them to wait before beginning their ministry till the Spirit should come upon them; {42.24.49}; {44.1.8}. (e) On the day of Pentecost the Spirit came upon the whole body of believers {44.2.1-4} (f) After Pentecost, so long as the Gospel was preached to Jews only, the Spirit was imparted to such as believed by the laying on of hands {44.8.17}; {44.9.17}. (g) When Peter opened the door of the kingdom to the Gentiles (Acts 10.), the Holy Spirit, without delay, or other condition than faith, was given to those who believed. {44.10.44}; {44.11.15-18}. This is the permanent fact for the entire church age. Every believer is born of the Spirit; {43.3.3}; {43.3.6}; {62.5.1} indwelt by the Spirit, whose presence makes the believer’s body a temple; {46.6.19}; {45.8.9-15}; {62.2.27}; {48.4.6} and baptized by the Spirit; {46.12.12}; {46.12.13}; {62.2.20}; {62.2.27} thus sealing him for God; {49.1.13}; {49.4.30}. (3) The N.T. distinguishes between having the Spirit, which is true of all believers, and being filled with the Spirit, which is the believer’s privilege and duty (cf) {44.2.4} with; {44.4.29-31}; {49.1.13}; {49.1.14} with {49.5.18}. --"One baptism, many fillings." (4) The Holy Spirit is related to Christ in His Conception {40.1.18-20}; {42.1.35} baptism; {40.3.16}; {41.1.10}; {42.3.22}; {43.1.32}; {43.1.33} walk and service {42.4.1}; {42.4.14} resurrection {45.8.11}, and as His witness throughout this age; {43.15.26}; {43.16.8-11}; {43.16.13}; {43.16.14}. (5) The Spirit forms the church {40.16.18} (See Scofield on {58.12.23}) by baptizing all believers into the body of Christ {46.12.12}; {46.12.13} imparts gifts for service to every member of that body {46.12.7-11}; {46.12.27}; {46.12.30} guide the members in their service; {42.2.27}; {42.4.1}; {44.16.6}; {44.16.7} and is Himself the power of that service; {44.1.8}; {44.2.4}; {46.2.4}. (6) The Spirit abides in the company of believers who constitute a local church, making of them, corporately, a temple {46.3.16}; {46.3.17}. (7) Christ indicates a threefold personal relationship of the Spirit to the believer: "With", "In", "upon" {43.14.17}; {42.24.49}; {44.1.8}. "With" indicates the approach of God to the soul, convicting of sin {43.16.9} presenting Christ as the object of faith {43.16.14} imparting faith {49.2.8} and regenerating {43.3.3-16}. "In" describes the abiding presence of the Spirit in the believer’s body {46.6.19} to give victory over the flesh; {45.8.2-4}; {48.5.16}; {48.5.17} to create the Christian character {48.5.22}; {48.5.23} to help infirmities {45.8.26} to inspire prayer {49.6.18} to give conscious access to God {49.2.18} to actualize to the believer his sonship {48.4.6} to apply the Scripture in cleansing and sanctification; {49.5.26}; {53.2.13}; {60.1.2} to comfort and intercede; {44.9.31}; {45.8.26} and to reveal Christ {43.16.14}. (8) Sins against the Spirit committed by unbelievers are: To blaspheme {40.12.31}, resist {44.7.51}, insult {58.10.29}, "despite," lit. insult). Believers’ sins against the Spirit are: To grieve Him by allowing evil in heart or life {49.4.30}; {49.4.31} and to quench Him by disobedience {52.5.19}. The right attitude toward the Spirit is yieldedness to His sway in walk and service, and in constant willingness that He shall "put away" whatever grieves Him or hinders His power {49.4.31}.
