said unto them The theme of Peter’s sermon at Pentecost is stated in {44.2.36}. It is, that Jesus is the Messiah. No message could have been more unwelcome to the Jews who had rejected His Messianic claims, and crucified Him. Peter, therefore, does not announce his theme until he has covered every possible Jewish objection. The point of difficulty with the Jews was the apparent failure of the clear and repeated prophetic promise of a regathered Israel established in their own land under their covenanted King (e.g).; {23.11.10-12}; {24.23.5-8}; {26.37.21-28}. Instead of explaining, as Rome first taught, followed by some Protestant commentators, that the covenant and promises were to be fulfilled in the church in a so-called "spiritual" sense, Peter shows {44.2.25-32} from Psalms 16. that David himself understood that the dead and risen Christ would fulfil the covenant and sit on his throne {42.1.32}; {42.1.33}. In precisely the same way James {44.15.14-17} met the same difficulty. See "Kingdom (O.T.)," {38.12.8} (N.T.),; {42.1.33}; {46.15.24}.

last days A distinction must be observed between "the last days" when the prediction relates to Israel, and the "last days" when the prediction relates to the church {54.4.1-3}; {55.3.1-8}; {58.1.1}; {58.1.2}; {60.1.4}; {60.1.5}; {61.3.1-9}; {62.2.18}; {62.2.19}; {65.1.17-19}. Also distinguish the expression the "last days" (plural) from "the last day" (singular); the latter expression referring to the resurrections and last judgment; {43.6.39}; {43.6.40}; {43.6.44}; {43.6.54}; {43.11.24}; {43.12.48}. The "last days" as related to the church began with the advent of Christ {58.1.2} but have especial reference to the time of declension and apostasy at the end of this age; {55.3.1}; {55.4.4}. The "last days" as related to Israel are the days of Israel’s exaltation and blessing, and are synonymous with the kingdom-age; {23.2.2-4}; {33.4.1-7}. They are "last" not with reference to this dispensation, but with reference to the whole of Israel’s history.

And he shall The appeal here is national to the Jewish people as such, not individuals as in Peter’s first sermon {44.2.38}; {44.2.39}. There those who were pricked in heart were exhorted to save themselves from (among) the untoward nation; here the whole people is addressed, and the promise to national repentance is national deliverance: "and he shall send Jesus Christ" to bring in the times which the prophets had foretold (See Scofield on {44.2.14}). The official answer was the imprisonment of the apostles, and the inhibition to preach, so fulfilling {42.19.14}.

voice Cf {44.22.9}; {44.26.14}. A contradiction has been imagined. The three statements should be taken together. The men heard the "voice" as a sound (Greek - ἀναφωνέω), but did not hear the "voice" as articulating the words, "Saul, Saul," etc).

that he is the Son of God Cf. {44.2.36}. Peter, while maintaining the deity of Jesus--"God hath made that same Jesus, whom ye have crucified, both Lord and Christ"--gives especial prominence to His Messiahship. Paul, fresh from the vision of the glory, puts the emphasis on His Deity. Peter’s charge was that the Jews had crucified the Son of David {44.2.25-30} Paul’s that they had crucified the Lord of glory {46.2.8}. In the A.V. the sense is largely lost. The point was, not that the Christ was God, a truth plainly taught by Isaiah.; {23.7.14}; {23.9.6}; {23.9.7} but that Jesus, the crucified Nazarene, was the Christ and therefore God the Son.

(3) {44.15.1-30}; {48.2.2-10}. (4) {44.21.17} to {44.23.35}.

While Peter yet spake {44.10.44} is one of the pivotal points of Scripture. Heretofore the Gospel has been offered to Jews only, and the Holy Spirit bestowed upon believing Jews through apostolic mediation. But now the normal order for this age is reached: the Holy Spirit is given without delay, mediation, or other condition than simple faith in Jesus Christ. Cf. (See Scofield on {44.2.4}) {46.6.19}.

Men and brethren Dispensationally, this is the most important passage in the N.T. It gives the divine purpose for this age, and for the beginning of the next. (1) The taking out from among the Gentiles of a people for His name, the distinctive work of the present, or church-age. The church is the ecclesia--the "called-out assembly." Precisely this has been in progress since Pentecost. The Gospel has never anywhere converted all, but everywhere has called out some. (2) "After this viz. the out-calling I will return." James quotes from {30.9.11}; {30.9.12}. The verses which follow in Amos describe the final regathering of Israel, which the other prophets invariably connect with the fulfilment of the Davidic Covenant (e.g.); {23.11.1}; {23.11.10-12}; {24.23.5-8}. (3) "And will build again the tabernacle of David," i.e. re-establish the Davidic rule over Israel {10.7.8-17}; {42.1.31-33}. (4) "That the residue of men Israelites may seek after the Lord" cf {38.12.7}; {38.12.8}; {38.13.1}; {38.13.2}. (5) "And all the Gentiles," etc. cf {33.4.2}; {38.8.21}; {38.8.22}. The decision might be otherwise stated in the terms of {45.6.14}. "Ye are not under the law, but under grace." Gentile believers were to show grace by abstaining from the practices offensive to godly Jews. {44.15.20}; {44.15.21}; {44.15.28}; {44.15.29} cf; {45.14.12-17}; {46.8.1-13}

Epicureans Disciples of Epicurus, B.C. 342-271, who abandoned as hopeless the search by reason for pure truth, cf. {43.18.38} seeking instead true pleasure through experience. Stoicks Disciples of Zeno, B.C. 280, and Chrysippus, B.C. 240. This philosophy was founded on human self-sufficiency, inculcated stern self-repression, the solidarily of the race, and the unity of Deity. Epicureans and Stocis divided the apostolic world.

The reference is to the creation-work of God in which He made man (i.e. mankind, the race in Adam) in his own likeness, {1.1.26}; {1.1.27} thus rebuking the thought that "the Godhead is like unto gold," etc. The word "Father" is not used, not does the passage affirm anything concerning fatherhood or sonship, which are relationships based on faith, and the new birth. Repent Repentance is the trans. of a (Greek - γένος ("metanoia-metanoeo") meaning "to have another mind," "to change the mind," and is used in the N).T. to indicate a change of mind in respect of sin, of God, and of self. This change of mind may, especially in the case of Christians who have fallen into sin, be preceded by sorrow {47.7.8-11} but sorrow for sin, though it may "work" repentance, is not repentance. The son in {40.21.28}; {40.21.29} illustrates true repentance. Saving faith: (See Scofield on {58.11.39}) includes and implies that change of mind which is called repentance.

his own hired house It has been much disputed whether Paul endured two Roman imprisonments, from A.D. 62 to 68 or one. The tradition from Clement to Eusebius favours two imprisonments with a year of liberty between. Erdman (W.J.) has pointed out the leaving of Trophimus sick at Miletus, mentioned in {55.4.20} could not have been an occurrence of Paul’s last journey to Jerusalem, for then Trophimus was not left; {44.20.4}; {44.21.29} nor of the journey to Rome to appear before Caesar, for then he did not touch at Miletus. To make this incident possible there must have been a release from the first imprisonment, and an interval of ministry and travel.

records.o: Book Introduction - Romans WRITER: The Apostle Paul ({45.1.1}). DATE: Romans, the sixth in chronological order of Paul’s Epistles, was written from Corinth during the apostle’s third visit to that city. {47.13.1} in A.D. 60. The Epistle has its occasion in the intention of the apostle soon to visit Rome. Naturally, he would wish to announce before his coming the distinctive truths which had been revealed to and through him. He would desire the Christians in Rome to have his own statement of the great doctrines of grace so bitterly assailed everywhere by legalistic teachers. THEME: The theme of Romans is "the Gospel of God" ({45.1.1}), the very widest possible designation of the whole body of redemption truth, for it is He with whom is "no respect of persons"; and who is not "the God of the Jews only," but "of the Gentiles also"; {45.2.11}; {45.3.29}. Accordingly, "all the world" is found guilty {45.3.19}, and a redemption is revealed as wide as the need, upon the alone condition of faith. Not only does Romans embody in the fullest way the doctrines of grace in relation to salvation, but in three remarkable chapters (Romans 9-11.) the great promises to Israel are reconciled with the promises concerning the Gentiles, and the fulfilment of the former shown to await the completion of the church and coming of the Deliverer out of Zion {45.11.25-27}. The key-phrase is "the righteousness of God"; {45.1.17}; {45.3.21}; {45.3.22}. The Epistle, exclusive of the introduction ({45.1.1-17}), is in seven parts. 1. The whole world guilty before God, {45.1.18} to {45.3.20}. 2. Justification through the righteousness of God by faith, the Gospel remedy for guilt, {45.3.21} to {45.5.11}. 3. Crucifixion with Christ, the resurrection life of Christ, and the walk in the Spirit, the Gospel provision for inherent sin, {45.5.12} to {45.8.13}. 4. The full result in blessing of the Gospel, {45.8.14-39}. 5. Parenthesis: the Gospel does not abolish the covenant promises to Israel, {45.9.1} to {45.11.36}. 6. Christian life and service, Romans 12:1-15:33. The outflow of Christian love, Romans 16:1-27.

salvation The Heb. and (Greek - ἀλεκτοροφωνία, safety, preservation, healing, and soundness). Salvation is the great inclusive word of the Gospel, gathering into itself all the redemptive acts and processes: as justification, redemption, grace, propitiation, imputation, forgiveness, sanctification, and glorification. Salvation is in three tenses: (1) The believer has been saved from the guilt and penalty of sin {42.7.50}; {46.1.18}; {47.2.15}; {49.2.5}; {49.2.8}; {55.1.9} and is safe. (2) the believer is being saved from the habit and dominion of sin {45.6.14}; {50.1.19}; {50.2.12}; {50.2.13}; {53.2.13}; {45.8.2}; {48.2.19}; {48.2.20}; {47.3.18}. (3) The believer is to be saved in the sense of entire conformity to Christ. {45.13.11}; {58.10.36}; {60.1.5}; {62.3.2}. Salvation is by grace through faith, is a free gift, and wholly without works; {45.3.27}; {45.3.28}; {45.4.1-8}; {45.6.23}; {49.2.8}. The divine order is: first salvation, then works; {49.2.9}; {49.2.10}; {56.3.5-8}.

righteousness of God The righteousness of God is neither an attribute of God, not the changed character of the believer, but Christ Himself, who fully met in our stead and behalf every demand of the law, and who is, but the act of God called imputation {3.25.50}; {59.2.23}, "made unto us. . righteousness" {46.1.30}. "The believer in Christ is now, by grace, shrouded under so complete and blessed a righteousness that the law from Mt. Sinai can find neither fault nor diminution therein. This is that which is called the righteousness of God by faith."--Bunyan. {47.5.21}; {45.4.6}; {45.10.4}; {50.3.9}; {45.3.26}

sinned Sin, Summary: The literal meanings of the Heb. and (Greek - ἀλεκτοροφωνία sin," "sinner," etc)., disclose the true nature of sin in its manifold manifestations. Sin is transgression, an overstepping of the law, the divine boundary between good and evil {19.51.1}; {42.15.29}, iniquity, an act inherently wrong, whether expressly forbidden or not; error, a departure from right; {19.51.9}; {45.3.23}, missing the mark, a failure to meet the divine standard; trespass, the intrusion of self-will into the sphere of divine authority {49.2.1}, lawlessness, or spiritual anarchy {54.1.9}, unbelief, or an insult to the divine veracity {43.16.9}. Sin originated with Satan {23.14.12-14}, entered the world through Adam {45.5.12}, was, and is, universal, Christ alone excepted; {45.3.23}; {60.2.22}, incurs the penalties of spiritual and physical death; {1.2.17}; {1.3.19}; {26.18.4}; {26.18.20}; {45.6.23} and has no remedy but in the sacrificial death of Christ; {58.9.26}; {44.4.12} availed of by faith {44.13.38}; {44.13.39}. Sin may be summarized as threefold: An act, the violation of, or want of obedience to the revealed will of God; a state, absence of righteousness; a nature, enmity toward God.

Redemption Redemption, "to deliver by paying a price." The N.T. doctrine. The N.T. records the fulfilment of the O.T. types and prophecies of redemption through the sacrifice of Christ. The completed truth is set forth in the three words which are translated redemption (1) agorazo, "to purchase in the market." The underlying thought is of a slave-market. The subjects of redemption are "sold under sin" {45.7.14} but are, moreover, under sentence of death; {26.18.4},; {43.3.18}; {43.3.19}; {45.3.19}; {48.3.10}, and the purchase price is the blood of the Redeemer who dies in their stead; {48.3.13}; {47.5.21}; {40.20.28},; {41.10.45}; {54.2.6}; {60.1.18}. (2) exagorazo, "to buy out of the market." The redeemed are never again to be exposed to sale; (3) lutroo, "to loose," "to set free by paying a price" {43.8.32}; {48.4.4}; {48.4.5}; {48.4.31}; {48.5.13}; {45.8.21}. Redemption is by sacrifice and by power (See Scofield on {2.14.30}) Christ paid the price, the Holy Spirit makes deliverance actual in experience {45.8.2}. (See Scofield on {23.59.20}; {45.1.16}). grace Grace (in salvation), {45.4.4-16}; {45.3.24}. (See Scofield on {43.1.17}).

propitiation Lit. a propitiatory sacrifice, through faith by his blood; (Greek - ἱλαστήριον, "place of propitiation)." The word occurs, {62.2.2}; {62.4.10} as the trans. of hilasmos, "that which propitiates," "a propitiatory sacrifice." Hilasterion is used by the Septuagint, and {58.9.5} for "mercy-seat." The mercy-seat was sprinkled with atoning blood in the day of atonement {3.16.14} in token that the righteous sentence of the law had been (typically) carried out, so that what must else have been a judgment-seat could righteously be a mercy-seat; {58.9.11-15}; {58.4.14-16}, a place of communion {2.25.21}; {2.25.22}. In fulfilment of the type, Christ is Himself the hilasmos, "that which propitiates," and the hilasterion, "the place of propitiation" --the mercy-seat sprinkled with His own blood-- the token that in our stead He so honoured the law by enduring its righteous sentence that God, who ever foresaw the cross, is vindicated in having "passed over" sins from Adam to Moses {45.5.13} and the sins of believers under the old covenant (See Scofield on {2.29.33}) and just in justifying sinners under the covenant. There is no thought in propitiation of placating a vengeful God, but of doing right by His holy law and so making it possible for Him righteously to show mercy. remission passing over of sins done aforetime, i.e. since Adam. Cf. {58.9.15}.

righteousness "His righteousness" here is God’s consistency with His own law and holiness in freely justifying a sinner who believes in Christ; that is, one in whose behalf Christ has met every demand of the law {45.10.4}.

Justification Justification, Summary: Justification and righteousness are inseparably united in Scripture by the fact that the same word (dikaios, "righteous"; dikaioo, "to justify") is used for both. The believing sinner is justified because Christ, having borne his sins on the cross, has been "made unto him righteousness" {46.1.30}. Justification originates in grace; {45.3.24}; {56.3.4}; {56.3.5} is through the redemptive and propitiatory work of Christ, who has vindicated the law; {45.3.24}; {45.3.25}; {45.5.9} is by faith, not works; {45.3.28-30}; {45.4.5}; {45.5.1}; {48.2.16}; {48.3.8}; {48.3.24} and may be defined as the judicial act of God whereby He justly declares righteous one who believes on Jesus Christ. It is the Judge Himself {45.8.31-34} who thus declares. The justified believer has been in court, only to learn that nothing is laid to his charge. {45.8.1}; {45.8.33}; {45.8.34}.

Do we then The sinner establishes the law in its right use and honour by confessing his guilt, and acknowledging that by it he is justly condemned. Christ, on the sinner’s behalf, establishes the law by enduring its penalty, death. Cf. {40.5.17}; {40.5.18}.

works Cf. {59.2.24}. These are two aspects of one truth. Paul speaks of that which justifies man before God, viz.: faith alone, wholly apart from works; James of the proof before men, that he who professes to have justifying faith really has it. Paul speaks of what God sees--faith; James of what men see--works, as the visible evidence of faith. Paul draws his illustration from {1.15.6} James from {1.22.1-19}. James’ key phrase is "ye see" {59.2.24} for men cannot see faith except as manifested through works.

The "wherefore" relates back to {45.3.19-23} and may be regarded as a continuation of the discussion of the universality of sin, interrupted; {45.3.24} to {45.5.11}; by the passage on justification and its results. have sinned The first sin wrought the moral ruin of the race. The demonstration is simple. (1) Death is universal ({45.4.12}; {45.4.14}), all die: sinless infants, moral people, religious people, equally with the depraved. For a universal effect there must be a universal cause; that cause is a state of universal sin ({45.5.12}). (2) But this universal state must have had a cause. It did. The consequence of Adam’s sin was that "the many were made sinners" ({45.5.19})--"By the offence of one judgment came upon all men unto condemnation" ({45.5.18}). (3) Personal sins are not meant here. From Adam to Moses death reigned ({45.5.14}), although, there being no law, personal guilt was not imputed ({45.5.13}). Accordingly, from {1.4.7} to {2.29.14} the sin-offering is not once mentioned. Then, since physical death from Adam to Moses was not due to the sinful acts of those who die ({45.5.13}), it follows that it was due to a universal sinful state, or nature, and that state is declared to be out inheritance from Adam. (4) the moral state of fallen man is described in Scripture {1.6.5}; {11.8.46}; {19.14.1-3}; {19.39.5}; {24.17.9}; {40.18.11}; {41.7.20}; {41.7.23}; {45.1.21}; {45.2.1-29}; {45.3.9-19}; {45.7.24}; {45.8.7}; {43.3.6}; {46.2.14}; {47.3.14}; {47.4.4}; {48.5.19-21}; {49.2.1-3}; {49.2.11}; {49.2.12}; {49.4.18-22}; {51.1.21}; {58.3.13}; {59.4.14}; {46.15.22}.

Adam to Moses Broadly, the contrast is: Adam: sin, death; Christ: righteousness, life. Adam drew down into his ruin the old creation {45.8.19-22} of which he was lord and head. Christ brings into moral unity with God, and into eternal life, the new creation of which he is Lord and Head. {49.1.22}; {49.1.23}. Even the animal and material creation, cursed for man’s sake. {1.3.17} will be delivered by Christ.; {23.11.6-9}; {45.8.19-22}.

old self The expression occurs elsewhere, in {49.4.22}; {51.3.9} and always means the man of old, corrupt human nature, the inborn tendency to evil in all men. In {45.6.6} it is the natural man himself; in; {49.4.22}; {51.3.9} his ways. Positionally, in the reckoning of God, the old man is crucified, and the believer is exhorted to make this good in experience, reckoning it to be so by definitely "putting off" the old man and "putting on" the new; {51.3.8-14}; {51.3.4}; {51.3.24}, (See Scofield on {49.4.24}), note 3.

What then The old relation to the law and sin, and the new relation to Christ and life are illustrated by the effect of death upon servitude {45.6.16-23} and marriage {45.7.1-6}. (1) The old servitude was nominally to the law, but, since the law had no delivering power, the real master continued to be sin in the nature. The end was death. The law could not give life, and "sin" (here personified as the old self) is in itself deathful. But death in another form, ie., crucifixion with Christ, has intervened to free the servant from his double bondage to sin ({45.6.6}; {45.6.7}), and to the law {45.7.4}; {45.7.6} (2) This effect of death is further illustrated by widowhood. Death dissolves the marriage relation {45.7.1-3}. As natural death frees a wife from the law of her husband, so crucifixion with Christ sets the believer free from the law. (See Scofield on {48.3.24}).
sin Sin. (See Scofield on {45.3.23}). holiness sanctification. (See Scofield on {66.22.11}).
married joined. {49.5.31}, same Greek word. Bride (of Christ). {47.11.1-3}; {43.3.29}; {66.19.6-8}.

newness Cf. {45.2.29}; {47.3.6}. "The letter" is a Paulinism for the law, as "spirit" in these passages is his word for the relationships and powers of new life in Christ Jesus. In 2 Corinthians 3. a series is presented of contrast of law with "spirit," of the old covenant and the new. The contrast is not between two methods of interpretation, literal, and spiritual, but between two methods of divine dealing: one through the law, the other through the Holy Spirit.

when the commandment The passage ({45.7.7-25}) is autobiographical. Paul’s religious experience was in three strongly marked phases: (1) He was a godly Jew under the law. That the passage does not refer to that period is clear from his own explicit statements elsewhere. At that time he held himself to be "blameless" as concerned the law {50.3.6}. He had "lived in all good conscience" {44.23.1}. (2) With his conversion came new light upon the law itself. He now perceived it to be "spiritual" ({45.7.14}). He now saw that, so far from having kept it, he was condemned by it. He had supposed himself to be "alive," but now the commandment really "came" ({45.7.9}) and he "died." Just when the apostle passed through the experience of {45.7.7-25} we are not told. Perhaps during the days of physical blindness at Damascus {44.9.9}, perhaps in Arabia {48.1.17}. It is the experience of a renewed man, under the law, and still ignorant of the delivering power of the Holy Spirit {45.8.2}. (3) With the great revelations afterward embodied in Galatians and Romans, the apostle’s experience entered it third phase. He now knew himself to be "dead to the law by the body of Christ," and, in the power of the indwelling Spirit, "free from the law of sin and death" {45.8.2} while "the righteousness of the law" was wrought in him (not by him) while he walked after the Spirit {45.8.4}, Romans 7. is the record of past conflicts and defeats experience as a renewed man under law. sin Sin. (See Scofield on {45.5.21}).

carnal Cf. {46.3.1}; {46.3.4}. "Carnal" = "fleshly" is Paul’s word for the Adamic nature, and for the believer who "walks," i.e. lives, under the power of it. I do I allow not The apostle personifies the strife of the two natures in the believer, the old or Adamic nature, and the divine nature received through the new birth {60.1.23}; {61.1.4}; {48.2.20}; {51.1.27}. The "I" which is Saul of Tarsus, and the "I" which is Paul the apostle are at strife, and "Paul" is in defeat. cast That Israel has not been forever set aside is the theme of this chapter. (1) The salvation of Paul proves that there is still a remnant ({45.11.1}) (2) The doctrine of the remnant proves it ({45.11.2-6}). (3) The present national unbelief was foreseen ({45.11.7-10}). (4) Israel’s unbelief is the Gentile opportunity ({45.11.11-25}). (5) Israel is judicially broken off from the good olive tree, Christ ({45.11.17-22}). (6) They are to be grafted in again ({45.11.23}; {45.11.24}). (7) The promised Deliverer will come out of Zion and the nation will be saved ({45.11.25-29}). (See Scofield on {1.15.18}) but Israel as a nation always has it own place, and is yet to have its greatest exaltation as the earthly people of God. Remnant Remnant, Summary: In the history of Israel, a "remnant" may be discerned, a spiritual Israel within the national Israel. In Elijah’s time 7,000 had not bowed the knee to Baal {11.19.18}. In Isaiah’s time it was the "very small remnant" for whose sake God still forbore to destroy the nation {23.1.9}. During the captivities the remnant appears in Jews like Ezekiel, Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, Esther, and Mordecai. At the end of the 70 years of Babylonian captivity it was the remnant which returned under Ezra and Nehemiah. At the advent of our Lord, John the Baptist, Simeon, Anna, and "them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem" {42.2.38} were the remnant. During the church-age the remnant is composed of believing Jews {45.11.4}; {45.11.5}. But the chief interest in the remnant is prophetic. During the great tribulation a remnant out of all Israel will turn to Jesus as Messiah, and will become His witnesses after the removal of the church {66.7.3-8}. Some of these will undergo martyrdom {66.6.9-11} some will be spared to enter the millennial kingdom {38.12.6} to {38.13.9}. Many of the Psalms express, prophetically, the joys and sorrows of the tribulation remnant. remnant Remnant. See, {23.1.9}. grace Grace (in salvation). vs. {47.8.9}; {45.3.24} See note, (See Scofield on {43.1.17}).

records.o: Book Introduction - 1 Corinthians WRITER: The Apostle Paul. His relation to the church at Corinth is set forth in {44.18.1-18} and in the Epistles to the Corinthians. DATE: First Corinthians was written in A.D. 59, at the close of Paul’s three year’s residence in Ephesus. {44.20.31}; {46.16.5-8}. THEME: The subjects treated are various, but may all be classified under the general theme, Christian conduct. Even the tremendous revelation of the truth concerning resurrection is made to bear upon that theme {46.15.58}. The occasion of the Epistle was a letter on inquiry from Corinth concerning marriage, and the use of meats offered to idols; {46.7.1}; {46.8.1-13} but the apostle was much more exercised by reports of the deepening divisions and increasing contentions in the church, and of a case of incest which had not been judged; {46.1.10-12}; {46.5.1}. The factions were not due to heresies, but to the carnality of the restless Corinthians, and to their Greek admiration of "wisdom" and eloquence. The abomination of human leadership in the things of God is here rebuked. Minor disorders were due to vanity, yielding to a childish delight in tongue and the sign gifts, rather than to sober instruction ({46.14.1-28}). Paul defends his apostleship because it involved the authority of the doctrine revealed through him. A rigid analysis of First Corinthians is not possible, The Epistle is not a treatise, but came from the Spirit through the apostle’s grief, solicitude, and holy indignation. The following analysis may, however, be helpful. 1. Introduction: The believer’s standing in grace, {46.1.1-9} 2. The contrast of their present factious state, 1 Co {46.1.10} to {46.4.21}. 3. Immorality rebuked; discipline enjoined, {46.5.1-6}; {46.5.8}. 4. The sanctity of the body, and Christian marriage, {46.6.9} to {46.7.40}. 5. Meats, and the limitations of Christian liberty, 1 Co {46.8.1} to {46.11.1}. 6. Christian order and the Lord’s Supper, {46.11.2-34} 7. Spiritual gifts in relation to the body, the church, and Christian ministry, {46.12.1} to {46.14.40}. 8. The resurrection of the dead, {46.15.1-58} 9. Special directions and greetings, {46.16.1-24}.

v: them {46.1.2-9}, in contrast with 1 Corinthians 10-13, illustrate a distinction constantly made in the Epistles between the believer’s position in Christ Jesus, in the family of God, and his walk, or actual state. Christian position in grace is the result of the work of Christ, and is fully entered the moment that Christ is received by faith; {43.1.12}; {43.1.13}; {45.8.1}; {45.8.15-17}; {46.1.2}; {46.1.30}; {46.12.12}; {46.12.13}; {48.3.26}; {49.1.3-14}; {49.2.4-9}; {60.2.9}; {66.1.6}; {66.5.9}; {66.5.10}. The weakest, most ignorant, and fallible believer has precisely the same relationships in grace as the most illustrious saint. All the after work of God in his behalf, the application of the word to walk and conscience; {43.17.17}; {49.5.26} the divine chastenings; {46.11.32}; {58.12.10}, the ministry of the Spirit {49.4.11}; {49.4.12} the difficulties and trials of the path {60.4.12}; {60.4.13} and the final transformation at the appearing of Christ {62.3.2} have for their object to make the believer’s character conform to his exalted position in Christ. He grows in grace, not into grace.

coming Three words are used in connection with the return of the Lord: (1) Parousia, "personal presence," also used by Paul of the "coming" of Stephanas {46.16.17} of Titus {47.7.6}; {47.7.7} and of his own "coming" to Philippi {50.1.26}. The word means simply personal presence, and is used of the return of the Lord as that event relates to the blessing of the saints; {46.15.23}; {52.4.14}; {52.4.17} and to the destruction of the man of sin {53.2.8}. (2) Apokalupsis, "unveiling," "revelation." The use of this word emphasizes the visibility of the Lord’s return. It is used of the Lord {53.1.7}; {60.1.7}; {60.1.13}; {60.4.13} of the sons of God in connection with the Lord’s return {45.8.19} and of the man of sin {53.2.3}; {53.2.6}; {53.2.8} and always implies visibility. (3) Epiphaneia, "appearing," trans. "brightness" {53.2.8} A.V.; "manifestation," R.V.), and means simply an appearing. It is used of both advents.; {55.1.10}; {53.2.8}; {54.6.14}; {55.4.1}; {55.4.8}; {56.2.13}. coming (Greek - revelation, unveiling).

A.V. has "day of Christ," {53.2.2} incorrectly, for "day of the Lord"; {23.2.12}; {66.19.11-21} The "day of Christ" relates wholly to the reward and blessing of saints at his coming, as "day of the Lord" is connected with judgment.

words (1) The writers of Scripture invariably affirm, where the subject is mentioned by them at all, that the words of their writings are divinely taught. This, of necessity, refers to the original documents, not to translations and versions; but the labours of competent scholars have brought our English versions to a degree of perfection so remarkable that we may confidently rest upon them as authoritative. (2) {46.2.9-14} gives the process by which a truth passes from the mind of God to the minds of His people. (a) The unseen things of God are undiscoverable by the natural man ({46.2.9}). (b) These unseen things God has revealed to chosen men ({46.2.10-12}). (c) The revealed things are communicated in Spirit-taught words ({46.2.13}). This implies neither mechanical dictation nor the effacement of the writer’s personality, but only that the Spirit infallibly guides in the choice of words from the writer’s own vocabulary ({46.2.13}). (d) These Spirit-taught words, in which the revelation has been expressed, are discerned, as to their true spiritual content, only by the spiritual among believers; {46.2.15}; {46.2.16}; (See Scofield on {66.22.19}).

natural man Paul divides men into three classes: psuchikos, "of the senses" {59.3.15}; {65.1.19} or "natural," i.e. the Adamic man, unrenewed through the new birth {43.3.3}; {43.3.5} pneumatikos, "spiritual," i.e. the renewed man as Spirit-filled and walking in the Spirit in full communion with God {49.5.18-20} and sarkikos, "carnal," "fleshly," i.e. the renewed man who, walking "after the flesh," remains a babe in Christ {46.3.1-4}. The natural man may be learned, gentle, eloquent, fascinating, but the spiritual content of Scripture is absolutely hidden from him; and the fleshly, or carnal, Christian is able to comprehend only its simplest truths, "milk" {46.3.2}.
one Paul refutes the notion that he and Cephas and Apollos are at variance, mere theologians and rival founders of sects: they are "one." {46.3.22}; {46.16.12}. reward {46.9.17}; {27.12.3}; {46.3.14}

reward God, in the N.T. Scriptures, offers to the lost, salvation, and, for the faithful service of the saved, rewards. The passages are easily distinguished by remembering that salvation is invariably spoken of as a free gift (e.g.) {43.4.10}; {45.6.23}; {49.2.8}; {49.2.9} while rewards are earned by works; {40.10.42}; {42.19.17}; {46.9.24}; {46.9.25}; {55.4.7}; {55.4.8}; {66.2.10}; {66.22.12}. A further distinction is that salvation is a present possession {42.7.50}; {43.3.36}; {43.5.24}; {43.6.47}, while rewards are a future attainment, to be given at the coming of the Lord; {40.16.27}; {55.4.8}; {66.22.12}. reward {46.9.17}; {27.12.3}; {46.3.14}

castaway (Greek - Ἀδμίν, "disapproved)." Dokimos, without the private a, is translated "approved" in {45.14.18}; {45.16.10}; {46.11.19}; {47.10.18}; {55.2.15}; {59.1.12}, by the word "tried." The prefix simply changes the word to a negative, i.e. not approved, or, disapproved. The apostle is writing of service, not of salvation. He is not expressing fear that he may fail of salvation but of his crown. See "Rewards"; {27.12.3}; {46.3.14}.

fell in one day Cf. {4.25.9}. A discrepancy has been imagined. {46.10.8}. gives the number of deaths in "one day"; {4.25.9}, the total number of deaths "in the plague." Some discrepant statements concerning numbers are, however, found in the existing manuscripts of the Hebrew Scriptures. These are most naturally ascribed to the fact that the Hebrews used letters in the place of numerals. The letters for Koph to Tau express hundreds up to four hundred. Five certain Hebrew letters, written in a different form, carry hundreds up to nine hundred, while thousands are expressed by two dots over the proper unit letter: e.g. the letter Teth, used alone, stands for 9; with two dots it stands for nine thousand. Error in transcription of Hebrew numbers thus becomes easy, preservation of numerical accuracy difficult.

If neglected, the Lord judges, and the result is chastisement, but never condemnation {46.11.32}; {10.7.14}; {10.7.15}; {10.12.13}; {10.12.14}; {46.5.5}; {54.1.20}; {58.12.7}. spiritual gifts The word pneumatika, lit. "spirituals," i.e. matters of or from the Holy Spirit, gives the key to Chapters 12, 13, 14. Chapter 12. concerns the Spirit in relation to the body of Christ. This relation is twofold: (1) The baptism with the Spirit forms the body by uniting believers to Christ the risen and glorified Head, and to each other ({46.12.12}; {46.12.13}). The symbol of the body thus formed is the natural, human body ({46.12.12}), and all the analogies are freely used ({46.12.14-26}). (2) To each believer is given a spiritual enablement and capacity for specific service. No believer is destitute of such gift ({46.12.7}; {46.12.11}; {46.12.27}), but in their distribution the Spirit acts in free sovereignty ({46.12.11}). There is no room for self-choosing, and Christian service is simply the ministry of such gift as the individual may have received (cf) {45.12.4-8}. The gifts are diverse ({46.12.6}; {46.12.8-10}; {46.12.28-30}), but all are equally honourable because bestowed by the same Spirit, administered under the same Lord, and energized by the same God.
gifts Cf. {49.4.8}; {49.4.11}; {49.4.12}. The Spirit gives gifts for service to men, Christ gives the gifted men to the churches.
prophecy The N.T. prophet is not ordinarily a foreteller, but rather a forth-teller, one whose gift enabled him to speak "to edification, and exhortation, and comfort" {46.14.3}.

more excellent Chapter 13. continues the pneumatika begun in Chapter 12. Gifts are good, but only if ministered in love. {46.13.1}; {46.13.2}. Benevolence is good, but not apart from love. {46.13.3} Love is described. {46.13.4-7} Love is better than our present incomplete knowledge, {46.13.8-12} and greater than even faith and hope {46.13.13}.

rather The subject is still the pneumatika. Chapter 12, described the gifts and the Body; Chapter 13. the love which alone gives ministry of gift any value; Chapter 14. regulates the ministry of gift in the primitive, apostolic assembly of saints. (1) The important gift is that of prophecy ({46.1.1}). The N.T. prophet was not merely a preacher, but an inspired preacher, through whom, until the N.T. was written, new revelations suited to the new dispensation were given {46.14.29}; {46.14.30}. (2) Tongues and the sign gifts are to cease, and meantime must be used with restraint, and only if an interpreter be present {46.14.1-19}; {46.14.27}; {46.14.28}. (3) In the primitive church there was liberty for the ministry of all the gifts which might be present, but for prophecy more especially {46.14.23-26}; {46.14.31}; {46.14.39}. (4) In such meetings, when "the whole church" came together "in one place," women were required to keep silence {46.14.34}; {46.14.35}; {46.11.3-16}; {54.2.11-14}. (5) These injunctions are declared to be "the commandments of the Lord" {46.14.36}; {46.14.37}.
be not children (Greek - Ἀδμίν, youths). be ye children babies.

born out of due time (Greek - ἀγαπητός, "before the due time)." Paul thinks of himself here as an Israelite whose time to be born again had not come, nationally (cf) {40.23.39} so that his conversion by the appearing of the Lord in glory {44.9.3-6} was an illustration, or instance before the time, of the future national conversion of Israel. See; {26.20.34-38}; {28.2.14-17}; {38.12.10} to {38.13.6}; {45.11.25-27}.

Adam Adam was a contrasting type of Christ, {46.15.45-47}; {45.5.14-19}. (1) "The first man Adam was made a living soul" {1.2.7}, i.e. he derived life from another, that is, God. "The last Adam was a life-giving spirit." So far from deriving life, He was Himself the fountain of life, and He gave that life to others; {43.1.4}; {43.5.21}; {43.10.10}; {43.12.24}; {62.5.12}. (2) In origin the first man was of the earth, earthy; the Second Man is the Lord from heaven. (3) Each is the head of a creation, and these also are in contrast: in Adam all die; in Christ all will be made alive; the Adamic creation is "flesh"; the new creation, "spirit." {43.3.6}.

kingdom Kingdom (N.T.), Summary: See "Kingdom (O.T.)" {1.1.26-28}. (See Scofield on {38.12.8}). Kingdom truth is developed in the N.T. in the following order: (1) The promise of the kingdom to David and his seed, and described in the prophets {10.7.8-17},; {38.12.8} enters the N.T. absolutely unchanged. {42.1.31-33}. The King was born in Bethlehem; {40.2.1}; {33.5.2} of a virgin.; {40.1.18-25}; {23.7.14}. (2) The kingdom announced as "at hand" (See Scofield on {40.4.17}), by John the Baptist, by the King, and by the Twelve, was rejected by the Jews, first morally, (See Scofield on {40.11.20}), and afterward officially {40.21.42}; {40.21.43} and the King, crowned with thorns, was crucified. (3) In anticipation of His official rejection and crucifixion, the King revealed the "mysteries" of the kingdom of heaven, (See Scofield on {40.13.11}) to be fulfilled in the interval between His rejection and His return in glory {40.13.1-50}. (4) Afterward He announced His purpose to "build" His church {40.16.18} another "mystery" revealed through Paul which is being fulfilled contemporaneously with the mysteries of the kingdom. The "mysteries of the kingdom of heaven" and the "mystery" of the church {49.3.9-11} occupy, historically, the same period, i.e, this present age. (5) The mysteries of the kingdom will be brought to an end by "the harvest" {40.13.39-43}; {40.13.49}; {40.13.50} at the return of the King in glory, the church having previously been caught up to meet Him in the air {52.4.14-17}. (6) Upon His return the King will restore the Davidic monarchy in His own person, re- gather dispersed Israel, establish His power over all the earth, and reign one thousand years {40.24.27-30}; {42.1.31-33}; {44.15.14-17}; {66.20.1-10}. (7) The kingdom of heaven (See Scofield on {40.3.2}) thus established under David’s divine Son, has for its object the restoration of the divine authority in the earth, which may be regarded as a revolted province of the great kingdom of God (See Scofield on {40.6.33}). When this is done ({46.14.24}; {46.14.25}) the Son will deliver up the kingdom (of heaven), {40.3.2} to "God, even the Father," that "God" (i.e. the triune God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) "may be all in all" ({46.14.28}). The eternal throne is that "of God, and of the Lamb" {66.22.1}. The kingdom-age constitutes the seventh Dispensation, (See Scofield on {49.1.10}). Then cometh Then, finally, when he delivers up the kingdom to God, even the Father; when he has done away with every rule, and every authority and power (for he must reign till he has put all enemies under his feet), the last enemy, death, is destroyed.
dead i.e. who, through the introductory rite of baptism, are taking the places in the ranks left vacant by Christians who have died.

raised Resurrection, Summary: (1) The resurrection of the dead was believed by the patriarchs {1.22.5}; {58.11.19}; {18.19.25-27} and revealed through the prophets; {23.26.19}; {27.12.2}; {27.12.13}; {28.13.14} and miracles of the dead restored to life are recorded in the O.T.; {12.4.32-35}; {12.13.21}. (2) Jesus Christ restored life to the dead {40.9.25}; {42.7.12-15}; {43.11.43}; {43.11.44} and predicted His own resurrection; {43.10.18}; {42.24.1-8}. (3) A resurrection of bodies followed the resurrection of Christ {40.27.52}; {40.27.53} and the apostles raised the dead; {44.9.36-41}; {44.20.9}; {44.20.10}. (4) Two resurrections are yet future, which are inclusive of "all that are in the graves" {43.5.28}. These are distinguished as "of life"; {46.15.22}; {46.15.23}; {52.4.14-17}; {66.20.4} and "of judgment"; {43.5.28}; {43.5.29}; {66.20.11-13}. They are separated by a period of one thousand years {66.20.5}. The "first resurrection," that "unto life," will occur at the second coming of Christ {46.15.23} the saints of the O.T. and church ages meeting Him in the air {52.4.16}; {52.4.17} while the martyrs of the tribulation, who also have part in the resurrection {66.20.4} are raised at the end of the great tribulation. (5) The mortal body will be related to the resurrection body as grain sown is related to the harvest {46.15.37}; {46.15.38} that body will be incorruptible, glorious, powerful, and spiritual {46.15.42-44}; {46.15.49}. (6) The bodies of living believers will, at the same time, be instantaneously changed {46.15.50-53}; {50.3.20}; {50.3.21}. This "change" of the living, and resurrection of the dead in Christ, is called the "redemption of the body"; {45.8.23}; {49.1.13}; {49.1.14}. (7) After the thousand years the "resurrection unto judgment" {43.5.29} occurs. The resurrection-body of the wicked dead is not described. They are judged according to their works, and cast into the lake of fire. {66.20.7-15}.
Anathema Maranatha Accursed; our Lord cometh. Christ is God’s final test.

records.o: Book Introduction - 2 Corinthians WRITER: The Apostle Paul DATE: A.D. 60; probably from Philippi, after the events of {44.19.23-41}; {44.20.1-13}. THEME: The Epistle discloses the touching state of the great apostle at this time. It was one of physical weakness, weariness, and pain. But his spiritual burdens were greater. These were two kinds--solicitude for the maintenance of the churches in grace as against the law-teachers, and anguish of heart over the distrust felt toward him by Jews and Jewish Christians. The chilling doctrines of the legalizers were accompanied by detraction, and by denial of his apostleship. It is evident that the really dangerous sect in Corinth was that which said, "and I of Christ" ({46.1.12}). They rejected the new revelation through Paul of the doctrines of grace; grounding themselves, probably, on the kingdom teachings of our Lord as "a minister of circumcision" ({45.15.8}); seemingly oblivious that a new dispensation had been introduced by Christ’s death. This made necessary a defence of the origin and extent of Paul’s apostolic authority. The Epistle is in three parts: 1. Paul’s principles of action, {47.1.1} to {47.7.16}. 2. The collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem, 2 Co {47.8.1} to {47.9.15}. 3. Paul’s defence of his apostolic authority, {47.10.1} to {47.13.14}.

come out from among them Separation, Summary: (1) Separation in Scripture is twofold: "from" whatever is contrary to the mind of God; and "unto" God Himself. The underlying principle is that in a moral universe it is impossible for God to fully bless and use His children who are in compromise or complicity with evil. The unequal yoke is anything which unites a child of God and an unbeliever in a common purpose {5.22.10}. (2) Separation from evil implies (a) separation in desire, motive, and act, from the world, in the ethically bad sense of this present world-system. (See Scofield on {66.13.8}) and (b) separation from believers, especially false teachers, who are "vessels unto dishonour" {55.2.20}; {55.2.21}; {63.1.9-11}. (3) Separation is not from contact with evil in the world or the church, but from complicity with and conformity to {43.17.15}; {47.6.14-18}; {48.6.1}. (4) The reward of separation is the full manifestation of the divine fatherhood {47.6.17}; {47.6.18} unhindered communion and worship {58.13.13-15} and fruitful service {55.2.21} as world-conformity involves the loss of these, though not of salvation. Here, as in all else, Christ is the model. He was "holy, harmless, undefiled, and separate from sinners" {58.7.26} and yet in such contact with them for their salvation that the Pharisees, who illustrate the mechanical and ascetic conception of separation (See Scofield on {40.3.7}), judged Him as having lost His Nazarite character. {42.7.39} Cf; {46.9.19-23}; {46.10.27}.
salvation (See Scofield on {45.1.16}). world kosmos = world-system. {48.6.14}; {43.7.7}. (See Scofield on {66.13.8}).

Moreover In 2 Corinthians 8, 9, the apostle sums up the Christian doctrine of giving. It may be thus summarized: (1) It is a "grace," i.e. a disposition created by the Spirit {47.8.7} (2) In contrast with the law, which imposed giving as a divine requirement, Christian giving is voluntary, and a test of sincerity and love {47.8.8-12}; {47.9.1}; {47.9.2}; {47.9.5}; {47.9.7} (3) The privilege is universal, belonging, according to ability, to rich and poor {47.8.1-3}; {47.8.12-15}; {46.16.1}; {46.16.2}. (4) Giving is to be proportioned to income {47.8.12-14}; {46.16.2}. The O.T. proportion was the tithe, a proportion which antedates the law {1.14.20}. (5) The rewards of Christian giving are (a) joy {47.8.2} (b) increased ability to give in proportion to that which has been already given {47.9.7-11} (c) increased thankfulness to God {47.9.12} (d) God and the Gospel glorified {47.9.13}; {47.9.14}
third heaven First heaven, of clouds; second, of stars; third, God’s abode.

thorn It has been conjectured that Paul’s "thorn in the flesh" was chronic ophthalmia, inducing bodily weakness, and a repulsive appearance {48.4.15}; {46.2.3}; {46.2.4}; {47.10.10}. This cannot be positively known, and the reserve of Scripture is as sure a mark of inspiration as its revelations. Paul’s particular "thorn" is not described that his consolations may avail for all to who any thorn is given.

records.o: Book Introduction - Galatians WRITER: The Apostle Paul (1:1) DATE: Galatians was probably written A.D. 60, during Paul’s third visit to Corinth, The occasion of the Epistle is evident. It had come to Paul’s knowledge that the fickle Galatians, who were not Greeks, but Gauls, "a stream from the torrent of barbarians which poured into Greece in the third century before Christ," had become the prey of the legalizers, the Judaizing missionaries from Palestine. THEME: The theme of Galatians is the vindication of the Gospel of the grace of God from any admixture of law-conditions, which qualify or destroy its character of pure grace. The Galatian error had two forms, both of which are refuted. The first is the teaching that obedience to the law is mingled with faith as the ground of the sinner’s justification; the second, that the justified believer is made perfect by keeping the law. Paul meets the first form of the error by a demonstration that justification is through the Abrahamic Covenant ({1.15.18}), and that the law, which was four hundred and thirty years after the confirmation of that covenant, and the true purpose of which was condemnation, not justification, cannot disannul a salvation which rests upon the earlier covenant. Paul meets the second and more subtle form by vindicating the office of the Holy Spirit as Sanctifier. The book is in seven parts: 1. Salutation {48.1.1-5} 2. Theme, {48.1.6-9}. 3. Paul’s Gospel is a revelation, {48.1.10} to {48.2.14}. 4, Justification is by faith without law, {48.2.15} to {48.3.24}. 5. The rule of the believer’s life is gracious, not legal, {48.3.25} to {48.5.15}. 6. Sanctification is through the Spirit, not the law, {48.5.16-24}. 7. Exhortations and conclusion, {48.5.25} to {48.6.18}.

v: grace The test of the Gospel is grace. If the message excludes grace, or mingles law with grace as the means of either of justification or sanctification {48.2.21}; {48.3.1-3} or denies the fact or guilt of sin which alone gives grace its occasion and opportunity, it is "another" gospel, and the preacher of it is under the anathema of God {48.1.8}; {48.1.9}.

For now do The demonstration is as follows: (1) The Galatians know Paul, that he is no seeker after popularity {48.1.10}. (2) He puts his known character back of the assertion that his Gospel of grace was a revelation from God ({48.1.11}; {48.1.12}). (3) As for the Judaizers, Paul had been a foremost Jew, and had forsaken Judaism for something better ({48.1.13}; {48.1.14}). (4) He had preached grace years before he saw any of the other apostles ({48.1.15-24}). (5) When he did meet the other apostles they had nothing to add to his revelations {48.2.1-6}. (6) The other apostles fully recognized Paul’s apostleship. {48.2.7-10}. (7) If the legalizers pleaded Peter’s authority, the answer was that he himself had claimed none when rebuked ({48.2.11-14}).
Jews’ religion The new dispensation of grace having come in, the Mosaic system, if still persisted in, becomes a mere "Jews’ religion."

religion In {48.1.13-14} the Greek word for "the Jews’ religion" is Ioudaismos (Judaism). In {44.26.5}; {59.1.26}; {59.1.27} threskeia--religious service--is translated "religion," and in {51.2.18}, "worshipping." Excepting {59.1.27}, "religion" has always a bad sense, and nowhere is it synonymous with salvation or spirituality.

We who are Paul here quotes from his words to Peter when he withstood him at Antioch to show the Galatians that, whatever the legalists may have pretended, Peter and he were in perfect accord doctrinally. Paul appealed to the common belief of Peter and himself as a rebuke of Peter’s inconsistent practice. sinners Sin. (See Scofield on {45.3.23}).

we seek That is, "we" Jews. {45.3.19-23}. The passage might be thus paraphrased: If we Jews, in seeking to be justified by faith in Christ, take our places as mere sinners, like the Gentiles, is it therefore Christ who makes us sinners? By no means. It is by putting ourselves again under law after seeking justification through Christ, that we act as if we were still unjustified sinners, seeking to become righteous through law-works. {48.5.1-4}. sinners Sin. grace Grace (in salvation). vs. {48.5.4}; {45.3.24}. (See Scofield on {43.1.17}). righteousness (See Scofield on {45.10.10}).

Wherefore then The answer is sixfold: (1) The law was added because of transgressions, i.e. to give to sin the character of transgression. (a) Men had been sinning before Moses, but in the absence of law their sins were not put to their account. {45.5.13}. The law gave to sin the character of "transgression," i.e. of personal guilt. (b) Also, since men not only continued to transgress after the law was given, but were provoked to transgress by the very law that forbade it {45.7.8}, the law conclusively proved the inveterate sinfulness of man’s nature {45.7.11-13}. (2) The law, therefore, "concluded all under sin" {45.3.19}; {45.3.20}; {45.3.23}. (3) The law was an ad interim dealing, "till the seed should come". {48.3.19}. (4) The law shut sinful man up to faith as the only avenue of escape. {48.3.23}. (5) The law was to the Jews what the pedagogue was in a Greek household, a ruler of children in their minority, and it had this character "unto" i.e. until Christ {48.3.24}. (6) Christ having come, the believer is no longer under the pedagogue. {48.3.25} because of for the sake, i.e. in order that sin might be made manifest as transgression. See, {45.4.15}; {45.5.20}; {45.7.7}; {45.7.13}.

law I. The law of Moses, Summary: (1) The Mosaic Covenant was given to Israel in three parts: the commandments, expressing the righteous will of God {2.20.1-26}, the "judgments," governing the social life of Israel {2.21.1} to {2.24.11}, and the "ordinances," governing the religious life of Israel; {2.24.12}; {2.31.18}. (2) The commandments and ordinances were one complete and inseparable whole. When an Israelite sinned, he was held "blameless" if he brought the required offering {42.1.6}; {50.3.6}. (3) Law, as a method of the divine dealing with man, characterized the dispensation extending from the giving of the law to the death of Jesus Christ {48.3.13}; {48.3.14}; {48.3.23}; {48.3.24}. (4) The attempt of legalistic teachers (e.g.) {44.15.1-31}; {48.2.1-5}, to mingle law with grace as the divine method for this present dispensation of grace, brought out the true relation of the law to the Christian, viz. II. The Christian doctrine of the law: (1) Law is in contrast with grace. Under the latter God bestows the righteousness which, under law, He demanded {2.19.5}; {43.1.17}. (See Scofield on {45.3.21}).; {45.10.3-10}; {46.1.30}. (2) The law is, in itself, holy, just, good, and spiritual {45.7.12-14}. (3) Before the law the whole world is guilty, and the law is therefore of necessity a ministry of condemnation, death, and the divine curse {45.3.19}; {47.3.7-9}; {48.3.10}. For Another Point of View: See Topic 301242 Other Factors to Consider: See Topic 301187 (4) Christ bore the curse of the law, and redeemed the believer both from the curse and from the dominion of the law {48.3.13}; {48.4.5-7}. (5) Law neither justifies a sinner nor sanctifies a believer {48.2.16}; {48.3.2}; {48.3.3}; {48.3.11}; {48.3.12}. (6) The believer is both dead to the law and redeemed from it, so that he is "not under the law, but under grace" {45.6.14}; {45.7.4}; {48.2.19}; {48.4.4-7}; {54.1.8}; {54.1.9}. (7) Under the new covenant of grace the principle of obedience to the divine will is inwrought {58.10.6}. So far is the life of the believer from the anarchy of self-will that he is "inlawed to Christ" {46.9.21} and the new "law of Christ"; {48.6.2}; {63.1.5} is his delight; while, through the indwelling Spirit, the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in him; {45.8.2-4}; {48.5.16-18}. The commandments are used in the distinctively Christian Scriptures as an instruction in righteousness; {55.3.16}; {45.13.8-10}; {49.6.1-3}; {46.9.8}; {46.9.9}. to bring us Omit "to bring us." unto up to, or until.

schoolmaster (Greek - παιδαγωγός, "child-conductor)." "among the Greeks and Romans, persons, for the most part slaves, who had it in charge to educate and give constant attendance upon boys till they came of age."--H.A.W. Meyer. The argument does not turn upon the extent or nature of the pedagogue’s authority, but upon the fact that it wholly ceased when the "child" {48.4.1} became a; {22.1.1}; {48.4.1-6} when the minor became an adult. The adult "son" does voluntarily that which formerly he did in fear of the pedagogue. But even if he does not, it is no longer a question between the son and the pedagogue (the law), but between the son and his Father--God. (Cf); {58.12.5-10}; {62.2.1}; {62.2.2}.

little children The allegory {48.4.22-31} is addressed to justified but immature believers (cf) {46.3.1}; {46.3.2} who, under the influence of legalistic teachers, "desire to be under the law," and has, therefore, no application to a sinner seeking justification. It raises and answers, for the fifth time in this Epistle, the question, Is the believer under the law?; {48.2.19-21}; {48.3.1-29}; {48.3.26}; {48.4.4-6}; {48.4.9-31}.

no effect grace no effect i.e. of no experimental effect: the sense of liberty is lost. {48.2.21}; {51.1.23}. grace Grace (in salvation). {49.1.6}; {49.1.7}; {45.3.24}. (See Scofield on {48.1.6}; {43.1.17}).
under the law i.e. not under bondage of effort to please God by law-works. {47.3.17}.

But the fruit Christian character is not mere moral or legal correctness, but the possession and manifestation of nine graces: love, joy, peace--character as an inward state; longsuffering, gentleness, goodness--character in expression toward man; faith, meekness, temperance-- character in expression toward God. Taken together they present a moral portrait of Christ, and may be taken as the apostle’s explanation of {48.2.20} "Not I, but Christ," and as a definition of "fruit" in {43.15.1-8} This character is possible because of the believer’s vital union to Christ; {43.15.5}; {46.12.12}; {46.12.13} and is wholly the fruit of the Spirit in those believers who are yielded to Him. {48.5.22}; {48.5.23}.

large (Greek - αὑτου̑).. .mine own hand." The apostle was, it appears from many considerations, afflicted with ophthalmia, a common disease in the East, to the point almost of total blindness (e.g.) {48.4.13-15}. Ordinarily, therefore, he dictated his letters. But now, having no amanuensis at hand, but urged by the spiritual danger of his dear Galatians, he writes, we cannot know with what pain and difficulty, with his own hand, in the "large letters" his darkened vision compelled him to use.
constrain you to be circumcised "Circumcision" stands here for externality in religion -- form rather than spirit. {51.2.16-23}.

records.o: Book Introduction - Ephesians WRITER: The Apostle Paul (1:1) DATE: Ephesians was written from Rome in A.D. 64. It is the first in order of the Prison Epistles. {44.20.1} to {44.27.44}. (See Scofield on {44.28.30}) and was sent by Tychicus, concurrently with Colossians and Philemon. It is probable that the two greater letters had their occasion in the return of Onesimus to Philemon. Ephesians is the most impersonal of Paul’s letters. Indeed the words, "to the Ephesians," are not in the best manuscripts. {51.4.16} mentions an epistle to the Laodiceans. It has been conjectured that the letter known to us as Ephesians is really the Laodicean letter. Probably it was sent to Ephesus and Laodicea without being addressed to any church. The letter would then be "to the saints and the faithful in Christ Jesus" anywhere. THEME: The doctrine of the Epistle confirms this view. It contains the highest church truth, but has nothing about church order. The church here is the true church, "His body," not the local church, as in Philippians, Corinthians, etc. Essentially, three lines of truth make up this Epistle: the believer’s exalted position through grace; the truth concerning the body of Christ; and a walk in accordance with that position. There is a close spiritual affinity between Ephesians and Joshua, the "heavenlies" answering in Christian position to Canaan in Israel’s experience. In both there is conflict, often failure, but also victory, rest, and possession {6.21.43-45}; {49.1.3}; {49.3.14-19}; {49.6.16}; {49.6.23}. As befits a complete revelation, the number seven is conspicuous in the structure of Ephesians. The divisions are, broadly, four: 1. The apostolic greeting {49.1.1-2} 2. Positional; the believer’s standing "Christ" and "in the heavenlies" through pure grace, {49.1.3} to {49.3.21}. 3. Walk and service, {49.4.1} to {49.5.17} 4. The walk and warfare of the Spirit-filled believer, {49.5.18} to {49.6.24}.

v: in Christ The believer’s place as a member of the body of Christ, vitally united to Him by the baptism with the Holy Spirit {46.12.12}; {46.12.13}.

in heavenly places Literally, the heavenlies. The same Greek word is used in {43.3.12} where "things" is added. In both places the word signifies that which is heavenly in contradistinction to that which is earthy. In Ephesians "places" is especially misleading. "The heavenlies" may be defined as the sphere of the believer’s spiritual experience as identified with Christ in nature. {61.1.4}, life,; {51.3.4}; {62.5.12}, relationships; {43.20.17}; {58.2.11} service,; {43.17.18}; {40.28.20}, suffering; {50.1.29}; {50.3.10}; {51.1.24} inheritance {45.8.16}; {45.8.17} and future glory in the kingdom; {45.8.18-21}; {60.2.9}; {66.1.6}; {66.5.10}. The believer is a heavenly man, and a stranger and pilgrim on the earth.; {58.3.1}; {60.2.11}.

predestinated Predestination is that effective exercise of the will of God by which things before determined by Him are brought to pass. See Election, (See Scofield on {60.1.2}). Foreknowledge, (See Scofield on {60.1.20}). adoption Adoption (huiothesia, "placing as a son") is not so much a word of relationship as of position. The believer’s relation to God as a child results from the new birth {43.1.12}; {43.1.13} whereas adoption is the act of God whereby one already a child is, through redemption from the law, placed in the position of an adult son. {48.4.1-5}. The indwelling Spirit gives the realization of this in the believer’s present experience {48.4.6} but the full manifestation of the believer’s sonship awaits the resurrection, change, and translation of saints, which is called "the redemption of the body"; {45.8.23}; {52.4.14-17}; {49.1.14}; {62.3.2}.

dispensation of the fullness of times The Dispensation of the Fulness of Times. This, the seventh and last of the ordered ages which condition human life on the earth, is identical with the kingdom covenanted to David. {10.7.8-17}; {38.12.8} Summary; {42.1.31-33}; {46.15.24}, and gathers into itself under Christ all past "times": (1) The time of oppression and misrule ends by Christ taking His kingdom. {23.11.3}; {23.11.4}. (2) The time of testimony and divine forbearance ends in judgment. {40.25.31-46}; {44.17.30}; {44.17.31}; {66.20.7-15}. (3) The time of toil ends in rest and reward. {53.1.6}; {53.1.7}. (4) The time of suffering ends in glory. {45.8.17}; {45.8.18}. (5) The time of Israel’s blindness and chastisement ends in restoration and conversion. {45.11.25-27}; {26.39.25-29}. (6) The times of the Gentiles end in the smiting of the image and the setting up of the kingdom of the heavens. {27.2.34}; {27.2.35}; {66.19.15-21}. (7) The time of creation’s thraldom ends in deliverance at the manifestation of the sons of God. {1.3.17}; {23.11.6-8}; {45.8.19-21}.

sealed The Holy Spirit is Himself the seal. In the symbolism of Scripture a seal signifies: (1) A finished transaction {24.32.9}; {24.32.10}; {43.17.4}; {43.19.30}. (2) Ownership {24.32.11}; {24.32.12}; {55.2.19} (3) Security {17.8.8}; {27.6.17}; {49.4.30}

dead Death (spiritual), Summary: Spiritual death is the state of the natural or unregenerate man as still in his sins. {49.2.1} alienated from the life of God {49.4.18}; {49.4.19} and destitute of the Spirit. Prolonged beyond the death of the body, spiritual death is a state of eternal separation from God in conscious suffering. This is called "the second death."; {66.2.11}; {66.20.6}; {66.20.14}; {66.21.8}. saved (See Scofield on {45.1.16}).
grace Grace (in salvation). Ep 5,7,8 {51.1.6}; {45.3.24}; {43.1.17} (See Scofield on {43.1.17}). saved See note, (See Scofield on {45.1.16}).

new man Here the "new man" is not the individual believer but the church, considered as the body of Christ in the sense of {49.1.22}; {49.1.23}; {46.12.12}; {46.12.13}; {51.3.10}; {51.3.11}. (See Scofield on {58.12.23}).

That the Gentiles That the Gentiles were to be saved was no mystery {45.9.24-33}; {45.10.19-21}. The mystery "hid in God" was the divine purpose to make of Jew and Gentile a wholly new thing--"the church, which is his Christ’s body," formed by the baptism with the Holy Spirit {46.12.12}; {46.12.13} and in which the earthly distinction of Jew and Gentile disappears; {49.2.14}; {49.2.15}; {51.3.10}; {51.3.11}. The revelation of this mystery, which was foretold, but not explained by Christ {40.16.18} was committed to Paul. In his writings alone we find the doctrine, position, walk, and destiny of the church.

gave In {46.12.8-28} the Spirit is seen as enduing the members of the body of Christ with spiritual gifts, or enablements for a varied service; here certain Spirit-endued men, viz. apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers, are themselves the gifts whom the glorified Christ bestows upon His body the church. In Corinthians the gifts are spiritual enablements for specific service; in Ephesians the gifts are men who have such enablements. some The Lord, in bestowing the gifted men, determines, providentially (e.g.) {44.11.22-26} or directly through the Spirit (e.g.); {44.13.1}; {44.13.2}; {44.16.6}; {44.16.7} the places of their service. "Some" (churches or places) need one gift, as, (e.g.) evangelist; "some" (churches or places) need rather a pastor or teacher. Absolutely nothing in Christ’s service is left to mere human judgment or self-choosing. Even an apostle was not permitted to choose his place of service {44.16.7}; {44.16.8}.

new man The new man is the regenerate man as distinguished from the old man (See Scofield on {45.6.6}) and is a new man as having become a partaker of the divine nature and life {61.1.4}; {51.3.3}; {51.3.4} and in no sense the old man made over, or improved; {47.5.17}; {48.6.15}; {49.2.10}; {51.3.10}. The new man is Christ, "formed" in the believer; {48.2.20}; {48.4.19}; {51.1.27}; {62.4.12}. righteousness (See Scofield on {45.10.10}).

even as Christ Christ’s love-work for the church is threefold: past, present, future: (1) For love He gave Himself to redeem the church ({49.5.25}); (2) in love He is sanctifying the church ({49.5.26}); (3) for the reward of His sacrifice and labour of love He will present the church to Himself in flawless perfection, "one pearl of great price" ({49.5.27}) {40.13.46}.

bride {49.5.30}; {49.5.31} are quoted from {1.2.23}; {1.2.24} and exclude the interpretation that the reference is to the church merely as the body of Christ. Eve, taken from Adam’s body, was truly "bone of his bones, and flesh of his flesh," but she was also his wife, united to him in a relation which makes of "twain.. . one flesh" {40.19.5}; {40.19.6} and so a clear type of the church as bride of Christ. {47.11.2}; {47.11.3}. The bride type are Eve {1.2.23}; {1.2.24} Rebecca (See Scofield on {1.24.1}). Asenath (See Scofield on {1.41.45}). (See Scofield on {1.37.2}). Zipporah {2.2.21}. (See Scofield on {28.2.2}). mystery (See Scofield on {40.13.11}).

records.o: Book Introduction - Philippians WRITER: The Apostle Paul ({50.1.1}) DATE: The date of Philippians cannot be positively fixed. It is one of the prison letters. Whether Paul was twice imprisoned, and if so, whether Philippians was written during the first or second imprisonment, affects in no way the message of the Epistle. A.D. 64 is the commonly received date. The immediate occasion of the Epistle is disclosed in {50.4.10-18}. THEME: The theme of Philippians is Christian experience. Soundness of doctrine is assumed. There is nothing in church order to set right. Philippi is a normal New Testament assembly--"saints in Christ Jesus, with the bishops (elders) and deacons." The circumstances of the apostle are in striking contrast with his Christian experience. As to the former, he was Nero’s prisoner. As to the latter, there was the shout of victory, the paean of joy. Christian experience, he would teach us, is not something which is going on around the believer, but something which is going on within him. The key-verse is, "For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain" ({50.1.21}). Right Christian experience, then, is the outworking, whatever one’s circumstances may be, of the life, nature, and mind of Christ living in us ({50.1.6}; {50.1.11}; {50.2.5}; {50.2.13}). The divisions are indicated by the chapters: Christ, the believer’s life, rejoicing in suffering, {50.1.1-30}. Christ, the believer’s pattern, rejoicing in lowly service, {50.2.1-30} Christ, the believer’s object, rejoicing despite imperfections, {50.3.1-21}. Christ, the believer’s strength, rejoicing over anxiety, {50.4.1-23}.

v: which are at Churches (local), Summary: A local church is an assembly of professed believers on the Lord Jesus Christ, living for the most part in one locality, who assemble themselves together in His name for the breaking of bread, worship, praise, prayer, testimony, the ministry of the word, discipline, and the furtherance of the Gospel, {58.10.25}; {44.20.7}; {46.14.26}; {46.5.4}; {46.5.5}; {50.4.14-18}; {52.1.8}; {44.13.1-4}. Such a church exists where two or three are thus gathered {40.18.20}. Every such local church has Christ in the midst, is a temple of God, and indwelt by the Holy Spirit {46.3.16}; {46.3.17}. When perfected in organization a local church consists of "saints, with the bishops elders and deacons."

form of God "Form," etc. (Greek - μορφή, the form by which a person or thing strikes the vision, the external appearance)."--Thayer. CF {43.17.15}. "The glory which I had with Thee before the world was." Nothing in this passage teaches that the Eternal Word {43.1.1} emptied Himself of either His divine nature, or His attributes, but only of the outward and visible manifestation of the Godhead. "He emptied, stripped Himself of the insignia of Majesty."--Lightfoot. "When occasion demanded He exercised His divine attributes."-- Moorehead. CF (See Scofield on {43.1.1}; {43.20.28}). robbery a thing to be grasped after. See, {1.3.5-6}.

records.o: Book Introduction - Colossians WRITER: The Apostle Paul ({51.1.1}) DATE: Colossians was sent by the same messenger who bore Ephesians and Philemon, and was probably written at the same time. THEME: Epaphras, who laboured in the Word in the assembly at Colosse, was Paul’s fellow-prisoner at Rome. Doubtless from him Paul learned the state of that church. As to fundamentals that state was excellent (1:3-8), but in a subtle way two forms of error were at work: The first was legality in its Alexandrian form of asceticism, "touch not, taste not," with a trace of the Judaic observance of "days"; the object of which was the mortification of the body (cf {45.8.13}). The second form of error was false mysticism, "intruding into those things which he hath not seen"--the result of philosophic speculation. Because these are ever present perils, Colossians was written, not for that day only, but for the warning of the church in all days. The Epistle is in seven divisions: 1. Introduction {51.1.1-8} 2. The apostolic prayer {51.1.9-14} 3. The exaltation of Christ, Creator, Redeemer, Indweller {51.1.15-29} 4. The Godhead incarnate in Christ, in whom the believer is complete, {51.2.1-23}. 5. The believer’s union with Christ in resurrection life and glory, {51.3.1-4} 6. Christian living, the fruit of union with Christ, {51.3.5} to {51.4.6} 7. Christian fellowship, {51.4.7-18}

v: reconciled Reconciliation. The Greek word signifies "to change thoroughly from," and occurs, {45.5.10}; {45.11.15}; {46.7.11}; {47.5.18}; {47.5.19}; {47.5.20}. Reconciliation looks toward the effect of the death of christ upon man, as propitiation (See Scofield on {45.3.25}), is the Godward aspect, and is that effect of the death of Christ upon the believing sinner which, through divine power, works in him a "thorough change" toward God from enmity and aversion to love and trust. It is never said that God is reconciled. God is propitiated, the sinner reconciled (cf) {47.5.18-21}.

mystery of God The "mystery of God" is Christ, as incarnating the fulness of the Godhead, and all the divine wisdom and knowledge for the redemption and reconciliation of man. mystery (See Scofield on {40.13.11}). and of The best authorities omit "and of the Father, and of Christ."

intruding into those things The errorists against whom Paul warns the Colossians, and against whom, in principle, the warning has perpetual significance, were called "Gnostics," from gnosis, "knowledge." These Gnostics "came most keenly into conflict with the exalted rank and redeeming rank of Christ, to whom they did not leave His full divine dignity, but assigned to Him merely the highest rank in the order of spirits, while they exalted angels as concerned in bringing the Messianic salvation."--H.A.W. Meyer. Paul’s characteristic word in Colossians for the divine revelation is epignosis, i.e. "full knowledge." {51.1.9}; {51.1.10}; {51.3.10} as against the pretended "knowledge" of the errorists. The warnings apply to all extra-biblical forms, doctrines, and customs, and to all ascetic practices. angels (See Scofield on {58.1.4}).
not in any Or, "which do not really honour God, but only satisfy the flesh" (i.e. by creating a reputation for superior sanctity).
